lessons.title: Ionic Bonding: Electron Transfer and Crystal Lattices (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: explain how ionic bonds form through electron transfer between metals and nonmetals and describe the structure and properties of ionic compounds
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time you gave something to someone because they needed it more than you. How did it change both of you?
lessons.do_now: Draw the Lewis dot structures for sodium (Na) and chlorine (Cl). Sodium has 1 valence electron and chlorine has 7. How could both atoms end up with 8 valence electrons? Sketch your idea.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Ionic compound sample set: NaCl, CaCO3, MgSO4 (Epsom salt)
Beakers with distilled water for dissolving tests
Crystal lattice model (NaCl, physical or digital 3D model)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Ionic Bonding: Electron Transfer and Crystal Lattices. Demo: Dissolve table salt in water and test conductivity — the bulb lights up. Then test solid salt — no conductivity. Then test sugar water — no conductivity. Ask: Why does salt conduct only when dissolved? What is special about salt at the particle level that sugar does not have? Record student hypotheses.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Ionic Bonding: Electron Transfer and Crystal Lattices. Students draw step-by-step diagrams of ionic bond formation for NaCl: (1) Lewis dot structures of separate Na and Cl atoms, (2) arrow showing electron transfer from Na to Cl, (3) resulting Na+ and Cl- ions with brackets and charges, (4) electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Then repeat for MgCl2 (Mg gives 2 electrons, one to each Cl). Students discuss in pairs: Why does Mg form +2 while Na forms +1?

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Ionic Bonding: Electron Transfer and Crystal Lattices. Teacher formalizes ionic bonding: metals lose electrons (form cations), nonmetals gain electrons (form anions), oppositely charged ions attract in a 3D crystal lattice. Show the NaCl crystal lattice model — each Na+ is surrounded by 6 Cl- and vice versa. Connect structure to properties: high melting points (strong electrostatic forces throughout the lattice), brittleness (shifting layers causes like charges to align and repel), conductivity when dissolved or melted (ions are free to move).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Ionic Bonding: Electron Transfer and Crystal Lattices. Property prediction: Given three unknown ionic compounds with melting point data (compound X: 770 C, compound Y: 2570 C, compound Z: 1418 C), students predict which has the strongest ionic bonds. Then students explain why ionic compounds dissolve in water but not in oil, using the concept of polar water molecules surrounding ions.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Ionic Bonding: Electron Transfer and Crystal Lattices. Exit ticket: (1) Draw the ionic bond formation between calcium (Ca) and fluorine (F), showing electron transfer and resulting ions. (2) Explain why NaCl has a high melting point using the crystal lattice model. (3) Why does solid NaCl not conduct electricity, but dissolved NaCl does?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a partially completed ionic bonding diagram with the Lewis structures pre-drawn; students only need to show the electron transfer and write the ion charges. Include a step-by-step guide for predicting ion charges from group number.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the ionic bonding diagrams and property analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on lattice energy — how the size and charge of ions affect the strength of the ionic bond (e.g., compare NaCl to MgO lattice energies and explain the difference).
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual glossary with diagrams of electron transfer labeled in English and Spanish; use color-coded ion charges (red for positive, blue for negative) throughout all materials.
differentiation.iep: Chunked worksheet with one ionic bond per page; provide a periodic table with ion charges clearly marked for common elements; extended time for exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the historical significance of salt across cultures: Roman soldiers were partially paid in salt (origin of 'salary'), salt mining in Timbuktu was central to West African trade empires, and Gandhi's Salt March (1930) was a pivotal act of civil disobedience against British rule in India. All of this over NaCl — an ionic compound.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'ionic compound': Ionic compounds have high melting points because___. Ionic compounds conduct electricity in solution, but not as solids, because___. Sodium loses one electron to form Na+, so chlorine___.

vocabulary.definition: A bond formed by the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, resulting from the transfer of electrons from a metal to a nonmetal
A repeating three-dimensional arrangement of ions in an ionic compound, held together by electrostatic forces

cer.phenomenon: A student tests two white crystalline substances. Substance A melts at 801 degrees C, dissolves in water, and the solution conducts electricity. Substance B melts at 186 degrees C, dissolves in water, but the solution does not conduct electricity.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Substance A is an ionic compound and Substance B is a molecular compound because___.
cer.evidence_source: Compare the melting point, solubility, and conductivity data for both substances to the expected properties of ionic and molecular compounds.
cer.reasoning_frame: Substance A has a high melting point because___, and its solution conducts electricity because___. Substance B has a low melting point because___, and its solution does not conduct because___, indicating it is made of___.

lessons.title: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing and Lewis Structures (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: explain how covalent bonds form through electron sharing and draw accurate Lewis structures for simple molecular compounds
lessons.circle_prompt: When is sharing better than giving something away completely? Can you think of a situation where sharing made both sides better off?
lessons.do_now: Two hydrogen atoms each have 1 valence electron and need 2 to be stable. Neither wants to completely give up its electron. How could both atoms get a full outer shell? Sketch your idea.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Molecular model kits (1 set per group)
Bond type spectrum diagram (nonpolar covalent — polar covalent — ionic)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing and Lewis Structures. Show two images: NaCl crystal (ionic) and H2O molecule (covalent). Ask: In NaCl, electrons are transferred. But in water, hydrogen and oxygen share electrons. Why would two nonmetals share rather than transfer? Introduce the concept: when two atoms have similar electronegativity, neither can pull electrons away completely, so they share.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing and Lewis Structures. Guided Lewis structure construction: Teacher demonstrates the step-by-step process for drawing Lewis structures: (1) count total valence electrons, (2) draw the skeletal structure with single bonds, (3) complete octets on outer atoms, (4) place remaining electrons on the central atom, (5) convert lone pairs to multiple bonds if the central atom lacks an octet. Students practice with H2, O2, N2, H2O, CO2, and NH3, checking each with molecular model kits.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing and Lewis Structures. Teacher explains single, double, and triple bonds as sharing 2, 4, or 6 electrons respectively. Distinguish between bonding pairs and lone pairs. Introduce the concept of bond strength and length: triple bonds are shortest and strongest, single bonds are longest and weakest. Discuss the difference between molecular covalent substances (discrete molecules like H2O) and network covalent substances (continuous lattice like diamond or SiO2).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing and Lewis Structures. Students draw Lewis structures for 6 additional molecules: HCl, CCl4, CH4, C2H4 (has a double bond), HCN (has a triple bond), and PCl3. For each, they identify the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs. Challenge: Why does PCl3 have a lone pair on phosphorus while CCl4 does not?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing and Lewis Structures. Exit ticket: (1) Draw the Lewis structure for carbon dioxide (CO2) and identify the type of bonds present. (2) How many total valence electrons are in a molecule of ammonia (NH3)? Draw its Lewis structure. (3) Explain why two oxygen atoms form a double bond rather than a single bond.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Lewis structure checklist card: Step 1 — count valence electrons (use periodic table), Step 2 — draw skeleton, etc. Include a worked example (HCl) at the top of the practice sheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete Lewis structure practice and model building as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Draw Lewis structures for molecules with expanded octets (SF6, PCl5) and explain why elements in Period 3 and beyond can exceed the octet rule.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual step-by-step Lewis structure guide with numbered diagrams; allow students to use molecular model kits to verify structures before drawing.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice molecules from 6 to 4; provide a valence electron reference card; allow use of molecular model kits during the exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Linus Pauling, one of only two people to win two unshared Nobel Prizes (Chemistry and Peace). His work on the nature of the chemical bond revolutionized our understanding of covalent bonding. Also discuss his later controversial advocacy for vitamin C megadoses — showing that even brilliant scientists can hold views not supported by evidence outside their expertise.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'covalent bond': Two oxygen atoms form a double bond because___. Both ionic and covalent bonds involve valence electrons, but___. Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more to complete its octet, so it forms___.

vocabulary.definition: A bond formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons
A covalent bond in which three pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms
A diagram showing all valence electrons in a molecule as dots or lines between atoms

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Metal samples: copper wire, aluminum foil, iron nail
Property cards for sorting activity (15 cards with properties)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Metallic Bonding and Bond Type Comparison. Demo: Bend a copper wire back and forth (malleable). Hit an NaCl crystal with a hammer (it shatters). Ask: Copper atoms and Na/Cl ions are both arranged in crystal lattices. Why does copper bend while NaCl shatters? Students discuss and predict.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Metallic Bonding and Bond Type Comparison. Students test metal samples for conductivity (as solids), malleability (bending), and luster. They record observations and compare to their previous data on ionic and covalent compounds. Then students examine the 'sea of electrons' model diagram: metal cations are arranged in a lattice, surrounded by delocalized valence electrons that flow freely.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Metallic Bonding and Bond Type Comparison. Teacher explains metallic bonding: metal atoms release their valence electrons into a shared 'sea' that holds the cations together. This delocalized electron cloud explains: conductivity (electrons flow freely), malleability/ductility (layers of cations can slide without breaking bonds because the electron sea reshapes around them), luster (free electrons absorb and re-emit light). Build a comprehensive comparison table: ionic (electron transfer, high MP, brittle, conducts when dissolved), covalent (electron sharing, low MP, nonconductor), metallic (delocalized electrons, variable MP, malleable, conducts as solid).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Metallic Bonding and Bond Type Comparison. Property sorting card activity: Students receive 15 cards with properties (e.g., 'conducts as a solid,' 'brittle,' 'low melting point,' 'forms a crystal lattice with delocalized electrons') and sort them into three columns: ionic, covalent, and metallic. Some properties may fit more than one category — students must justify their placement.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Metallic Bonding and Bond Type Comparison. Exit ticket: A mystery substance is shiny, conducts electricity as a solid, has a high melting point, and is malleable. (1) What type of bonding does it have? (2) Describe the bonding model. differentiation.approaching: Provide the comparison table partially completed with ionic column filled in; include a visual diagram of each bonding model with labeled key features for reference during the sorting activity.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the property testing, comparison table, and sorting activity as designed.

differentiation.ell: Provide property sorting cards with diagrams alongside text descriptions; include a bilingual comparison chart with visual icons for each property (flame icon for high MP, lightning bolt for conductivity).
differentiation.iep: Reduce sorting cards from 15 to 10; provide a reference sheet with the three bonding models side by side; allow partner work for the sorting activity.

cer.phenomenon: Copper is used for electrical wiring in homes. Sodium chloride is used to de-ice roads in winter. Sugar (C12H22O11) is used to sweeten food. Each substance serves a different purpose because of its unique properties, which are determined by its bonding.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that copper is used for wiring because of its___ bonding, NaCl de-ices roads because of its___ bonding, and sugar dissolves easily because of its___ bonding.
cer.evidence_source: For each substance, identify the bond type, describe the bonding model, and connect it to the specific property that makes it useful for its purpose.
cer.reasoning_frame: Copper's metallic bonding means it has___, which is essential for wiring because___. NaCl's ionic bonding means it___ when dissolved in water, which lowers the freezing point because___. Sugar's covalent bonding means it___, so___.

lessons.title: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: predict the three-dimensional shape of a molecule using VSEPR theory and the number of bonding and lone pairs around the central atom
lessons.circle_prompt: If you had to arrange 4 balloons tied together at a central point so they were as far apart as possible, what shape would they make? What about 3 balloons? 2?
lessons.do_now: Draw the Lewis structure for water (H2O) and methane (CH4). Count the number of electron groups (bonding pairs + lone pairs) around the central atom in each. Predict: Will these molecules be the same shape? Why or why not?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Balloon sets (4-6 per group for geometry modeling)
Molecular model kits (1 set per group)
3D molecular geometry posters or digital models

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry. Balloon demo: Inflate 4 balloons and tie them together at a central point. Ask: What shape do they naturally form? (tetrahedral) Why? (They repel each other and maximize the space between them.) Now pop one balloon — what shape do the remaining 3 form? (trigonal pyramidal) This is exactly how electron pairs around a central atom determine molecular shape.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry. Students use molecular model kits to build five molecules: BeCl2 (2 bonding pairs, linear), BF3 (3 bonding pairs, trigonal planar), CH4 (4 bonding pairs, tetrahedral), NH3 (3 bonding + 1 lone pair, trigonal pyramidal), H2O (2 bonding + 2 lone pairs, bent). For each, they record: Lewis structure, number of bonding pairs, number of lone pairs, 3D shape name, and approximate bond angle.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry. Teacher introduces VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory: electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves to minimize repulsion. Key shapes and angles: linear (180 degrees), trigonal planar (120 degrees), tetrahedral (109.5 degrees), trigonal pyramidal (~107 degrees), bent (~104.5 degrees). Emphasize that lone pairs take up more space than bonding pairs, so they compress bond angles.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry. Students predict the molecular geometry for 6 additional molecules by drawing Lewis structures first, then counting electron groups: CO2, SO2, CCl4, PCl3, H2S, and CHCl3. They build each with model kits to verify their predictions.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry. Exit ticket: (1) Draw the Lewis structure for ammonia (NH3) and name its molecular geometry. (2) Explain why H2O is bent even though oxygen has 4 electron groups. (3) Predict the shape of CO2 and explain why it is different from H2O, even though both have 2 atoms bonded to a central atom.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a VSEPR decision flowchart: 'How many electron groups? -> How many are lone pairs? -> Shape name and angle.' Include model kit building instructions with photographs for each shape.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the model building and geometry predictions as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Extend to 5 and 6 electron group geometries (trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral) and predict shapes for SF4, ClF3, and XeF2.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual VSEPR chart with 3D photographs of each geometry labeled in English and native language; allow students to take photos of their model kit structures as evidence.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice molecules from 6 to 4; provide a completed Lewis structure for each molecule so students focus only on geometry prediction; allow use of model kits during the exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding molecular geometry is critical in pharmaceutical chemistry — the shape of a drug molecule determines whether it can fit into a receptor in the body (like a key in a lock). Highlight Tu Youyou, the Chinese chemist who won the Nobel Prize for discovering artemisinin, an antimalarial drug, by studying traditional Chinese herbal medicine and understanding the molecular structure of the active compound.

lessons.title: Polarity: Bond Polarity and Molecular Polarity (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: determine whether a bond is polar or nonpolar using electronegativity differences and predict whether a molecule is polar or nonpolar based on its geometry
lessons.circle_prompt: In a tug-of-war, what happens when both sides pull equally? What happens when one side is much stronger?
lessons.do_now: Use the electronegativity values on your reference table to find the difference between: (a) H and Cl, (b) Na and Cl, (c) Cl and Cl. Which pair shares most equally? Which pair has the biggest difference?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Charged rod and water stream demonstration materials (plastic rod, fur, buret with water)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Polarity: Bond Polarity and Molecular Polarity. Demo: Run a thin stream of water from a buret. Bring a charged plastic rod near the stream — the water bends toward the rod. Repeat with hexane — no bending. Ask: Why does water respond to the charged rod but hexane does not? Both are clear liquids. The answer lies in molecular polarity.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Polarity: Bond Polarity and Molecular Polarity. Students calculate electronegativity differences for 10 atom pairs and classify each bond as nonpolar covalent (0-0.4), polar covalent (0.4-1.7), or ionic (>1.7). They draw arrows on bond diagrams pointing from the less electronegative atom to the more electronegative atom (dipole arrows). Then they examine 4 molecules (CO2, H2O, CCl4, HCl) and draw dipole arrows for each bond.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Polarity: Bond Polarity and Molecular Polarity. Teacher explains the two-step process for determining molecular polarity: (1) Are the individual bonds polar? (Use electronegativity difference.) (2) Does the molecular geometry cause the dipoles to cancel or reinforce? Symmetric molecules (CO2, CCl4) have polar bonds that cancel — the molecule is nonpolar. Asymmetric molecules (H2O, NH3, HCl) have dipoles that do not cancel — the molecule is polar. Use vector addition analogy: arrows in opposite directions cancel; arrows in the same direction add up.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Polarity: Bond Polarity and Molecular Polarity. Students determine molecular polarity for 6 molecules: BF3, CHCl3, SO2, CH4, PH3, and HF. For each, they draw the Lewis structure, determine geometry, draw dipole arrows, and conclude polar or nonpolar. Students discuss why CHCl3 is polar while CCl4 is not, even though both contain polar C-Cl bonds.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Polarity: Bond Polarity and Molecular Polarity. Exit ticket: (1) Is a C-O bond polar or nonpolar? Justify using electronegativity values. (2) CO2 has two polar bonds but is a nonpolar molecule. Explain. (3) Predict whether SCl2 is polar or nonpolar. Draw the Lewis structure, show molecular geometry, and use dipole arrows to justify.

differentiation.approaching: Provide an electronegativity difference table pre-calculated for common atom pairs; include a visual polarity decision tree: 'Step 1: Are any bonds polar? Step 2: Does the geometry cause them to cancel?'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the bond classification and molecular polarity analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research how molecular polarity affects the solubility of vitamins (fat-soluble vs. water-soluble) and explain why vitamin C dissolves in water but vitamin E does not.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Charged rod and water stream demonstration materials (plastic rod, fur, buret with water)

engage.description: Brief review of Day 1 concepts through a warm-up problem or quick discussion. Building on previous days: Demo: Run a thin stream of water from a buret. Bring a charged plastic rod near the stream — the water bends toward the rod. Repeat with hexane — no bending. Ask: Why does water respond to the charged rod but hexane does not? Both are clear liquids. The answer lies in molecular polarity.

explore.description: Students work through practice problems or applications in pairs or small groups. Building on previous days: Students calculate electronegativity differences for 10 atom pairs and classify each bond as nonpolar covalent (0-0.4), polar covalent (0.4-1.7), or ionic (>1.7). They draw arrows on bond diagrams pointing from the less electronegative atom to the more electronegative atom (dipole arrows). Then they examine 4 molecules (CO2, H2O, CCl4, HCl) and draw dipole arrows for each bond.

explain.description: Address common misconceptions from practice; model problem-solving strategies. Building on previous days: Teacher explains the two-step process for determining molecular polarity: (1) Are the individual bonds polar? (Use electronegativity difference.) (2) Does the molecular geometry cause the dipoles to cancel or reinforce? Symmetric molecules (CO2, CCl4) have polar bonds that cancel — the molecule is nonpolar. Asymmetric molecules (H2O, NH3, HCl) have dipoles that do not cancel — the molecule is polar. Use vector addition analogy: arrows in opposite directions cancel; arrows in the same direction add up.

elaborate.description: CER activity connecting evidence to claims about the topic. Building on previous days: Students determine molecular polarity for 6 molecules: BF3, CHCl3, SO2, CH4, PH3, and HF. For each, they draw the Lewis structure, determine geometry, draw dipole arrows, and conclude polar or nonpolar. Students discuss why CHCl3 is polar while CCl4 is not, even though both contain polar C-Cl bonds.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket with application-level problems requiring multi-step reasoning. Building on previous days: Exit ticket: (1) Is a C-O bond polar or nonpolar? Justify using electronegativity values. (2) CO2 has two polar bonds but is a nonpolar molecule. Explain. (3) Predict whether SCl2 is polar or nonpolar. Draw the Lewis structure, show molecular geometry, and use dipole arrows to justify.

differentiation.approaching: Review key concepts from the full sequence before assessment. Provide an electronegativity difference table pre-calculated for common atom pairs; include a visual polarity decision tree: 'Step 1: Are any bonds polar? Step 2: Does the geometry cause them to cancel?'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the bond classification and molecular polarity analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Complete extension challenge connecting to real-world applications. Research how molecular polarity affects the solubility of vitamins (fat-soluble vs. water-soluble) and explain why vitamin C dissolves in water but vitamin E does not.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual guide showing dipole arrows as colored vectors on 3D molecule drawings; use the tug-of-war analogy with labeled diagrams throughout.

lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: identify the types of intermolecular forces present in a substance and rank them by strength to predict physical properties like boiling point
lessons.circle_prompt: What holds your friend group together? Is it one strong connection or many small ones? Can weak connections add up to be strong?
lessons.do_now: Water boils at 100 degrees C, but methane (CH4) boils at -161 degrees C. Both are small molecules. What is different about how their molecules interact with each other?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: IMF card sorting set (20 molecules with properties, 1 per group)
Boiling point data table for various substances (printed)
Demonstration materials: water, rubbing alcohol, cooking oil in petri dishes for evaporation race

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Intermolecular Forces. Evaporation race demo: Place a drop of water, rubbing alcohol, and acetone on three separate glass slides. Students observe which evaporates fastest. Ask: If evaporation means molecules are escaping from the liquid, which substance has the weakest attraction between its molecules? How can we predict this from molecular structure?

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Intermolecular Forces. Data analysis: Students examine a table showing the boiling points and molecular structures of 12 substances organized into groups: (1) noble gases (He, Ne, Ar — showing increasing BP with size), (2) similar-sized molecules with different polarity (CH4 vs. NH3 vs. H2O), (3) molecules with and without -OH groups. Students look for patterns and formulate hypotheses about what molecular features lead to higher boiling points.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Intermolecular Forces. Teacher introduces three types of intermolecular forces (IMFs) in order of increasing strength: (1) London dispersion forces (LDFs) — present in ALL molecules, increase with molecular size/electron count; the only IMF in nonpolar substances. (2) Dipole-dipole forces — present in polar molecules; stronger than LDFs for similar-sized molecules. (3) Hydrogen bonding — a strong dipole-dipole force occurring when H is bonded to N, O, or F; explains water's unusually high boiling point. Key distinction: IMFs act BETWEEN molecules; intramolecular bonds (ionic, covalent) act WITHIN molecules.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Intermolecular Forces. IMF card sort: Each group receives 10 molecule cards. For each, students determine: (1) Is it polar or nonpolar? (2) What IMFs are present? (3) Rank the 10 molecules from lowest to highest expected boiling point based on IMF strength. Groups then compare their rankings to actual boiling point data and discuss any surprises.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Intermolecular Forces. Exit ticket: (1) Identify all intermolecular forces present in HF. (2) Explain why H2O (MW=18) has a much higher boiling point than CH4 (MW=16) even though they are similar in size. (3) Rank these substances from lowest to highest boiling point: Ar, HCl, HF, CH4. Justify.

differentiation.approaching: Provide an IMF identification flowchart: 'Is the molecule polar? If yes, does it have H bonded to N, O, or F? If yes = hydrogen bonding. If no = dipole-dipole. If nonpolar = London dispersion only.' Include a strength ranking reference card.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the data analysis and card sorting activity as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research why ice floats (hydrogen bonding creates an open crystalline structure less dense than liquid water) and explain the ecological significance of this anomaly for aquatic life.
differentiation.ell: Provide the IMF flowchart with visual diagrams showing each type of IMF at the molecular level; include bilingual labels on all card sorting materials.
differentiation.iep: Reduce card sort from 10 molecules to 6; provide a pre-completed example for each type of IMF; allow use of flowchart and reference materials during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Connection to gecko adhesion: Geckos can climb smooth glass walls using London dispersion forces between billions of tiny hairs (setae) on their feet and the surface. Engineers are developing gecko-inspired adhesives — connecting molecular forces to biomimicry in engineering. Discuss how indigenous observations of nature have long inspired innovation.

cer.claim_starter: I claim that ethanol has a much higher boiling point than dimethyl ether because___.
cer.evidence_source: Examine the structural formulas of both molecules, identify the intermolecular forces present in each, and explain how the presence of the -OH group in ethanol creates an additional type of IMF.
cer.reasoning_frame: Ethanol has an -OH group, which allows it to form___ with neighboring molecules because___. Dimethyl ether lacks an -OH group, so its strongest IMF is___. Since hydrogen bonds are___ than dipole-dipole forces, ethanol requires___ energy to boil, resulting in a___ boiling point.

lessons.title: Structure-Property Relationships: Connecting Bonding to Bulk Properties (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: predict the melting point, solubility, and conductivity of a substance based on its type of bonding and intermolecular forces
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about how the smallest details can have the biggest effects. What is something tiny in your life that has a huge impact?
lessons.do_now: Diamond and graphite are both made entirely of carbon atoms. Diamond is the hardest known natural substance, while graphite is soft enough to use as pencil lead. How can the same element have such different properties?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Substance cards with structure diagrams and property data (20 cards)
Sorting mats (ionic, molecular, network covalent, metallic)
Samples if available: NaCl, sugar, paraffin wax, copper wire, graphite pencil
Reference table of common substances and their properties

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Structure-Property Relationships: Connecting Bonding to Bulk Properties. Show four substances: a salt crystal, a sugar cube, a copper wire, and a piece of graphite. State their melting points: NaCl = 801 degrees C, sugar = 186 degrees C, copper = 1085 degrees C, graphite > 3600 degrees C. Ask: Can you predict which type of bonding each has just from the melting point? What patterns do you see?

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Structure-Property Relationships: Connecting Bonding to Bulk Properties. Substance sorting challenge: Each group receives 12 substance cards, each showing the substance name, a particle-level structure diagram, melting point, conductivity data, and solubility in water. Students sort the cards into four categories (ionic, molecular, network covalent, metallic) using the property data as evidence. They must justify each placement.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Structure-Property Relationships: Connecting Bonding to Bulk Properties. Teacher builds a comprehensive property summary: (1) Ionic — high MP, soluble in water, conducts when dissolved/melted. (2) Molecular — low MP, may or may not dissolve in water (polar dissolves in water, nonpolar does not), does not conduct. (3) Network covalent — very high MP, insoluble, does not conduct (except graphite). (4) Metallic — variable MP, insoluble in water, conducts as solid. Key principle: the strength of the forces holding particles together determines the energy needed to overcome them.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Structure-Property Relationships: Connecting Bonding to Bulk Properties. Prediction challenge: Students receive descriptions of 4 unknown substances with partial property data and must predict the missing properties. Example: 'Substance X melts at 2072 degrees C and does not conduct electricity. Predict its solubility in water and what type of bonding it has.' Students write CER-style justifications for each prediction.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Structure-Property Relationships: Connecting Bonding to Bulk Properties. Exit ticket: (1) A substance melts at 45 degrees C, does not conduct electricity, and does not dissolve in water. What type of bonding does it most likely have? Explain. (2) Why do network covalent substances like diamond have extremely high melting points? (3) Explain at the particulate level why the smartphone glass in the Regents sample cluster is an insulator.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a property prediction reference card organized by bond type with key properties listed; include guided questions for each sorting card ('Does it conduct? If yes as a solid = metallic. If yes only when dissolved = ionic.').
differentiation.on_level: Complete the substance sorting and prediction challenge as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and explain the properties of graphene — a single layer of graphite — and why it conducts electricity (delocalized pi electrons) while diamond does not, despite both being pure carbon.
differentiation.ell: Provide sorting mats with property checklists in bilingual format; include particle-level diagrams on each sorting mat showing the bond type visually.
differentiation.iep: Reduce sorting cards from 12 to 8; provide a completed example card in each category; allow use of all reference materials during the exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect to the smartphone chemistry cluster from the Regents exam: aluminosilicate glass (network covalent/ionic), indium tin oxide conductor (metallic), lithium battery (ionic/metallic). Discuss how understanding structure-property relationships enables material scientists — many of whom come from underrepresented backgrounds like Mildred Dresselhaus, the 'Queen of Carbon Science' — to design new materials for technology.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'structure-property relationship': Diamond has an extremely high melting point because___. Both diamond and table salt have crystal lattice structures, but they melt at very different temperatures because___. The particulate-level structure of a substance determines its bulk properties, so knowing the bonding type allows us to___.

vocabulary.definition: A substance in which atoms are connected by covalent bonds in a continuous three-dimensional network, resulting in very high melting points and hardness
Observable, macroscopic properties of a substance (melting point, conductivity, solubility) that result from its particulate-level structure
A substance that allows the flow of electrical current, due to the presence of mobile charged particles (free electrons or ions)

lessons.title: Writing Chemical Formulas for Ionic Compounds (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: write correct chemical formulas for ionic compounds, including those with polyatomic ions, by balancing the charges of cations and anions
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a partnership where both sides have to balance — like a seesaw. What makes a good balance?
lessons.do_now: Sodium forms Na+ ions and chlorine forms Cl- ions. The compound they make is NaCl. Calcium forms Ca2+ ions and chlorine forms Cl- ions. Why is the formula CaCl2 and not CaCl? What rule determines the subscripts?
materials: Ion charge reference card (common cations and anions with charges)
Ion charge cards for criss-cross method practice (laminated, 1 set per group)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Writing Chemical Formulas for Ionic Compounds. Show labels from common household products: baking soda (NaHCO3), table salt (NaCl), chalk (CaCO3), plaster of Paris (CaSO4). Ask: What do all these formulas have in common? (They all contain a metal or positive ion paired with a negative ion.) How do chemists know the correct subscripts? Today we learn the formula-writing system.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Writing Chemical Formulas for Ionic Compounds. Students practice the criss-cross method for binary ionic compounds: write the cation first, anion second, criss-cross the charges to get subscripts, reduce to lowest ratio. Practice set 1 (binary): NaCl, MgO, Al2O3, CaBr2, K2S, FeCl3. Teacher circulates and provides feedback. Then introduce polyatomic ions: students receive the polyatomic ion reference table and practice formulas with SO4(2-), NO3(-), CO3(2-), OH(-), PO4(3-), NH4(+).

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Writing Chemical Formulas for Ionic Compounds. Teacher formalizes the rules: (1) Ionic compounds are always neutral — total positive charge equals total negative charge. (2) Use the criss-cross method, then reduce. (3) Polyatomic ions are treated as a single unit — use parentheses when the subscript is greater than 1 (e.g., Ca(OH)2, not CaOH2). (4) Transition metals require Roman numerals in the name to indicate charge (e.g., FeCl2 = iron(II) chloride, FeCl3 = iron(III) chloride).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Writing Chemical Formulas for Ionic Compounds. Practice set 2 (mixed): Students write formulas for 10 compounds including polyatomic ions and transition metals: ammonium sulfate, calcium phosphate, iron(III) oxide, copper(II) nitrate, aluminum hydroxide. Then reverse: given the formula Mg3(PO4)2, students identify the ions and their charges.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Writing Chemical Formulas for Ionic Compounds. Exit ticket: (1) Write the formula for aluminum sulfate. (2) Write the formula for iron(II) hydroxide. (3) What is wrong with the formula NaCl2? Explain why this formula is incorrect for a compound of sodium and chlorine.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a step-by-step criss-cross method template with numbered boxes; include a common ion charge chart color-coded by charge; work through the first two problems of each set as a class.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the formula writing practice as designed with the ion reference card.
differentiation.advanced: Write formulas for compounds with transition metals that have multiple oxidation states without being given the charge (e.g., determine the charge of iron in Fe2O3 from the formula).
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual criss-cross method guide with arrows and color-coded charges; allow verbal explanation of the error in NaCl2; bilingual ion reference card.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice sets from 6+10 to 4+6; provide a pre-organized workspace with columns for cation, anion, charges, and final formula; allow use of reference card during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how chemical formulas are a universal language — a chemist in Japan, Nigeria, and Brazil all read NaCl the same way. Connect to the development of chemical notation by Jons Jacob Berzelius (Sweden, 1813), who replaced alchemical symbols with the letter-based system we still use today. Discuss how alchemical traditions existed in many cultures: Chinese alchemy, Islamic alchemy (jabir ibn Hayyan), and European alchemy.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'chemical formula': The formula for calcium chloride is CaCl2 because___. Both sodium and calcium form ionic compounds with chlorine, but their formulas are different because___. An ionic compound must be electrically neutral, so the formula for aluminum oxide is___.

vocabulary.definition: A representation of a compound using element symbols and subscripts to show the ratio of atoms
A technique for writing ionic compound formulas by crossing the numerical charges of the ions to become subscripts

lessons.title: Naming Ionic and Covalent Compounds (IUPAC Nomenclature) (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: name ionic compounds (including those with polyatomic ions and transition metals) and covalent compounds using IUPAC nomenclature rules
lessons.circle_prompt: Naming things gives them identity. What is the story behind your name — who named you and why?
lessons.do_now: Match these common names to their chemical names: (a) table salt, (b) baking soda, (c) water, (d) rust. Choices: sodium chloride, iron(III) oxide, dihydrogen monoxide, sodium hydrogen carbonate. What patterns do you notice in the chemical names?
materials: Greek prefix chart for covalent naming (mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, hexa-)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Naming Ionic and Covalent Compounds (IUPAC Nomenclature). Show two chemical labels side by side: 'dihydrogen monoxide' and 'H2O.' Ask: Would you drink something called dihydrogen monoxide? (Students often say no, thinking it sounds dangerous.) Reveal it is water. Discuss why systematic naming matters — it tells us exactly what is in a compound, but common names can be misleading.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Naming Ionic and Covalent Compounds (IUPAC Nomenclature). Two-part naming practice. Part A — Ionic compounds: Students name 8 ionic compounds from formulas using the rules: metal name + nonmetal name with '-ide' ending (NaCl = sodium chloride); polyatomic ions keep their names (CaCO3 = calcium carbonate); transition metals get Roman numerals (FeCl3 = iron(III) chloride). Part B — Covalent compounds: Students name 6 covalent compounds using Greek prefixes (CO2 = carbon dioxide; N2O4 = dinitrogen tetroxide; PCl5 = phosphorus pentachloride).

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Naming Ionic and Covalent Compounds (IUPAC Nomenclature). Teacher summarizes the two naming systems. Key distinction: Ionic compounds never use Greek prefixes (not 'disodium monoxide' — just 'sodium oxide'). Covalent compounds use Greek prefixes because two nonmetals can form multiple compounds (CO vs. CO2). Review common mistakes: forgetting Roman numerals for transition metals, using prefixes for ionic compounds, not changing the second element's ending to '-ide' for binary compounds.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Naming Ionic and Covalent Compounds (IUPAC Nomenclature). Nomenclature card matching game: In pairs, students match 20 compound name cards with their formula cards. Cards include a mix of ionic (binary and polyatomic) and covalent compounds. After matching, they sort the pairs into 'ionic' and 'covalent' categories and identify the clues that distinguish them.

cer.claim_starter: I claim that the Roman numerals in the names indicate___, which explains why the two compounds have different colors and formulas:___.
cer.evidence_source: Write the chemical formulas for both compounds using the charges indicated by the Roman numerals, and explain why the same two elements can form different compounds.
cer.reasoning_frame: Cobalt(II) chloride means cobalt has a___ charge, so the formula is___ to balance with Cl-. Cobalt(III) chloride means cobalt has a___ charge, so the formula is___. These are different compounds because___, which is why they have different___ and different___.

lessons.title: The Mole Concept and Avogadro's Number (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: explain what a mole is, use Avogadro's number to convert between moles and particles, and explain why chemists need the mole as a counting unit
lessons.circle_prompt: We use words like 'dozen' (12) and 'pair' (2) to count everyday objects. What would you need a really, really large counting word for?
lessons.do_now: A single grain of sand has a mass of about 0.004 grams. How many grains would you need to equal 1 gram? Now consider: a single carbon atom has a mass of 0.00000000000000000000002 grams. How could a chemist count atoms? There must be a better way.
materials: Mole scale analogy cards (printed — showing relative sizes)
Mole Day celebration props (optional: for October 23, 6:02 AM)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: The Mole Concept and Avogadro's Number. Scale challenge: If you had a mole (6.02 x 10^23) of pennies and stacked them, the stack would reach from Earth to the Sun and back over 400 billion times. If you had a mole of grains of sand, it would cover the entire United States to a depth of about 3 feet. Ask: Why would scientists need a number this incredibly large? Because atoms are incredibly small.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: The Mole Concept and Avogadro's Number. Students practice mole-to-particle and particle-to-mole conversions using Avogadro's number (6.02 x 10^23). Practice set: (1) How many molecules are in 2.5 moles of water? (2) How many moles is 3.01 x 10^23 atoms of iron? (3) How many atoms are in 0.75 moles of gold? Students use dimensional analysis setup: given quantity x conversion factor = desired quantity.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: The Mole Concept and Avogadro's Number. Teacher formalizes: A mole is 6.02 x 10^23 of anything — the chemist's counting unit. Just as a dozen = 12, a mole = 6.02 x 10^23. One mole of any element contains Avogadro's number of atoms. One mole of any molecular compound contains Avogadro's number of molecules. Key: distinguish between atoms and molecules (1 mole of H2O = 6.02 x 10^23 molecules, but 3 x 6.02 x 10^23 atoms because each molecule has 3 atoms).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: The Mole Concept and Avogadro's Number. Multi-step conversion challenge: (1) How many oxygen atoms are in 2.0 moles of CO2? (Students must first convert moles of CO2 to molecules, then multiply by 2 for the two oxygen atoms per molecule.) (2) If a sample contains 1.806 x 10^24 atoms of hydrogen and all the hydrogen is in the form of H2 gas, how many moles of H2 are present?

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: The Mole Concept and Avogadro's Number. Exit ticket: (1) Define 'mole' in your own words. (2) How many molecules are in 4.00 moles of CO2? (3) A sample contains 1.204 x 10^24 molecules of water. How many moles is this? How many individual hydrogen atoms does this sample contain?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a dimensional analysis template with blanks: '___ x (6.02 x 10^23 / 1 mol) = ___' and guide students through the first two problems step by step; include a calculator use guide for scientific notation.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the mole conversion practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate how long it would take to count a mole of objects at a rate of 1 per second, and express the answer in years. Discuss why this illustrates the necessity of the mole concept.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual dimensional analysis setup with arrows showing the conversion path; use the dozen-to-mole analogy with visual comparisons; bilingual vocabulary definitions.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice problems by half; provide a conversion factor reference card; allow calculator use throughout; break multi-step problems into numbered steps.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Amedeo Avogadro (Italian physicist, 1776-1856) whose hypothesis about equal volumes of gases was not accepted during his lifetime but became foundational to chemistry. The number was named in his honor by Jean Baptiste Perrin (French physicist). Discuss how scientific contributions are sometimes recognized only after a scientist's death, and how naming conventions in science honor diverse contributors.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'mole': A mole of any substance contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles because___. A mole of carbon and a mole of gold contain the same number of atoms, but they have different masses because___. Atoms are too small to count individually, so chemists use the mole to___.

vocabulary.definition: The SI unit for amount of substance; one mole contains exactly 6.02 x 10^23 representative particles (atoms, molecules, or formula units)
The smallest unit of a substance: atoms for elements, molecules for covalent compounds, or formula units for ionic compounds

cer.phenomenon: A chemistry teacher places two sealed containers on the front table. Container A holds 12.0 g of carbon (graphite). Container B holds 55.8 g of iron (filings). The teacher claims that both containers contain the same number of atoms.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the teacher is___ (correct/incorrect) because both containers contain approximately___ atoms, even though their masses are different.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the number of moles of each element using molar mass, then convert to atoms using Avogadro's number.
cer.reasoning_frame: Container A: 12.0 g C / ___ g/mol = ___ mol C x 6.02 x 10^23 = ___ atoms. Container B: 55.8 g Fe / ___ g/mol = ___ mol Fe x 6.02 x 10^23 = ___ atoms. Both containers hold approximately 1 mole, which contains___ atoms, demonstrating that the mole concept connects___ to___.

lessons.title: Molar Mass and Mole-Mass Conversions (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: calculate the molar mass of a compound from its formula and convert between moles, mass, and number of particles using dimensional analysis
lessons.circle_prompt: When you go grocery shopping, some things are sold by weight and others by count (eggs by the dozen, bananas by the bunch). Why do we use different units for different things?
lessons.do_now: The periodic table says carbon has an atomic mass of 12.01 amu and oxygen has 16.00 amu. If CO2 has one carbon and two oxygens, predict the mass of one mole of CO2 molecules. Show your calculation.
materials: Triple-beam balances and element samples for verification (optional)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Molar Mass and Mole-Mass Conversions. Show students three piles: 12.0 g of carbon (charcoal), 55.8 g of iron filings, and 18.0 g of water. State: Each pile contains the same number of particles — one mole, or 6.02 x 10^23. Ask: Why do they have different masses? Because each atom or molecule has a different mass. The mass of one mole is called the molar mass, and it equals the atomic or formula mass in grams.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Molar Mass and Mole-Mass Conversions. Students calculate molar masses for 8 compounds: H2O, NaCl, CO2, C6H12O6 (glucose), Ca(OH)2, Fe2O3, H2SO4, and C9H8O4 (aspirin — connecting to the anchoring phenomenon). They show all work: list each element, multiply atomic mass by number of atoms, sum all contributions.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Molar Mass and Mole-Mass Conversions. Teacher presents the mole conversion 'road map': Particles <-> (Avogadro's number) <-> Moles <-> (Molar mass) <-> Grams. All conversions use dimensional analysis. Work through three example problems: (1) How many grams are in 3.50 moles of NaCl? (2) How many moles are in 25.0 g of water? (3) How many molecules are in 10.0 g of CO2? (This requires two steps: grams to moles, then moles to molecules.)

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Molar Mass and Mole-Mass Conversions. Aspirin tablet challenge (connecting to the anchoring phenomenon): A 500 mg aspirin tablet contains 500 mg of C9H8O4. Students calculate: (1) the molar mass of aspirin, (2) how many moles of aspirin are in one tablet, (3) how many molecules of aspirin are in one tablet, (4) how many individual atoms of all types are in one tablet.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Molar Mass and Mole-Mass Conversions. Exit ticket: (1) Calculate the molar mass of calcium phosphate, Ca3(PO4)2. (2) How many grams are in 0.250 moles of glucose (C6H12O6)? (3) A sample has a mass of 44.0 g of CO2. How many moles is this, and how many oxygen atoms does it contain?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a molar mass calculation template with columns: element, atomic mass, number of atoms, subtotal; include the road map diagram with arrows and conversion factor labels for reference.
differentiation.on_level: Complete molar mass calculations and conversion problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Determine how many aspirin tablets a pharmaceutical company can produce from 1.00 kg of pure aspirin, and calculate the total number of molecules in the entire batch.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual road map with color-coded conversion arrows and worked examples in each direction; include bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce the number of molar mass calculations from 8 to 5; provide a molar mass example card; break multi-step problems into sequential numbered steps; allow calculator throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect to the pharmaceutical industry: Precision in measuring moles and masses is critical in drug manufacturing. Discuss how access to affordable medication varies globally — the same aspirin formula costs different amounts in different countries. Highlight the work of organizations like Doctors Without Borders that rely on precise chemical manufacturing to provide medications to underserved communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'molar mass': The molar mass of water is 18.02 g/mol because___. One mole of carbon and one mole of iron contain the same number of atoms, but their masses are different because___. To convert from grams to moles, you divide by the molar mass, so 44.0 g of CO2 equals___.

vocabulary.definition: The mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in grams per mole (g/mol), numerically equal to the formula mass in amu
A ratio of equivalent measurements used to convert from one unit to another in dimensional analysis

cer.phenomenon: A 500 mg aspirin tablet (C9H8O4) seems like a tiny amount of material. Yet it contains approximately 1.67 x 10^21 molecules — far more molecules than there are grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth (estimated at 7.5 x 10^18).
cer.claim_starter: I claim that a tiny 500 mg aspirin tablet contains___ molecules, which is more than the number of grains of sand on Earth, because___.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the molar mass of aspirin, convert 500 mg to moles, then convert moles to molecules using Avogadro's number. Compare to the estimated number of sand grains.
cer.reasoning_frame: The molar mass of aspirin is___ g/mol. 500 mg = ___ g, which equals___ moles. Multiplying by Avogadro's number: ___ x 6.02 x 10^23 = ___ molecules. This is larger than 7.5 x 10^18 sand grains because atoms and molecules are___, so even a small mass contains___.

lessons.title: Percent Composition (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: calculate the percent composition of each element in a compound from its chemical formula
lessons.circle_prompt: If you had to describe the composition of your ideal pizza by percentage — what percent crust, sauce, cheese, toppings — what would it be?
lessons.do_now: A compound has the formula H2O. It contains hydrogen and oxygen. Without calculating, predict: Is water mostly hydrogen or mostly oxygen by mass? (Hint: Think about the atomic masses.) Write your prediction and reasoning.

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Percent Composition. Show a nutrition label from a food package. Ask: What does 'percent daily value' mean? It tells you what fraction of your daily needs is in one serving. Chemists use percent composition the same way — to describe what fraction of a compound's mass comes from each element. This is used in mining (what percent of ore is useful metal?), nutrition (what percent of a compound is a useful element?), and forensics.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Percent Composition. Students calculate percent composition for 5 compounds: H2O, NaCl, CO2, C6H12O6, and Fe2O3. Process: (1) Find molar mass of compound. (2) Find total mass contribution of each element (atomic mass x number of atoms). (3) Divide element mass by total molar mass x 100%. Students verify that all percentages add to 100% (within rounding). They create pie charts for two of the compounds.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Percent Composition. Teacher formalizes the percent composition formula: %element = (mass of element in one mole of compound / molar mass of compound) x 100%. Discuss real-world applications: iron ore analysis (what % of Fe2O3 is iron? 69.9% — this tells miners the maximum iron they can extract), and fertilizer labels (N-P-K numbers represent percent nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium by mass).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Percent Composition. Application problems: (1) A mining company has 500 kg of hematite ore (Fe2O3). What is the maximum mass of iron that can be extracted? (2) A fertilizer bag says it is 46% nitrogen by mass and lists the compound as CO(NH2)2 (urea). Verify this percentage. (3) Two iron compounds: FeO and Fe2O3. Which contains a higher percentage of iron?

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Percent Composition. Exit ticket: (1) Calculate the percent composition of each element in calcium carbonate (CaCO3). (2) A compound is 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen, and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Does this match the percent composition of ethanol (C2H6O)? Show your work.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a step-by-step percent composition template with labeled columns (element, atomic mass, number of atoms, total mass, percent); work through the first example (H2O) as a class.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the percent composition calculations and application problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Given percent composition data for an unknown compound, work backwards to determine a possible molecular formula (preview of empirical formula determination).
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual percent composition calculation guide with color-coded steps; use the pizza analogy throughout with labeled diagrams; bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice compounds from 5 to 3; reduce application problems from 3 to 2; provide a molar mass reference for common compounds; allow calculator and periodic table during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how percent composition is critical in mining and resource extraction — connecting to the global demand for lithium (Li2CO3 in batteries) and the environmental and social impact of lithium mining on indigenous communities in Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina (the 'Lithium Triangle'). Chemistry concepts have real consequences for real communities.

cer.phenomenon: A fertilizer bag is labeled '46-0-0,' meaning it is 46% nitrogen by mass. The active ingredient is urea, CO(NH2)2. A farmer needs to know if this label is accurate before applying it to their crops.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the fertilizer label of 46% nitrogen is___ (accurate/inaccurate) because the actual percent nitrogen in urea is___.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the molar mass of urea and the percent composition of nitrogen. Compare your calculated percentage to the label.
cer.reasoning_frame: Urea (CO(NH2)2) has a molar mass of___. It contains___ nitrogen atoms, contributing a total mass of___. The percent nitrogen = ___/___  x 100% = ___%. Compared to the label value of 46%, this is___, confirming that___.

lessons.title: Empirical and Molecular Formulas (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: determine the empirical formula of a compound from percent composition data and use molar mass to find the molecular formula
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever simplified a recipe — like doubling or halving it? How do you keep the proportions the same when you scale up or down?
lessons.do_now: Two compounds both contain only carbon and hydrogen. Compound A is 75.0% carbon and 25.0% hydrogen. Compound B is also 75.0% carbon and 25.0% hydrogen, but Compound B's molar mass is twice as large. Can they have the same formula? Discuss with your partner.
materials: Lab data cards (simulated experimental data for 4 unknown compounds)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Empirical and Molecular Formulas. Present a mystery: Formaldehyde (CH2O, molar mass 30), acetic acid (C2H4O2, molar mass 60), and glucose (C6H12O6, molar mass 180) all have the same percent composition: 40% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O. How is this possible? They all have the same simplest ratio of atoms (1:2:1) but different actual numbers. The simplest ratio is the empirical formula; the actual number is the molecular formula.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Empirical and Molecular Formulas. Step-by-step empirical formula determination: Students practice with two compounds. (1) A compound is 63.5% Fe and 36.5% O. Convert percentages to grams (assume 100 g sample), divide by atomic mass to get moles, divide by smallest mole value to get the ratio, round to nearest whole number. Result: Fe2O3. (2) A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O. Result: CH2O.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Empirical and Molecular Formulas. Teacher formalizes the process: (1) Assume 100 g sample (so percentages become grams). (2) Convert grams to moles for each element. (3) Divide each by the smallest number of moles. (4) If ratios are not whole numbers, multiply all by the smallest integer that gives whole numbers (e.g., 1.5 -> multiply all by 2). For molecular formula: (5) Divide the given molar mass by the empirical formula mass to get the multiplier. (6) Multiply all subscripts by the multiplier.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Empirical and Molecular Formulas. Lab data card challenge: Students receive simulated lab data for 4 unknown compounds (percent composition from combustion analysis or decomposition experiments). They determine the empirical formula for each. For 2 of the 4, they are also given the molar mass and must find the molecular formula. One example connects to the anchoring phenomenon: determine the molecular formula of aspirin from percent composition data and molar mass 180.16.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Empirical and Molecular Formulas. Exit ticket: (1) A compound is 82.8% carbon and 17.2% hydrogen. Determine the empirical formula. (2) If the molar mass of the compound in question 1 is 58.12 g/mol, what is the molecular formula? (3) Explain in one sentence the difference between an empirical formula and a molecular formula.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a color-coded step-by-step template with boxes for each calculation step; include a 'common ratios to watch for' card (1.33 -> multiply by 3, 1.5 -> multiply by 2, 1.25 -> multiply by 4).
differentiation.on_level: Complete the empirical formula practice and lab data card challenge as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Given combustion analysis data (mass of CO2 and H2O produced from burning a sample), determine the empirical formula of an unknown hydrocarbon.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual flowchart showing the empirical formula process with arrows and color-coded steps; include bilingual calculation templates.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice to 2 empirical formula problems plus 1 molecular formula; provide a completed example showing every step; allow use of all reference materials during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how empirical formula determination was historically critical in identifying new substances — Justus von Liebig and Friedrich Wohler (Germany, 1800s) developed combustion analysis to determine the composition of organic compounds. This technique was later refined by scientists worldwide and remains essential in pharmaceutical development, helping identify new drug compounds from natural sources used in traditional medicine across cultures.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'empirical formula': CH2O is the empirical formula for glucose, formaldehyde, and acetic acid because___. These three compounds have the same empirical formula, but they are different substances because___. The molecular formula is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, so if the empirical formula mass is 30 and the molar mass is 180, the multiplier is___.

vocabulary.definition: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound

lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply and compare concepts and fluently convert between compound names, formulas, moles, mass, particles, and percent composition in multi-step problems
lessons.circle_prompt: Share one connection you made between yesterday's topic and something in your daily life.
lessons.do_now: Recall from yesterday: explain one key idea from yesterday about how to define and describe key concepts related to: fluently convert between compound names, formulas, moles, mass, particles, and percent composition in multi-step problems.
materials: Periodic table and reference tables (1 per student)

engage.description: Review warm-up connecting Day 1 vocabulary to a new example or context. Continuing: Connect back to the anchoring phenomenon: A pharmaceutical company produces 500 mg aspirin tablets. Now students can fully solve the problem: name the compound (acetylsalicylic acid), write its formula (C9H8O4), calculate its molar mass, determine moles per tablet, and find the number of molecules per tablet. Walk through the complete solution as a class.

explore.description: Structured practice — students work through increasingly complex problems with scaffolds. Continuing: Station rotation review (4 stations, 3 min each): Station 1 — Formula writing and naming (8 compounds). Station 2 — Molar mass calculation for 4 compounds and 2 mole-mass conversions. Station 3 — Mole-particle conversions (3 problems including multi-step). Station 4 — Percent composition and empirical formula determination (2 problems).

explain.description: Mini-lesson addressing patterns from practice; introduce additional complexity. Continuing: Whole-class review of most commonly missed concepts from the unit: (1) When to use parentheses in formulas. (2) The difference between moles of molecules and moles of atoms. (3) The empirical vs. molecular formula distinction. Address student questions from the station rotation.

elaborate.description: Partner work on application problems with real-world contexts. Continuing: Regents-style practice cluster: Students answer a 5-question cluster based on a phenomenon (e.g., analyzing the composition of a mineral sample from a local quarry). Questions integrate naming, formula writing, molar mass, mole conversions, and percent composition.

evaluate.description: Formative assessment — students solve 2-3 problems independently and self-check. Continuing: Cumulative exit ticket: (1) Write the formula for iron(III) phosphate. (2) Calculate its molar mass. (3) How many moles are in 75.0 g of this compound? (4) What is the percent composition of iron in this compound? (5) If the empirical formula of a compound is CH2 and its molar mass is 56.0 g/mol, what is the molecular formula?

differentiation.approaching: Provide completed examples from Day 1 as reference. Provide a unit reference sheet summarizing all formulas and procedures; reduce station problems by 50%; allow use of reference sheet during the exit ticket.
differentiation.on_level: Complete all station rotation problems and the practice cluster as designed.
differentiation.advanced: After completing the practice cluster, students create a 3-question mini-cluster based on a phenomenon of their choice, integrating at least three different calculation types from the unit.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual reference sheets at each station; include sentence frames for constructed-response questions in the practice cluster.
differentiation.iep: Reduce cumulative exit ticket to 3 questions instead of 5; provide formula and procedure reference cards; allow extended time and calculator use.

cer.phenomenon: A geologist brings a 250.0 g sample of limestone (assumed to be pure calcium carbonate, CaCO3) to a chemistry lab. The lab needs to determine how many moles of calcium carbonate are in the sample and what percentage of the sample's mass is calcium.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the 250.0 g limestone sample contains___ moles of CaCO3 and is___% calcium by mass.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the molar mass of CaCO3, convert grams to moles, and calculate the percent composition of calcium. Show all work with dimensional analysis.
cer.reasoning_frame: The molar mass of CaCO3 is___ g/mol. 250.0 g / ___ g/mol = ___ moles. The percent calcium = (40.08 / ___) x 100% = ___%. This means that___ g of the sample is pure calcium, which is important because___.
