lessons.title: Evidence of Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Mass (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: identify evidence that a chemical reaction has occurred and demonstrate that mass is conserved during chemical reactions
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever seen something dramatic happen — like a firework, a cooking mishap, or rust appearing on metal? What made you think something chemical was going on?
lessons.do_now: Two clear, colorless solutions are mixed together and a bright yellow solid forms at the bottom of the beaker. List all the evidence that a chemical reaction occurred. Predict: Will the mass of the products equal the mass of the reactants? Why or why not?
materials: Lead nitrate and potassium iodide solutions (teacher demo only)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Evidence of Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Mass. Teacher demo: Mix lead nitrate and potassium iodide solutions in a beaker — an instant bright yellow precipitate of lead iodide forms (the 'golden rain' demo). Students identify all evidence of a chemical reaction (color change, precipitate formation). Then ask: Did matter appear from nothing? Where did the yellow solid come from?

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Evidence of Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Mass. Conservation of mass lab: Students measure the mass of a sealed bag containing baking soda and a small cup of vinegar. They tilt the bag to mix the reactants (gas produced, bag inflates). They measure the mass again. Students record before and after masses. Then teacher demo: burn steel wool on a balance — mass increases slightly. Discuss: Where did the extra mass come from? (Oxygen from air bonded to iron.)

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Evidence of Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Mass. Teacher formalizes the Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier, 1789): In a chemical reaction, matter is neither created nor destroyed — the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products. At the atomic level, atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed. This is why chemical equations must be balanced — same number of each type of atom on both sides.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Evidence of Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Mass. Students analyze three scenarios where it appears mass is not conserved and explain why it actually is: (1) Burning wood produces ash that weighs less than the wood (gases escaped — CO2 and H2O). (2) A nail rusts and becomes heavier (gained oxygen from air). (3) Baking soda + vinegar in an open container loses mass (CO2 gas escaped). Students explain each using conservation of mass.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Evidence of Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Mass. Exit ticket: (1) State the Law of Conservation of Mass in your own words. (2) A 10.0 g piece of magnesium is burned in air and produces 16.6 g of magnesium oxide. What mass of oxygen reacted? (3) In the Regents sample cluster about blueberry fields, students are asked to 'cite numerical evidence to demonstrate the claim that atoms, and therefore mass, are conserved.' Explain what this means.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a data table template with before/after mass columns and a 'difference' column; include a sentence frame: 'Mass was conserved because___ equals___.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the conservation of mass lab and scenario analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Design an experiment to prove conservation of mass for a reaction that produces a gas, accounting for how to capture and measure the gas.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual diagram of the baking soda + vinegar reaction with labeled before/after particle models; bilingual sentence frames for the exit ticket.
differentiation.iep: Pair with a lab partner; provide a simplified data table with guiding questions at each step; reduce scenario analysis from 3 to 2.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Antoine Lavoisier, the 'father of modern chemistry,' who established the Law of Conservation of Mass. Also discuss his wife Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, who was his essential collaborator — translating scientific texts, illustrating experiments, and managing the lab — yet received little credit for decades. Connect to the invisible labor of women and marginalized collaborators in science.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'conservation of mass': When wood burns, the ash weighs less than the original wood because___. It seems like mass disappears during burning, but mass is actually conserved because___. Atoms are rearranged during a chemical reaction but not created or destroyed, so the total mass of products___.

vocabulary.definition: A process in which one or more substances (reactants) are converted into one or more new substances (products) with different properties
In a chemical reaction, the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products; matter is neither created nor destroyed

cer.phenomenon: A student places an open beaker containing baking soda on a balance and records a mass of 85.0 g. They add vinegar and observe bubbling. After the reaction stops, the balance reads 82.3 g. The student concludes that mass was not conserved.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the student's conclusion is incorrect because mass was conserved, but___ explains the apparent loss of 2.7 g.
cer.evidence_source: Identify the gas produced in the reaction (CO2), explain why it escaped the open beaker, and describe how the experiment could be redesigned to demonstrate conservation of mass.
cer.reasoning_frame: The reaction between baking soda and vinegar produces___ gas, which is___ and escaped the open beaker into the air. The 'missing' 2.7 g is the mass of the___. If the reaction were conducted in a___, the mass before and after would be___, demonstrating that___.

lessons.title: Balancing Chemical Equations (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: balance chemical equations by adjusting coefficients to ensure the same number of each type of atom appears on both sides
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time you had to make things 'come out even' — dividing food equally, splitting a bill, balancing a budget. What strategies did you use?
lessons.do_now: The unbalanced equation is: _Fe + _O2 -> _Fe2O3. Count the atoms on each side. What is unbalanced? Try adding numbers in front of the formulas (not changing subscripts) to make both sides equal.
materials: Atom counting chips or colored tiles (for visual balancing)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Balancing Chemical Equations. Visual demo: Show the equation H2 + O2 -> H2O using molecular model kits. Build 1 H2 and 1 O2 on the left, and try to build H2O on the right. Problem: you have 2 oxygen atoms but only need 1 for H2O. You cannot break the O2 (that would change the formula). Solution: make 2 H2O molecules, but now you need 2 H2 molecules. Final: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Students see the physical reason for coefficients.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Balancing Chemical Equations. Level 1 balancing practice: Students balance 8 equations starting simple (synthesis and decomposition) and progressing to moderate difficulty. Strategy guide: (1) Start with the most complex formula. (2) Balance metals first, then nonmetals, then oxygen, then hydrogen. (3) Never change subscripts — only add coefficients. (4) Check your work by counting all atoms on both sides. Students use whiteboards for quick practice and teacher circulation.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Balancing Chemical Equations. Teacher reviews common balancing strategies and addresses errors: changing subscripts vs. coefficients (subscripts change the compound, coefficients change the amount), dealing with polyatomic ions that appear intact on both sides (balance them as a unit), and handling odd-even mismatches (e.g., if you have an odd oxygen on one side and O2 on the other, double everything first).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Balancing Chemical Equations. Level 2 balancing practice: 6 more challenging equations including combustion reactions (hydrocarbons + O2 -> CO2 + H2O), reactions with polyatomic ions, and equations requiring larger coefficients. Students work in pairs and compare strategies.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Balancing Chemical Equations. Exit ticket: Balance these three equations and prove they are balanced by counting all atoms: (1) _Al + _HCl -> _AlCl3 + _H2 (2) _C3H8 + _O2 -> _CO2 + _H2O (3) _Ca(OH)2 + _H3PO4 -> _Ca3(PO4)2 + _H2O

differentiation.approaching: Provide atom counting chips (colored tiles representing different elements) so students can physically manipulate the atoms; include a pre-made atom counting table for each equation with rows for each element.
differentiation.on_level: Complete Level 1 and Level 2 balancing practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Balance oxidation-reduction (redox) equations using the half-reaction method (preview of electrochemistry).
differentiation.ell: Provide visual balancing guides with color-coded atoms and arrows showing where coefficients go; include bilingual strategy cards.
differentiation.iep: Reduce Level 1 to 5 equations and Level 2 to 3 equations; provide an atom counting template for each equation; allow use of strategy card during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect equation balancing to the Regents sample cluster on blueberry fields, where students must 'cite numerical evidence from Equation 3 to demonstrate the claim that atoms, and therefore mass, are conserved.' Emphasize that this skill is tested directly on the new Regents exam in a phenomena-driven context.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'balanced equation': We use coefficients instead of changing subscripts because___. The unbalanced equation H2 + O2 -> H2O has 2 oxygen atoms on the left but only 1 on the right, so___. A balanced equation has the same number of each type of atom on both sides because___.

vocabulary.definition: A symbolic representation of a chemical reaction using formulas and symbols to show reactants, products, and their physical states
A number in a chemical formula that indicates the number of atoms of the preceding element; cannot be changed when balancing

lessons.title: Balancing Chemical Equations (Day 3 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can evaluate and explain my understanding to balance chemical equations by adjusting coefficients to ensure the same number of each type of atom appears on both sides
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could teach one thing from this week's lessons to a younger student, what would it be?
lessons.do_now: Review: Using what you've learned this week, explain one key idea from yesterday about how to apply and compare concepts and balance chemical equations by adjusting coefficients to ensure the same number of each type of atom appears on both sides.
materials: Atom counting chips or colored tiles (for visual balancing)

engage.description: Present a novel scenario that requires synthesis of concepts from Days 1-2. Building on previous days: Visual demo: Show the equation H2 + O2 -> H2O using molecular model kits. Build 1 H2 and 1 O2 on the left, and try to build H2O on the right. Problem: you have 2 oxygen atoms but only need 1 for H2O. You cannot break the O2 (that would change the formula). Solution: make 2 H2O molecules, but now you need 2 H2 molecules. Final: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Students see the physical reason for coefficients.

explore.description: CER activity — students construct evidence-based arguments about the topic. Building on previous days: Level 1 balancing practice: Students balance 8 equations starting simple (synthesis and decomposition) and progressing to moderate difficulty. Strategy guide: (1) Start with the most complex formula. (2) Balance metals first, then nonmetals, then oxygen, then hydrogen. (3) Never change subscripts — only add coefficients. (4) Check your work by counting all atoms on both sides. Students use whiteboards for quick practice and teacher circulation.

explain.description: Whole-class discussion of CER responses; address remaining misconceptions. Building on previous days: Teacher reviews common balancing strategies and addresses errors: changing subscripts vs. coefficients (subscripts change the compound, coefficients change the amount), dealing with polyatomic ions that appear intact on both sides (balance them as a unit), and handling odd-even mismatches (e.g., if you have an odd oxygen on one side and O2 on the other, double everything first).

elaborate.description: Extension or enrichment activity connecting to real-world applications. Building on previous days: Level 2 balancing practice: 6 more challenging equations including combustion reactions (hydrocarbons + O2 -> CO2 + H2O), reactions with polyatomic ions, and equations requiring larger coefficients. lessons.title: Types of Chemical Reactions: Synthesis, Decomposition, and Combustion (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: classify chemical reactions as synthesis, decomposition, or combustion and predict products for each type
lessons.circle_prompt: Building something up, breaking something down, and burning something — which of these three processes do you do most often in daily life?
lessons.do_now: Classify each scenario: (a) Two elements combine to form a compound. (b) A compound breaks apart into simpler substances. (c) A substance burns in oxygen. Write one real-world example for each.
materials: Demo materials: steel wool + O2, hydrogen peroxide + MnO2 catalyst, candle burning

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Types of Chemical Reactions: Synthesis, Decomposition, and Combustion. Three quick demos: (1) Synthesis — burn steel wool in oxygen (2Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3 sparks). (2) Decomposition — add MnO2 to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2 -> H2O + O2, rapid bubbling). (3) Combustion — light a candle (wax + O2 -> CO2 + H2O). Ask: What pattern do you see in each type? Students turn-and-talk.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Types of Chemical Reactions: Synthesis, Decomposition, and Combustion. Students examine 12 balanced equations and classify each as synthesis (A + B -> AB), decomposition (AB -> A + B), or combustion (CxHy + O2 -> CO2 + H2O). They identify the pattern for each type: synthesis combines simpler substances into one, decomposition breaks one compound into simpler substances, combustion always involves a fuel reacting with O2 to produce CO2 and H2O. Students then predict products for 4 unwritten reactions.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Types of Chemical Reactions: Synthesis, Decomposition, and Combustion. Teacher formalizes the three reaction types with general equations. Synthesis: A + B -> AB (two or more substances combine to form one product). Decomposition: AB -> A + B (one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances). Combustion: hydrocarbon + O2 -> CO2 + H2O (always produces carbon dioxide and water). Key connection to the Regents gas stoves cluster: combustion of methane (CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O) and its environmental impact.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Types of Chemical Reactions: Synthesis, Decomposition, and Combustion. Application problems: (1) In the airbag phenomenon, sodium azide decomposes: 2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2. Classify this reaction and explain why it is useful (produces a large volume of inert gas quickly). (2) Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Is this synthesis or something else? (Discuss how some reactions do not fit neatly into one category.) (3) Predict the products of the combustion of ethanol (C2H5OH).

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Types of Chemical Reactions: Synthesis, Decomposition, and Combustion. Exit ticket: (1) Classify and balance: Mg + N2 -> Mg3N2. (2) Predict the products and balance: C2H6 + O2 -> ___. (3) The Regents gas stoves cluster states that 'a student incorrectly identifies the products of the combustion of methane as oxygen and water.' Write the correct products and explain the error using patterns of chemical properties.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a reaction type decision tree: 'How many reactants? How many products? Is O2 a reactant with a hydrocarbon?' with examples for each branch.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the classification practice and product prediction as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and explain how the combustion of different fuels (methane, octane, ethanol) produces different amounts of CO2 per unit of energy, connecting to carbon footprint calculations.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual reaction type chart with diagrams using colored blocks (A + B -> AB for synthesis) and real-world photo examples; bilingual labels.
differentiation.iep: Reduce classification practice from 12 to 8 equations; provide the reaction type patterns on a reference card; allow use of reference card during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the chemistry of fireworks — a celebration of synthesis and combustion reactions used across cultures: invented in China over 1,000 years ago, central to Diwali celebrations in South Asia, used in New Year celebrations worldwide, and integral to Fourth of July traditions. Different metal salts produce different colors (Sr = red, Ba = green, Cu = blue) through synthesis reactions.

Both synthesis and combustion require energy to start, but combustion always involves___ as a reactant, so___. The decomposition of sodium azide produces nitrogen gas, so it is used in airbags because___.

cer.phenomenon: New York State banned gas stoves powered by methane in new residential construction. Methane (CH4) undergoes combustion when burned in a stove. A student incorrectly predicts that the products of methane combustion are oxygen and water.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the correct products of methane combustion are___ and___, not oxygen and water, because combustion reactions follow the pattern___.
cer.evidence_source: Write the balanced equation for the combustion of methane. Use patterns of chemical properties (combustion always produces CO2 and H2O) to correct the student's error.
cer.reasoning_frame: Combustion reactions always involve a hydrocarbon reacting with___ to produce___ and___. Methane is a hydrocarbon (CH4), so: CH4 + 2O2 ->___. The student's error was predicting___ as a product, but oxygen is actually a___ in combustion, not a product. This matters environmentally because___ is a greenhouse gas.

lessons.title: Single and Double Replacement Reactions (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: classify reactions as single or double replacement, use the activity series to predict whether a single replacement reaction will occur, and use solubility rules to predict precipitates in double replacement reactions
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about switching partners in a dance or trading cards. When does a trade happen, and when does someone refuse? What determines whether a trade is worth it?
lessons.do_now: Prediction: If you place a piece of zinc metal into a solution of copper sulfate (CuSO4, blue solution), what do you think will happen? Will the zinc react? Will anything change color? Draw or describe your prediction.
materials: Activity series reference table (printed and laminated)
Zinc metal strips and copper sulfate solution (for demo or student lab)
Test tubes and solutions for double replacement demo (NaCl + AgNO3)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Single and Double Replacement Reactions. Demo: Place a strip of zinc into copper sulfate solution. Within minutes, students see the zinc become coated with reddish-brown copper and the blue solution begins to fade. Ask: What happened? The zinc 'replaced' the copper in the solution. Zinc is more reactive than copper — it is higher on the activity series. But what if we placed copper into zinc sulfate solution? (Nothing happens — copper is less reactive.)

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Single and Double Replacement Reactions. Two-part exploration. Part A — Single replacement: Students use the activity series to predict whether 6 single replacement reactions will occur. For those that do, they write balanced equations. Key rule: a metal will replace a less active metal in solution; a metal will replace hydrogen from an acid if it is above hydrogen on the activity series. Part B — Double replacement: Teacher demos NaCl + AgNO3 -> AgCl (white precipitate) + NaNO3. Students use solubility rules to identify the precipitate. They practice predicting products and identifying precipitates for 4 additional reactions.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Single and Double Replacement Reactions. Teacher formalizes: Single replacement (A + BC -> AC + B): an element replaces another in a compound; use the activity series to determine if the reaction occurs. Double replacement (AB + CD -> AD + CB): ions in two compounds exchange partners; a reaction occurs if one product is an insoluble precipitate (check solubility rules), a gas, or water. Review how to read the activity series and solubility rules from the reference table.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Single and Double Replacement Reactions. Predict and classify: Students receive 8 potential reactions. For each, they must: (1) classify the expected reaction type (single or double replacement), (2) predict whether the reaction will occur (using activity series or solubility rules), (3) if it occurs, write and balance the equation and identify any precipitate. Includes 'no reaction' cases to reinforce that not all mixed substances react.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Single and Double Replacement Reactions. Exit ticket: (1) Will magnesium react with hydrochloric acid? Use the activity series to justify your answer and write the balanced equation if it occurs. (2) Predict the products when solutions of sodium sulfate and barium chloride are mixed. Use solubility rules to identify any precipitate. (3) Classify the reaction: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a highlighted activity series with the most common metals starred; include a decision flowchart: 'Is the single element higher on the activity series than the element it would replace? If yes, reaction occurs.' For double replacement, provide a simplified solubility table.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the reaction prediction practice as designed with reference tables.
differentiation.advanced: Write net ionic equations for the double replacement reactions, identifying spectator ions.
differentiation.ell: Provide visual activity series and solubility rules with color-coded categories; include translated instructions and sentence frames for prediction justifications.
differentiation.iep: Reduce prediction problems from 8 to 5; provide a completed example for each reaction type; allow use of all reference tables during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect to water quality testing in communities: double replacement reactions are the basis of many water tests — adding reagents that form precipitates with specific contaminants (e.g., adding silver nitrate to test for chloride ions, adding barium chloride to test for sulfate ions). Discuss how communities in places like Flint, Michigan, used these chemistry principles to independently verify lead contamination when official reports were inaccurate.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'activity series': Zinc reacted with copper sulfate solution because___. Copper is below zinc on the activity series, but if we placed copper in zinc sulfate solution, no reaction would occur because___. The activity series ranks metals by their reactivity, so a more active metal will___.

cer.phenomenon: A student places a copper penny into a clear solution of silver nitrate (AgNO3). After 24 hours, the penny is covered with shiny silver crystals and the solution has turned blue. The student places another copper penny into zinc nitrate solution and observes no change after 24 hours.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that copper reacted with silver nitrate but not with zinc nitrate because of its position on the activity series:___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the activity series to compare the positions of copper, silver, and zinc, and explain why one reaction occurred and the other did not.
cer.reasoning_frame: On the activity series, the order from most to least active is: Zn > Cu > Ag. Copper replaced silver because copper is___ the activity series than silver. However, copper did not replace zinc because copper is___ the activity series than zinc. The blue color appeared because___, and the silver crystals formed because___.

lessons.title: Mole Ratios and Introduction to Stoichiometry (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: interpret the coefficients in a balanced equation as mole ratios and use them to calculate the amount of product formed from a given amount of reactant
lessons.circle_prompt: If a recipe for 12 cookies calls for 2 eggs and 3 cups of flour, how many eggs do you need for 36 cookies? What mathematical relationship did you just use?
lessons.do_now: The balanced equation for the formation of water is: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. According to this equation, how many molecules of hydrogen react with each molecule of oxygen? If you had 6 molecules of H2, how many molecules of O2 would you need? How many molecules of H2O would form?
materials: Stoichiometry road map (printed — showing moles A -> mole ratio -> moles B)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Mole Ratios and Introduction to Stoichiometry. Recipe analogy: Show a recipe for s'mores: 1 chocolate bar + 2 graham crackers + 1 marshmallow = 1 s'more. If you have 10 chocolate bars, how many graham crackers do you need? How many s'mores can you make? The ratio (1:2:1:1) is fixed by the 'recipe.' In chemistry, the balanced equation IS the recipe, and the coefficients give the ratio.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Mole Ratios and Introduction to Stoichiometry. Students practice reading mole ratios from 5 balanced equations. For each equation, they write all possible mole ratios. Example: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O gives ratios of 2 mol H2 : 1 mol O2, 2 mol H2 : 2 mol H2O, 1 mol O2 : 2 mol H2O. Then they use these ratios to solve basic mole-to-mole problems: 'If 4.0 moles of H2 react, how many moles of H2O are produced?'

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Mole Ratios and Introduction to Stoichiometry. Teacher introduces stoichiometry as the quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a balanced equation. The process: (1) Start with the given amount in moles. (2) Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation as a conversion factor. (3) Get the desired amount in moles. Demonstrate with the airbag reaction: 2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2. If we decompose 5.0 moles of NaN3, how many moles of N2 are produced? (5.0 mol NaN3 x 3 mol N2 / 2 mol NaN3 = 7.5 mol N2)

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Mole Ratios and Introduction to Stoichiometry. Practice problems with increasing complexity: (1) Mole-to-mole: How many moles of CO2 are produced from 3.0 moles of C3H8 in combustion? (2) Connect to the blueberry field cluster: In the equation 2S + 3O2 + 6H2O -> 4H3O+ + 2SO4(2-), if 0.50 moles of sulfur react, how many moles of H3O+ are produced? Students set up each problem using dimensional analysis with the mole ratio clearly shown.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Mole Ratios and Introduction to Stoichiometry. Exit ticket: Given the balanced equation: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 (the Haber process for making ammonia). (1) Write the mole ratio of H2 to NH3. (2) How many moles of NH3 are produced from 9.0 moles of H2? (3) If a factory needs to produce 100.0 moles of NH3, how many moles of N2 are required?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a mole ratio setup template: '___ mol given x (___ mol desired / ___ mol given) = ___ mol desired' with the balanced equation written above and arrows connecting coefficients to the conversion factor.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the mole ratio practice and stoichiometry problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Extend to real-world scale: If the Haber process plant produces 1000 kg of NH3 per day, how many kg of N2 and H2 are consumed daily?
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual stoichiometry road map with color-coded arrows; use the recipe analogy consistently with visual examples; bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice problems by half; provide a clear mole ratio template; allow use of a completed example as reference; calculator provided.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the Haber-Bosch process: Fritz Haber (German-Jewish chemist) developed the process for synthesizing ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, which enabled mass production of fertilizers that now feed billions of people. However, the same process was used to manufacture explosives in World War I. This dual-use nature of chemistry raises ethical questions about scientific responsibility. Carl Bosch (German engineer) scaled the process industrially.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'mole ratio': The balanced equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O tells us that 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen because___. The coefficients give the mole ratio but not the mass ratio, so we need to convert between moles and grams because___. If we double the amount of reactants, the amount of products doubles because___.

vocabulary.definition: The calculation of quantities (moles, mass, volume) of reactants and products in a chemical reaction using the balanced equation
The number in front of a formula in a balanced equation that represents the number of moles of that substance

cer.phenomenon: An airbag contains 130 g of sodium azide (NaN3). The decomposition reaction is: 2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2. Engineers need to know exactly how many moles of N2 gas will be produced to ensure the bag inflates to the correct volume.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that 130 g of NaN3 will produce___ moles of N2 gas because___.
cer.evidence_source: Convert grams of NaN3 to moles, then use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to find moles of N2 produced.
cer.reasoning_frame: First, the molar mass of NaN3 is___ g/mol, so 130 g / ___ = ___ moles NaN3. The balanced equation shows a mole ratio of___ mol N2 : ___ mol NaN3. So ___ mol NaN3 x ___/___ = ___ moles N2. This is critical for airbag design because___.

lessons.title: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: perform mass-to-mass stoichiometric calculations by converting grams of a given substance to grams of a desired substance using molar mass and mole ratios
lessons.circle_prompt: When you buy ingredients for a recipe, you measure in grams or cups — not in 'number of molecules.' How do we connect what we measure on a scale to what happens between atoms?
lessons.do_now: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, if you start with 4.0 g of H2, how many grams of water will be produced? Think about what steps you need: grams -> moles -> mole ratio -> moles -> grams. Set up the road map.
materials: Stoichiometry road map poster (grams -> moles -> mole ratio -> moles -> grams)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry. Connect to the anchoring phenomenon: The airbag contains 130 g of NaN3. We calculated moles of N2 last lesson. But the engineer needs to know the mass of nitrogen gas produced (to calculate volume using gas laws). Today we complete the full calculation: grams of reactant -> grams of product. This is the central skill of stoichiometry.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry. Students solve the airbag problem end-to-end: 130 g NaN3 -> moles NaN3 -> moles N2 -> grams N2. Then they practice with 3 additional problems of increasing difficulty: (1) How many grams of iron are produced from 100.0 g of Fe2O3 in a thermite reaction? (2) How many grams of CO2 are produced when 50.0 g of propane (C3H8) undergoes combustion? (3) Connect to the Regents smartphone cluster: How many grams of Al2O3 are needed to produce 10.32 g of aluminum?

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry. Teacher reviews the complete stoichiometry road map: Grams A -> (divide by molar mass A) -> Moles A -> (multiply by mole ratio B/A) -> Moles B -> (multiply by molar mass B) -> Grams B. Emphasize that this can be written as one continuous dimensional analysis chain. Work through the smartphone aluminum problem step by step, showing units cancellation throughout.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry. Multi-step application problems: (1) A bakery uses 500 g of baking soda (NaHCO3) in a recipe. When it decomposes during baking (2NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2), what mass of CO2 gas makes the bread rise? (2) Reverse problem: How many grams of aluminum must be used to produce 50.0 g of aluminum oxide in the reaction 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry. Exit ticket: The Haber process: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. (1) How many grams of NH3 can be produced from 28.0 g of N2? (2) How many grams of H2 are needed to react completely with 28.0 g of N2? (3) Verify conservation of mass: add the mass of reactants and compare to the mass of products.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a dimensional analysis template with blanks for each conversion: '___ g A x (1 mol A / ___ g A) x (___ mol B / ___ mol A) x (___ g B / 1 mol B) = ___ g B'; include a completed example next to the template.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the mass-to-mass practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Solve reverse-engineering problems: Given the mass of a product, determine the minimum mass of each reactant needed (connecting to industrial chemistry).
differentiation.ell: Provide a color-coded road map with each step in a different color matching the dimensional analysis template; include bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice to 2 problems; provide a completed dimensional analysis example as a reference; break each problem into 3 numbered steps (grams to moles, mole ratio, moles to grams); allow calculator and all reference materials.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect to the Regents smartphone chemistry cluster: Question 3 asks students to 'construct a mathematical representation and calculate the number of grams of aluminum oxide required to produce the aluminum necessary to manufacture one smartphone.' This is exactly a mass-to-mass stoichiometry problem. Discuss how these calculations scale up to industrial chemistry in factories worldwide.

The mole ratio connects reactants to products, so the calculation goes grams -> moles -> mole ratio -> moles -> grams because___. Engineers need stoichiometry to design airbags because___.

cer.phenomenon: A popular smartphone requires 10.32 g of aluminum. The aluminum is extracted from aluminum oxide (Al2O3) using the reaction: 2Al2O3 + 3C -> 4Al + 3CO2. The smartphone manufacturer needs to determine how much aluminum oxide ore to order.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that___ grams of Al2O3 are needed to produce 10.32 g of aluminum for one smartphone because___.
cer.evidence_source: Set up and solve the mass-to-mass stoichiometry problem using the balanced equation, molar masses, and mole ratios. Show all steps of dimensional analysis.
cer.reasoning_frame: Step 1: 10.32 g Al / ___ g/mol = ___ mol Al. Step 2: ___ mol Al x ___ mol Al2O3 / ___ mol Al = ___ mol Al2O3. Step 3: ___ mol Al2O3 x ___ g/mol = ___ g Al2O3. Therefore, the manufacturer needs___ g of aluminum oxide per smartphone, which demonstrates that stoichiometry is essential for___.

lessons.title: Limiting Reagent and Excess Reagent (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: identify the limiting reagent in a chemical reaction and calculate the maximum amount of product that can be formed
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever run out of one ingredient while cooking and had leftovers of another? What determined when you had to stop?
lessons.do_now: You have 10 slices of bread and 3 slices of cheese. Each sandwich requires 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. How many sandwiches can you make? What runs out first? What is left over?
materials: Colored blocks or beads for physical limiting reagent simulation

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Limiting Reagent and Excess Reagent. S'mores factory simulation: Give each group 8 graham crackers, 3 marshmallows, and 5 chocolate bars. The recipe: 2 graham crackers + 1 marshmallow + 1 chocolate = 1 s'more. Which ingredient limits production? How many s'mores can they make? What is left over? The limiting ingredient is the 'limiting reagent' in chemistry.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Limiting Reagent and Excess Reagent. Students solve the limiting reagent problem systematically: Given the reaction 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, if you have 5.0 moles of H2 and 3.0 moles of O2, which is the limiting reagent? Method: Calculate how much product each reactant could make separately. Whichever makes LESS product is the limiting reagent. H2: 5.0 mol x (2 mol H2O / 2 mol H2) = 5.0 mol H2O. O2: 3.0 mol x (2 mol H2O / 1 mol O2) = 6.0 mol H2O. H2 is limiting (makes less product). Students practice with 3 additional mole-based problems.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Limiting Reagent and Excess Reagent. Teacher formalizes the limiting reagent concept: The limiting reagent is consumed first and determines the maximum amount of product. The excess reagent is left over. Two methods to identify: (1) Calculate moles of product from each reactant — the smaller value indicates the limiting reagent. (2) Divide moles of each reactant by its coefficient — the smallest ratio is the limiting reagent. Demonstrate mass-to-mass limiting reagent problem: If 10.0 g of Zn reacts with 15.0 g of HCl (Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2), find the limiting reagent and the mass of H2 produced.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Limiting Reagent and Excess Reagent. Application problems: (1) In the airbag reaction (2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2), there is only one reactant so there is no limiting reagent — all NaN3 is consumed. But in the aluminum extraction (2Al2O3 + 3C -> 4Al + 3CO2), if a factory has 500 g of Al2O3 and 100 g of C, which is limiting? How much aluminum is produced? cer.phenomenon: A chemistry student mixes 20.0 g of iron filings with 20.0 g of sulfur powder and heats the mixture. The reaction is: Fe + S -> FeS. After the reaction, some yellow sulfur powder is visible in the crucible, but no unreacted iron remains.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that iron is the limiting reagent and sulfur is the excess reagent because___.
cer.evidence_source: Convert both reactants to moles, compare using the 1:1 mole ratio, and identify which is consumed first. Calculate the mass of excess sulfur remaining.
cer.reasoning_frame: 20.0 g Fe / ___ g/mol = ___ mol Fe. 20.0 g S / ___ g/mol = ___ mol S. The 1:1 ratio requires equal moles, but we have more moles of___ than___. So___ is limiting. The excess sulfur remaining is: ___ mol excess x ___ g/mol = ___ g. This explains the visual observation of leftover yellow sulfur because___.

lessons.title: Percent Yield (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: calculate the theoretical yield, actual yield, and percent yield of a chemical reaction and explain why actual yield is often less than theoretical yield
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a goal you set for yourself — how close did you get to achieving 100% of it? What factors prevented you from reaching the full goal?
lessons.do_now: A recipe says it makes 24 cookies, but you only got 20. What is your 'percent yield'? (20/24 x 100% = 83.3%) Why might you get fewer cookies than expected?

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Percent Yield. Ask: If stoichiometry tells us exactly how much product should form, do real reactions always produce exactly that amount? Show data from a class lab: the theoretical yield of a precipitate was 5.00 g, but students obtained amounts ranging from 3.8 g to 4.7 g. Why? Sources of error: incomplete reactions, side reactions, loss during transfer, impure reagents. The actual amount obtained is called actual yield.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Percent Yield. Students practice with 4 percent yield problems: Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%. (1) A student calculates a theoretical yield of 15.0 g and obtains 12.6 g. What is the percent yield? (2) If the theoretical yield of iron from a reaction is 100.0 g and the percent yield is 85%, what mass of iron was actually obtained? (3) Reverse: If 8.0 g of product was obtained and the percent yield was 80%, what was the theoretical yield?

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Percent Yield. Teacher defines the three yields: Theoretical yield = maximum product possible from stoichiometry (always calculated). Actual yield = amount actually obtained in the lab (always measured). Percent yield = (actual/theoretical) x 100%. Discuss why percent yield is never over 100% in a properly conducted experiment (if it is, something is wrong — impurity, measurement error). Discuss industrial significance: pharmaceutical companies aim for high percent yields to minimize waste and cost.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Percent Yield. Full stoichiometry-to-percent-yield problem: When 15.0 g of zinc reacts with excess hydrochloric acid (Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2), 0.38 g of hydrogen gas is collected. (1) Calculate the theoretical yield of H2. (2) Calculate the percent yield. (3) Give two reasons why the actual yield might be less than theoretical.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Percent Yield. Exit ticket: In the reaction 2Al + 3CuSO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + 3Cu, a student starts with 5.40 g of aluminum and excess CuSO4. (1) Calculate the theoretical yield of copper. (2) The student actually obtains 17.5 g of copper. Calculate the percent yield. (3) List two factors that could account for the difference between theoretical and actual yield.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a percent yield formula card and a step-by-step template: 'Step 1: Calculate theoretical yield using stoichiometry. Step 2: Record actual yield from lab. Step 3: Divide actual by theoretical and multiply by 100%.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the percent yield practice and full stoichiometry problem as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research industrial percent yields for common processes (Haber process ~15%, aspirin synthesis ~85%) and discuss how engineers improve percent yield through temperature, pressure, and catalyst optimization.
differentiation.ell: Provide the percent yield formula with visual arrow diagrams showing the relationship between the three yields; include bilingual word problems with key vocabulary highlighted.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice to 2 problems; provide a completed stoichiometry example showing how to find theoretical yield; allow use of all reference materials during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how percent yield impacts the pharmaceutical industry and access to medication worldwide. A low percent yield means more raw materials are needed, increasing cost and environmental impact. Highlight the work of chemists in developing countries who optimize reaction conditions to produce medications more efficiently and affordably — making life-saving drugs accessible to more people.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'percent yield': The actual yield is usually less than the theoretical yield because___. A percent yield of 100% would mean the reaction was perfect, but this rarely happens because___. Pharmaceutical companies invest in research to increase percent yield, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The maximum amount of product that can be formed from given amounts of reactants, calculated using stoichiometry
The ratio of actual yield to theoretical yield, expressed as a percentage: (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%

cer.phenomenon: A pharmaceutical company produces aspirin (C9H8O4) by reacting salicylic acid (C7H6O3) with acetic anhydride (C4H6O3): C7H6O3 + C4H6O3 -> C9H8O4 + C2H4O2. Starting with 100.0 g of salicylic acid and excess acetic anhydride, the company obtains 115.2 g of aspirin.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the percent yield of this aspirin synthesis is___%, which means the reaction was___% efficient.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the theoretical yield of aspirin from 100.0 g of salicylic acid using stoichiometry, then calculate the percent yield using the actual yield of 115.2 g.
cer.reasoning_frame: Theoretical yield: 100.0 g C7H6O3 / ___ g/mol = ___ mol x (1 mol aspirin / 1 mol salicylic acid) x ___ g/mol = ___ g aspirin. Percent yield = 115.2 / ___ x 100% = ___%. The reaction achieved___% of the theoretical maximum, and the remaining___% was lost due to___.

lessons.title: Gas Stoichiometry Introduction (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: use the molar volume of a gas at STP (22.4 L/mol) to convert between moles and liters in stoichiometric calculations involving gases
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about blowing up a balloon. How much air does it take to fill it? Is there a way to predict exactly how big a balloon will get from a chemical reaction?
lessons.do_now: The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide produces oxygen gas: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2. If 1.0 mole of O2 is produced, the gas occupies 22.4 liters at standard temperature and pressure (STP: 0 degrees C, 1 atm). How many liters would 2.0 moles of O2 occupy?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Molar volume reference card (22.4 L/mol at STP)
Extended stoichiometry road map poster (adding liters)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Gas Stoichiometry Introduction. Return to the airbag phenomenon: We calculated the moles and grams of N2 gas produced. But the engineer needs to know the VOLUME of the gas — will it fill the airbag? At STP, one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 liters. This is the molar volume. It is the same for ALL gases at STP because gas particles are so far apart that their size does not matter. Today we add volume to our stoichiometry road map.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Gas Stoichiometry Introduction. Students practice basic mole-to-volume and volume-to-mole conversions at STP: (1) How many liters does 3.5 moles of N2 occupy at STP? (2) How many moles of gas are in 44.8 L at STP? Then integrate into stoichiometry: (3) In the airbag reaction (2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2), if 2.0 moles of NaN3 decompose, what volume of N2 is produced at STP? (4) What volume of O2 at STP is needed to completely combust 5.0 g of methane?

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Gas Stoichiometry Introduction. Teacher extends the stoichiometry road map: Grams <-> Moles <-> Mole Ratio <-> Moles <-> Grams, with a new branch: Moles <-> Liters (at STP, multiply by 22.4 L/mol). Important: 22.4 L/mol is only valid at STP. Preview that the combined gas law (Unit 6+) allows calculations at other conditions. Work through a complete problem: How many liters of CO2 at STP are produced by burning 100.0 g of octane (C8H18)?

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Gas Stoichiometry Introduction. Real-world application: (1) Complete the airbag problem end-to-end: 130 g NaN3 -> moles NaN3 -> moles N2 -> liters N2 at STP. Is this enough to fill a typical airbag (~60 L)? (Note: airbags deploy at higher temperatures, so the actual volume is larger — preview of gas laws.) (2) A car engine burns 1.00 kg of octane per trip. What volume of CO2 gas at STP is released into the atmosphere?

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Gas Stoichiometry Introduction. Exit ticket: (1) What is the volume of 0.500 moles of any gas at STP? (2) In the reaction CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, what volume of CO2 at STP is produced from the decomposition of 25.0 g of calcium carbonate? (3) Why does molar volume work the same for all gases at STP, regardless of the gas's identity?

differentiation.approaching: Provide the extended road map with the volume branch clearly marked and the conversion factor (22.4 L/mol) pre-printed; include a step-by-step template for gas stoichiometry problems.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the gas stoichiometry practice and application problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the volume of gas produced at non-STP conditions using the ideal gas law (PV = nRT) for one problem, previewing Unit 6 content.
differentiation.ell: Provide the extended road map with color-coded branches (blue for mass, green for volume, red for particles); bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice to 2 problems; provide a completed example showing the full grams-to-liters pathway; allow use of all reference materials.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect to environmental science: The volume of greenhouse gases released by burning fossil fuels can be calculated using gas stoichiometry. Discuss how these calculations inform climate policy — for example, calculating that burning 1 gallon of gasoline produces approximately 8,887 grams of CO2, which occupies about 4,540 liters at STP. This connects chemistry to environmental justice and the disproportionate impact of air pollution on low-income communities near highways and industrial areas.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'molar volume': At STP, one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 liters because___. Hydrogen gas and carbon dioxide gas have very different molar masses, but one mole of each occupies the same volume at STP because___. We can calculate the volume of gas produced by a reaction, so engineers use stoichiometry to___.

elaborate.description: CER activity connecting evidence to claims about the topic. Building on previous days: Real-world application: (1) Complete the airbag problem end-to-end: 130 g NaN3 -> moles NaN3 -> moles N2 -> liters N2 at STP. Is this enough to fill a typical airbag (~60 L)? (Note: airbags deploy at higher temperatures, so the actual volume is larger — preview of gas laws.) (2) A car engine burns 1.00 kg of octane per trip. What volume of CO2 gas at STP is released into the atmosphere?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket with application-level problems requiring multi-step reasoning. Building on previous days: Exit ticket: (1) What is the volume of 0.500 moles of any gas at STP? (2) In the reaction CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, what volume of CO2 at STP is produced from the decomposition of 25.0 g of calcium carbonate? (3) Why does molar volume work the same for all gases at STP, regardless of the gas's identity?

differentiation.approaching: Review key concepts from the full sequence before assessment. Provide the extended road map with the volume branch clearly marked and the conversion factor (22.4 L/mol) pre-printed; include a step-by-step template for gas stoichiometry problems.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the gas stoichiometry practice and application problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Complete extension challenge connecting to real-world applications. Calculate the volume of gas produced at non-STP conditions using the ideal gas law (PV = nRT) for one problem, previewing Unit 6 content.
differentiation.ell: Provide the extended road map with color-coded branches (blue for mass, green for volume, red for particles); bilingual problem setups.
differentiation.iep: Reduce practice to 2 problems; provide a completed example showing the full grams-to-liters pathway; allow use of all reference materials.

Discuss how these calculations inform climate policy — for example, calculating that burning 1 gallon of gasoline produces approximately 8,887 grams of CO2, which occupies about 4,540 liters at STP. This connects chemistry to environmental justice and the disproportionate impact of air pollution on low-income communities near highways and industrial areas.

cer.phenomenon: A car airbag must inflate to approximately 60 liters of N2 gas in under 40 milliseconds to protect the driver during a collision. The reaction is: 2NaN3 -> 2Na + 3N2. Engineers need to determine exactly how much sodium azide to include in the airbag module.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the airbag needs approximately___ grams of NaN3 to produce 60 liters of N2 at STP because___.
cer.evidence_source: Work backwards from 60 L of N2 at STP to moles of N2, then use mole ratios to find moles of NaN3, and finally convert to grams.
cer.reasoning_frame: 60 L N2 / 22.4 L/mol = ___ mol N2. Using the mole ratio: ___ mol N2 x (2 mol NaN3 / 3 mol N2) = ___ mol NaN3. Converting to grams: ___ mol x ___ g/mol = ___ g NaN3. Note: In reality, the gas is produced at a much higher temperature than STP, so___, meaning less NaN3 is actually needed because___.

This demonstrates the full power of stoichiometry.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Stoichiometry Unit Review and Regents Exam Preparation. Station rotation review (4 stations, 3 min each): Station 1 — Balance 4 equations and classify by reaction type. Station 2 — Mole-to-mole stoichiometry (2 problems). explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Stoichiometry Unit Review and Regents Exam Preparation. Brief whole-class review of key strategies for Regents-style question clusters: (1) Read the entire cluster introduction and all stimuli before answering. (2) For calculation questions, show all work with units. (3) For constructed-response questions, use CER format. (4) Look for conservation of mass as a unifying theme. Address top student questions.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Stoichiometry Unit Review and Regents Exam Preparation. Questions integrate reaction identification, equation balancing, stoichiometric calculations, conservation of mass evidence, and a constructed-response explanation.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Stoichiometry Unit Review and Regents Exam Preparation. Cumulative exit ticket: (1) Balance: _Fe + _H2SO4 -> _FeSO4 + _H2. (2) If 25.0 g of iron reacts with excess sulfuric acid, how many grams of hydrogen gas are produced? (3) If only 0.75 g of hydrogen is actually collected, what is the percent yield? (4) Cite numerical evidence from the balanced equation to demonstrate that atoms, and therefore mass, are conserved. (5) Classify the reaction type.

differentiation.on_level: Complete all station rotation problems and the practice cluster as designed.

differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual reference sheets and sentence frames for constructed-response questions; include visual road maps at each station.
differentiation.iep: Reduce cumulative exit ticket to 3 questions; provide all reference materials; allow extended time; break multi-step problems into guided steps.

lessons.crse_connection: Culminating CRSE connection: Discuss how the skills learned in this unit — balancing equations, stoichiometric calculations, understanding reaction types — are used by environmental scientists to monitor air and water quality, by agricultural chemists to optimize fertilizer use, and by public health officials to ensure clean drinking water. These are tools of empowerment that enable citizens to advocate for their communities using quantitative evidence, as demonstrated in Flint, Michigan, and communities around the world.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion spanning the entire unit. Start with: 'Reactions transform matter.' Students expand: 'Chemical reactions transform matter by rearranging atoms from reactants into products in predictable patterns that can be represented by balanced equations, quantified through stoichiometric calculations using mole ratios, and verified by the Law of Conservation of Mass, which states that the total mass and number of each type of atom remain constant throughout any chemical change.'

vocabulary.definition: The quantitative study of reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation, using mole ratios to calculate amounts of substances

cer.phenomenon: A community garden uses ammonium sulfate ((NH4)2SO4) as a fertilizer. The garden coordinator purchases a 50.0 kg bag and wants to know how many moles of nitrogen atoms the garden will receive, and what mass of nitrogen is in the bag.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that 50.0 kg of ammonium sulfate contains___ moles of nitrogen atoms and___ kg of nitrogen because___.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the molar mass of (NH4)2SO4, convert 50.0 kg to moles, and use the formula to determine the number of moles and mass of nitrogen. Note that each formula unit contains 2 nitrogen atoms.
cer.reasoning_frame: The molar mass of (NH4)2SO4 is___ g/mol. 50,000 g / ___ = ___ moles of (NH4)2SO4. Each formula unit contains___ nitrogen atoms, so ___ x 2 = ___ moles of nitrogen atoms. Mass of nitrogen: ___ mol x 14.01 g/mol = ___ g = ___ kg. The percent nitrogen is___%, which matches the fertilizer label if it reads '___-0-0.' This calculation helps the coordinator determine how much fertilizer to apply because___.

units.title: Energy in Chemical Reactions
units.anchoring_phenomenon: A disposable hand warmer heats up when you open the package and expose it to air, but an instant cold pack gets cold when you squeeze it and break the inner pouch. Both involve chemical reactions — why does one release heat while the other absorbs it?
essential_questions: How can we measure and predict the energy changes that occur during chemical reactions?
What role does bond breaking and bond forming play in determining whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic?
How do potential energy diagrams help us visualize the energy changes in a reaction?
units.crse_theme: Students examine how energy transformations in chemical reactions connect to cultural practices and real-world applications, including traditional metallurgy in West Africa (iron smelting requiring understanding of exothermic reactions), the chemistry of cooking across cultures, and the environmental justice implications of industrial energy use in communities of color.

formative: Exit tickets on exothermic vs. endothermic classification
summative: Unit 6 Exam: Energy in Chemical Reactions

investigations: Investigation 6: Calorimetry — Measuring the Heat of Dissolution

lessons.title: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: classify a chemical reaction as exothermic or endothermic based on temperature change data and explain the direction of energy flow between the system and surroundings
lessons.circle_prompt: What is the hottest or coldest thing you have ever touched? What happened to your body when you touched it?
lessons.do_now: A student mixes baking soda and vinegar in a beaker. The temperature drops 5 degrees C. Is this reaction exothermic or endothermic? How do you know?
materials: Thermometers or temperature probes (1 per group)
Commercial hand warmer and cold pack (1 each for demo)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions. Pass around an activated hand warmer and an activated cold pack. Students touch both and record the temperature sensation. Ask: Both involve chemicals reacting — why does one feel hot and the other cold? Where is the energy coming from or going to? Students write initial hypotheses in notebooks.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions. In pairs, students conduct two mini-experiments. Experiment A: Dissolve calcium chloride in water and record the temperature change every 30 seconds for 3 minutes. Experiment B: Dissolve ammonium nitrate in water and record temperature changes on the same schedule. Students graph both data sets on the same axes using different colors.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions. Teacher defines system (the chemicals reacting) and surroundings (everything else, including the water and cup). In exothermic reactions, energy flows from system to surroundings, so surroundings get warmer. In endothermic reactions, energy flows from surroundings to system, so surroundings get cooler. Students label their graphs and complete an energy flow diagram showing arrows for each reaction type.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions. Students classify five real-world processes as exothermic or endothermic: combustion of gasoline, photosynthesis, cooking an egg, ice melting, and rusting of iron. For each, they identify the system and surroundings and draw the energy flow arrow.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions. Exit ticket: A student dissolves a mystery salt in water and the temperature rises from 22 degrees C to 35 degrees C. (1) Is this process exothermic or endothermic? (2) Did the system release or absorb energy? (3) Draw an energy flow diagram with labeled arrows.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-drawn energy flow diagram template with labeled boxes for system and surroundings; include sentence starters for classifying reactions: 'This reaction is ___ because the temperature of the surroundings ___.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the two dissolution experiments and classification activity as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and explain why ammonium nitrate cold packs are used in first aid instead of ice, and calculate which provides more cooling per gram using provided enthalpy data.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual vocabulary card with visual energy flow diagrams labeled in English and Spanish; use color-coding (red for exothermic, blue for endothermic) consistently throughout materials.
differentiation.iep: Pre-formatted data table with time intervals already filled in; partner with a peer for temperature readings; reduce classification problems from five to three.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the chemistry of traditional cooking methods across cultures — tandoori ovens (sustained exothermic combustion), Korean ondol floor heating (using combustion heat transfer), and the endothermic process of evaporative cooling used in Nigerian clay pot refrigerators (zeer pots). Highlight how communities engineered energy solutions long before formal thermochemistry.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'exothermic reaction': The hand warmer feels hot because___. Both the hand warmer and the cold pack involve chemical reactions, but___. The temperature of the surroundings increased, so we know the reaction is___.

vocabulary.definition: A process that releases energy to the surroundings, usually observed as an increase in temperature
The specific part of the universe being studied, typically the reactants and products in a chemical reaction
The transfer of thermal energy between objects at different temperatures

cer.phenomenon: A camping supply company sells two products: a hand warmer that uses iron powder exposed to air, and a cold pack that contains ammonium nitrate and water separated by a thin membrane. When you squeeze the cold pack, the membrane breaks and the pack gets very cold.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the hand warmer undergoes a(n) ___ reaction and the cold pack undergoes a(n) ___ reaction because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use temperature data from the dissolution experiments and energy flow diagrams to support your classification of each product.
cer.reasoning_frame: The hand warmer releases energy to the surroundings because___. This is consistent with a(n) ___ reaction where the energy of the products is ___ than the energy of the reactants. The cold pack, however,___ because___.

lessons.title: Potential Energy Diagrams and Activation Energy (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: draw and interpret a potential energy diagram for exothermic and endothermic reactions, labeling reactants, products, activation energy, and enthalpy change
lessons.circle_prompt: Think of something that needed a push to get started but then kept going on its own — like pushing a car downhill. What was the initial push?
lessons.do_now: A match will not light on its own, but once you strike it, it burns completely. Why does the match need that initial strike if burning releases energy?
materials: Potential energy diagram template (printed, 2 per student)
PE diagram card sorting activity (set of 12 cards per group)
PhET simulation: 'Reactions & Rates' (projected or on devices)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Potential Energy Diagrams and Activation Energy. Analogy: Show an image of a person pushing a boulder up and over a hill. On the other side, the boulder rolls down to a lower elevation. Ask: The boulder ends up lower than where it started — it lost energy overall. But it needed energy to get over the hill first. How is this like a chemical reaction? Students sketch the hill analogy and label it.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Potential Energy Diagrams and Activation Energy. Card sorting: Each group receives 12 cards showing PE diagrams with various features (high activation energy, low activation energy, large exothermic change, small endothermic change, with and without catalysts). Students sort them into categories and identify patterns. Then using the PhET Reactions & Rates simulation, students adjust activation energy and observe how it affects whether reactions proceed.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Potential Energy Diagrams and Activation Energy. Teacher builds a labeled PE diagram step-by-step on the board. Key features: (1) reactant energy level, (2) activated complex at the peak, (3) product energy level, (4) activation energy (Ea) as the difference between reactants and the peak, (5) enthalpy change (delta H) as the difference between reactants and products. Students draw both an exothermic diagram (products lower) and endothermic diagram (products higher) with all labels.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Potential Energy Diagrams and Activation Energy. Students receive a PE diagram showing a reaction with and without a catalyst. They identify how the catalyst changes the diagram (lowers the activation energy peak but does not change delta H). Then they answer: A catalyst speeds up a reaction. Using the diagram, explain why lowering Ea makes the reaction faster. Connect to real-world catalysts: catalytic converters in cars, enzymes in digestion.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Potential Energy Diagrams and Activation Energy. Exit ticket: Given numerical values (reactant PE = 80 kJ, product PE = 30 kJ, activation energy = 60 kJ), students (1) draw a labeled PE diagram, (2) calculate delta H, (3) classify the reaction as exothermic or endothermic, (4) determine the PE of the activated complex.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a PE diagram template with axes pre-labeled and dotted lines showing where to draw reactant and product energy levels; include a step-by-step checklist for labeling each feature.
differentiation.on_level: Complete PE diagram construction and interpretation as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Given a PE diagram for a reversible reaction, students draw the PE diagram for the reverse reaction and compare the activation energies and delta H values for forward and reverse directions.
differentiation.ell: Color-coded PE diagram with a bilingual key (activation energy in red, delta H in blue, labels in English and native language); sentence frames for describing energy changes.
differentiation.iep: Enlarged PE diagram templates; reduce the exit ticket to two parts instead of four; allow use of reference card showing labeled sample diagrams.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the role of catalysts in industrial chemistry and connect to the work of Elinor Ostrom on managing common resources, and the contributions of Gertrude Elion, a Nobel Prize-winning biochemist whose work on enzyme inhibitors (which function by altering activation energy pathways) led to drugs treating leukemia, herpes, and organ transplant rejection. She was initially denied lab positions because of gender discrimination.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: 'Activation energy, the minimum energy required for reactants to form the activated complex and begin reacting, determines how easily a reaction starts.' 'A catalyst, a substance that lowers the activation energy without being consumed in the reaction, increases the reaction rate without changing the overall energy change.'

vocabulary.definition: A graph that shows the energy changes that occur during a chemical reaction, with the reaction pathway on the x-axis and potential energy on the y-axis
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by lowering the activation energy without being consumed or permanently changed

cer.phenomenon: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) decomposes very slowly at room temperature into water and oxygen gas. When a small amount of manganese dioxide (MnO2) is added, the decomposition happens rapidly with visible bubbling, but the MnO2 can be recovered unchanged after the reaction.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that manganese dioxide acts as a ___ in this reaction because___.

lessons.title: Calorimetry and Calculating Heat (q = mCdeltaT) (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: use the equation q = mCdeltaT to calculate the heat absorbed or released during a physical or chemical change and interpret the sign of q
lessons.circle_prompt: What is a food or drink that you eat at a specific temperature — really hot or really cold? Why does the temperature matter for that food?
lessons.do_now: You heat 100 grams of water and 100 grams of iron to the same temperature and then let them cool. Which one cools faster? Why might different materials lose heat at different rates?
materials: Thermometers or digital temperature probes (1 per group)
Metal samples: aluminum, copper, iron (pre-heated in hot water bath)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Calorimetry and Calculating Heat (q = mCdeltaT). Scenario: A lifeguard walks barefoot across a concrete pool deck and then steps onto a metal diving board. Both surfaces are in the same sunlight at the same air temperature. The metal feels much hotter. Ask: If they are at the same temperature, why does the metal feel hotter? Introduce the idea that different materials transfer heat at different rates, which connects to specific heat capacity.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Calorimetry and Calculating Heat (q = mCdeltaT). Calorimetry lab: Each group receives a pre-heated metal sample (identity unknown). They measure the mass of the metal and the mass and initial temperature of water in their calorimeter. They add the hot metal to the cool water, stir gently, and record the final equilibrium temperature. Groups then use q = mCdeltaT to calculate the heat gained by the water and, assuming no heat loss, set this equal to the heat lost by the metal to solve for the specific heat capacity of the unknown metal.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Calorimetry and Calculating Heat (q = mCdeltaT). Teacher formalizes the calorimetry equation: q = mCdeltaT, where q is heat in joules, m is mass in grams, C is specific heat capacity in J/g degrees C, and deltaT is the change in temperature. Key points: positive q means heat is absorbed, negative q means heat is released. In a calorimeter, q(water) = -q(metal). Students compare their calculated specific heat values to a reference table to identify their unknown metal.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Calorimetry and Calculating Heat (q = mCdeltaT). Practice problems: (1) How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 250 g of water from 20 degrees C to 80 degrees C? (2) A 50 g piece of copper (C = 0.385 J/g degrees C) cools from 95 degrees C to 25 degrees C. How much heat did it release? (3) If 5000 J of heat is added to 200 g of an unknown substance and the temperature rises by 12.5 degrees C, what is the specific heat capacity?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Calorimetry and Calculating Heat (q = mCdeltaT). Exit ticket: A student heats 150 g of water in a calorimeter from 22.0 degrees C to 34.5 degrees C by dissolving a salt. (1) Calculate the heat absorbed by the water (C of water = 4.18 J/g degrees C). (2) Was the dissolution exothermic or endothermic? Explain using the sign of q for the salt.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a calorimetry calculation template with the formula written out and blanks for each variable; include a worked example alongside each practice problem.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the calorimetry lab and calculation problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the percent error between experimental specific heat and accepted value; analyze sources of heat loss in the calorimeter and propose design improvements.
differentiation.ell: Provide a formula card with variable definitions in English and native language; use color-coding to match variables in the equation to their positions in the data table.
differentiation.iep: Allow calculator use for all problems; provide pre-organized data tables; reduce practice problems to two; allow extended time on lab calculations.

lessons.crse_connection: Highlight the work of Wilbur Scoville, who developed the Scoville scale for measuring pepper heat using dilution methods, and connect to the chemistry of capsaicin. Discuss how communities in Mexico, India, and West Africa cultivated hot peppers for millennia — the sensation of heat from capsaicin is a chemical interaction with nerve receptors, not an actual temperature change, contrasting perceived heat with measurable heat (q).

Metals feel hotter in the sun than wood at the same temperature, but their actual temperatures are the same, so___. The specific heat capacity of a substance is large, so it takes ___ energy to change its temperature.
