cer.phenomenon: Two students each dissolve a different salt in 100 g of water at 22 degrees C. Student A's solution reaches 35 degrees C. Student B's solution drops to 15 degrees C. Both used the same mass of salt (10 g).
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Student A's salt underwent a(n) ___ dissolution and Student B's salt underwent a(n) ___ dissolution because___.
cer.evidence_source: Calculate q for each student's experiment using q = mCdeltaT and use the sign of q to classify each process.
cer.reasoning_frame: Student A's water temperature ___, meaning the water ___ heat from the dissolving salt. Therefore q for the water is ___ and q for the salt is ___, which means the dissolution is ___. Student B's water temperature ___, so___.

lessons.title: Enthalpy, Bond Energy, and Energy in Reactions (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: explain how breaking bonds requires energy and forming bonds releases energy, and use bond energy data to determine whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about building something and then taking it apart — like a LEGO set or a puzzle. Which takes more effort: putting it together or breaking it apart?
lessons.do_now: In the reaction H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, bonds in H2 and Cl2 must break before new H-Cl bonds can form. If breaking bonds requires energy, where does the energy come from to start the reaction?
materials: Bond energy data table (printed, 1 per student)
Molecular model kits (1 set per group)
Colored pencils (red for energy absorbed, green for energy released)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Enthalpy, Bond Energy, and Energy in Reactions. Molecular model demo: Build H2 and Cl2 molecules using model kits in front of class. Physically pull them apart (break bonds) and say: 'This required energy — I had to do work.' Then connect the atoms into 2 HCl molecules and say: 'Forming new bonds releases energy.' Ask: If the energy released by forming H-Cl bonds is greater than the energy needed to break H-H and Cl-Cl bonds, what happens to the extra energy?

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Enthalpy, Bond Energy, and Energy in Reactions. Using bond energy tables, students work in groups to calculate the total energy required to break all bonds in the reactants and the total energy released by forming all bonds in the products for three reactions: (1) H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, (2) N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, (3) CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. For each, they determine whether the net energy change is positive (endothermic) or negative (exothermic).

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Enthalpy, Bond Energy, and Energy in Reactions. Teacher formalizes: delta H = (energy to break bonds in reactants) - (energy released forming bonds in products). If more energy is released than absorbed, delta H is negative (exothermic). If more energy is absorbed than released, delta H is positive (endothermic). Students create energy bar charts showing energy in vs. energy out for each of their three reactions.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Enthalpy, Bond Energy, and Energy in Reactions. Application: Students examine why combustion reactions (burning fuels) are always exothermic. They compare bond energies in hydrocarbons (C-H and C-C bonds broken) with the very strong bonds formed (C=O in CO2 and O-H in H2O). The strong product bonds release more energy than is needed to break the weaker reactant bonds.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Enthalpy, Bond Energy, and Energy in Reactions. Exit ticket: Given bond energies (H-H = 436 kJ/mol, O=O = 498 kJ/mol, O-H = 463 kJ/mol), calculate delta H for 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Show all work and classify the reaction.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a bond-counting organizer that walks students through each molecule step by step: 'In H2, how many H-H bonds? ___ x ___ kJ = ___ kJ total.' Include a completed example for the first reaction.
differentiation.on_level: Complete bond energy calculations and energy bar charts as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Compare bond energy estimates of delta H to actual experimental delta H values from a reference table and explain why they differ (bond energies are averages, real bonds vary with molecular environment).
differentiation.ell: Provide bond energy vocabulary card with visual diagrams showing bonds breaking (with a '+' energy arrow) and forming (with a '-' energy arrow); sentence frames for explaining calculations.
differentiation.iep: Pre-counted bond inventory for each reaction; reduced number of reactions from three to two; allow partner work for calculations; enlarged bond energy table.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the work of Marie Maynard Daly, the first African American woman to earn a PhD in chemistry (1947, Columbia University). Her research on cholesterol metabolism and the biochemistry of heart attacks involved understanding how bond energies in biological molecules relate to metabolic energy. Also connect to how Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest used controlled burns (exothermic combustion) for land management, demonstrating intuitive understanding of energy release in reactions.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'bond energy': Breaking bonds in the reactants requires energy because___. The reaction releases heat overall, but energy was still needed to break bonds first, so___. The bonds in the products are stronger than the bonds in the reactants, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of energy required to break one mole of a specific bond in a gaseous molecule, measured in kJ/mol
The net energy change in a reaction, equal to energy absorbed by bond breaking minus energy released by bond forming

Molecular model kits (1 set per group)

engage.description: Present a novel scenario that requires synthesis of concepts from Days 1-2. Building on previous days: Molecular model demo: Build H2 and Cl2 molecules using model kits in front of class. Physically pull them apart (break bonds) and say: 'This required energy — I had to do work.' Then connect the atoms into 2 HCl molecules and say: 'Forming new bonds releases energy.' Ask: If the energy released by forming H-Cl bonds is greater than the energy needed to break H-H and Cl-Cl bonds, what happens to the extra energy?

explore.description: CER activity — students construct evidence-based arguments about the topic. Building on previous days: Using bond energy tables, students work in groups to calculate the total energy required to break all bonds in the reactants and the total energy released by forming all bonds in the products for three reactions: (1) H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, (2) N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, (3) CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. For each, they determine whether the net energy change is positive (endothermic) or negative (exothermic).

explain.description: Whole-class discussion of CER responses; address remaining misconceptions. Building on previous days: Teacher formalizes: delta H = (energy to break bonds in reactants) - (energy released forming bonds in products). If more energy is released than absorbed, delta H is negative (exothermic). If more energy is absorbed than released, delta H is positive (endothermic). Students create energy bar charts showing energy in vs. energy out for each of their three reactions.

elaborate.description: Extension or enrichment activity connecting to real-world applications. Building on previous days: Application: Students examine why combustion reactions (burning fuels) are always exothermic. They compare bond energies in hydrocarbons (C-H and C-C bonds broken) with the very strong bonds formed (C=O in CO2 and O-H in H2O). The strong product bonds release more energy than is needed to break the weaker reactant bonds.

differentiation.advanced: Complete extension challenge connecting to real-world applications. Compare bond energy estimates of delta H to actual experimental delta H values from a reference table and explain why they differ (bond energies are averages, real bonds vary with molecular environment).
differentiation.ell: Provide bond energy vocabulary card with visual diagrams showing bonds breaking (with a '+' energy arrow) and forming (with a '-' energy arrow); sentence frames for explaining calculations.
differentiation.iep: Pre-counted bond inventory for each reaction; reduced number of reactions from three to two; allow partner work for calculations; enlarged bond energy table.

cer.claim_starter: I claim that the classmate's statement is incorrect because___.

lessons.title: Hess's Law and Enthalpy Calculations (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: apply Hess's Law to calculate the enthalpy change of a reaction by combining two or more thermochemical equations
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever taken a detour to get somewhere? Did the total distance change depending on the path you took, or was something about the trip the same regardless?
lessons.do_now: The direct flight from New York to Los Angeles is about 3,950 km. If you fly from New York to Chicago (1,150 km) and then Chicago to Los Angeles (2,800 km), the total is 3,950 km. What pattern do you notice? How might this relate to energy in chemical reactions?
materials: Thermochemical equation cards (set of 8 per group for puzzle activity)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Hess's Law and Enthalpy Calculations. Elevation analogy: Show a diagram of a hiker going from point A (sea level) to point B (mountaintop, 2000 m). Path 1 is direct; Path 2 goes through an intermediate valley and then up. Ask: Does the overall elevation change depend on the path? No — it only depends on the starting and ending points. Introduce Hess's Law: the total enthalpy change depends only on the initial and final states, not the pathway.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Hess's Law and Enthalpy Calculations. Puzzle activity: Groups receive thermochemical equation cards and a target reaction. They must arrange and combine the given equations (reversing or multiplying as needed) so they add up to the target reaction. When equations are combined, their delta H values are added. Groups work through two puzzles of increasing difficulty on their whiteboards.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Hess's Law and Enthalpy Calculations. Teacher formalizes the rules of Hess's Law: (1) If a reaction is reversed, the sign of delta H is reversed. (2) If a reaction is multiplied by a coefficient, delta H is multiplied by the same coefficient. (3) When reactions are added, their delta H values are added. Walk through a complete worked example: Calculate delta H for C(s) + 1/2 O2(g) -> CO(g) using the given reactions for C -> CO2 and CO -> CO2.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Hess's Law and Enthalpy Calculations. Students solve two additional Hess's Law problems independently. Problem 1: Calculate delta H for the formation of nitrogen dioxide from nitrogen and oxygen using two step reactions. Problem 2: Use three given thermochemical equations to find delta H for the combustion of ethanol.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Hess's Law and Enthalpy Calculations. Exit ticket: Given two thermochemical equations — (1) S(s) + O2(g) -> SO2(g), delta H = -297 kJ and (2) 2SO2(g) + O2(g) -> 2SO3(g), delta H = -198 kJ — calculate delta H for S(s) + 3/2 O2(g) -> SO3(g). Show all steps.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a step-by-step Hess's Law procedure card: Step 1 — Identify the target reaction. Step 2 — Check if each given reaction needs to be reversed. Step 3 — Check if coefficients need adjusting. Step 4 — Add equations and delta H values. Include a fully worked example alongside.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the puzzle activity and practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Apply Hess's Law to calculate the enthalpy of formation of glucose (C6H12O6) from combustion data and compare to the energy stored in food, calculating how many grams of glucose provide 2000 Calories.
differentiation.ell: Provide thermochemical equation cards with visual molecule diagrams alongside chemical formulas; use color-coded arrows for reversed reactions; bilingual procedure card.
differentiation.iep: Reduce puzzle complexity to single reversal or single multiplication; provide completed first step for each practice problem; allow partner work; extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Germain Hess, a Swiss-Russian chemist who formulated Hess's Law in 1840, and the broader international nature of thermochemistry. Connect to modern applications: Hess's Law is used in food science to calculate the caloric content of complex meals. Explore how different cultural diets (Mediterranean, Japanese, West African) are analyzed using calorimetry and enthalpy calculations for nutritional science.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'Hess's Law': Hess's Law states that enthalpy change is independent of pathway because___. We cannot directly measure the enthalpy change of some reactions, but we can use Hess's Law, so___. The reaction was reversed, so the sign of delta H was___.

vocabulary.definition: The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same regardless of whether the reaction occurs in one step or multiple steps

cer.phenomenon: A scientist wants to determine the enthalpy change for the reaction C(s) + 2H2(g) -> CH4(g), but this reaction does not occur easily in a calorimeter. However, the enthalpies of combustion for carbon, hydrogen, and methane are well known and can be measured accurately.

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Energy in Reactions Review and Performance Task. explain.description: Review solutions as a class. Emphasize: catalysts lower activation energy but do NOT change ΔH or equilibrium position.

units.title: Reaction Rates & Equilibrium
units.anchoring_phenomenon: When you open a bottle of soda, it fizzes vigorously and goes flat over time. But if you recap the bottle tightly, the fizzing slows and eventually seems to stop — even though CO2 is still dissolved in the liquid. Why does the fizzing stop in a sealed bottle?
essential_questions: What conditions must be met for a chemical reaction to occur, and how can we control how fast it happens?
What does it mean for a chemical system to be in equilibrium, and how do changes in conditions shift the equilibrium?
How can we use equilibrium expressions to predict the relative amounts of reactants and products?
units.crse_theme: Students explore how reaction rates and equilibrium are embedded in cultural food practices — fermentation in West African, Korean, and Latin American cuisines, tea brewing across Asian cultures, and yogurt-making in Middle Eastern and South Asian traditions. Students also examine how Le Chatelier's principle applies to industrial chemistry and environmental justice issues like acid rain formation.

lessons.title: Collision Theory and Factors Affecting Reaction Rate (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: explain how collision theory accounts for reaction rates and predict how changing temperature, concentration, surface area, or adding a catalyst will affect the rate of a reaction
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a crowd of people trying to get through a doorway. What conditions make it faster or slower for everyone to get through?
lessons.do_now: A student drops a whole Alka-Seltzer tablet into cold water and a crushed tablet into hot water. Which setup will react faster? List as many reasons as you can.
materials: Alka-Seltzer tablets (whole and crushed, 8 per group)
Ice, room temperature water, and hot water
Hydrochloric acid at two concentrations: 0.5 M and 2.0 M (for teacher demo)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Collision Theory and Factors Affecting Reaction Rate. Show a time-lapse video of iron rusting (very slow reaction) next to a video of an explosion (very fast reaction). Ask: Both are chemical reactions. What makes one take years and the other a fraction of a second? Students brainstorm factors that might affect how fast a reaction occurs and share with the class.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Collision Theory and Factors Affecting Reaction Rate. Controlled experiment: Groups test how four factors affect the rate of Alka-Seltzer dissolving in water. Each group tests one variable while controlling others: (1) Temperature — cold vs. hot water with whole tablets; (2) Surface area — whole vs. crushed tablet in room-temp water; (3) Concentration — the teacher demos HCl at 0.5 M vs. 2.0 M reacting with zinc metal; (4) Catalyst — not tested directly but discussed. Groups record time to complete dissolution and calculate relative rates.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Collision Theory and Factors Affecting Reaction Rate. Teacher introduces collision theory: for a reaction to occur, particles must (1) collide, (2) with sufficient energy (greater than or equal to activation energy), and (3) with proper orientation. Connect each factor to the theory: Higher temperature means faster particles and more energetic collisions. Higher concentration means more particles in the same space, so more frequent collisions. Greater surface area exposes more particles to collide. Catalysts lower Ea so more collisions have sufficient energy.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Collision Theory and Factors Affecting Reaction Rate. Students analyze two Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves — one at low temperature and one at high temperature. They shade the area representing particles with energy greater than Ea and explain why increasing temperature dramatically increases reaction rate. They then sketch what happens when a catalyst lowers Ea on the same curve.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Collision Theory and Factors Affecting Reaction Rate. Exit ticket: A factory produces ammonia gas. The plant manager wants to speed up the reaction. For each proposed change (raising temperature, increasing pressure/concentration of reactants, adding a catalyst), explain using collision theory WHY each would increase the rate.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a collision theory reference card with diagrams showing effective vs. ineffective collisions; pre-formatted data table for the Alka-Seltzer experiment with column headers filled in.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the experimental investigation and collision theory analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Design an additional experiment to quantify the relationship between temperature and rate — predict whether doubling temperature doubles the rate, and justify using collision theory and the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
differentiation.ell: Visual collision theory diagrams with bilingual labels; sentence frames for explaining each factor: 'Increasing ___ causes the reaction rate to ___ because___.'
differentiation.iep: Assign one variable per group rather than rotating; provide a completed example of one factor's analysis; allow verbal explanation as alternative to written exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss traditional fermentation practices across cultures as examples of controlling reaction rate: Korean kimchi fermentation (temperature and salt concentration control the rate of bacterial activity), Ethiopian injera preparation (time and temperature for wild yeast fermentation), and Mexican pulque production. Highlight how these communities empirically controlled reaction rates for thousands of years before collision theory was formalized.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'reaction rate': Crushing a solid reactant increases the reaction rate because___. Both reactions use the same chemicals, but the one at higher temperature reacts faster, so___. A catalyst does not change the products of a reaction, but it does increase the rate because___.

vocabulary.definition: The speed at which reactants are converted to products, measured as the change in concentration over time
A collision between reactant particles that has enough energy and the correct orientation to form products

With cold water, the same tablets take over 2 minutes. The teacher asks students to explain this observation using collision theory.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that Alka-Seltzer dissolves faster in warm water because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use data from the class experiment (time to dissolve at different temperatures) and principles of collision theory to support your explanation.
cer.reasoning_frame: According to collision theory, a reaction occurs when particles collide with___. At higher temperatures, the water molecules have ___ kinetic energy, which means___. This results in ___ effective collisions per unit time, so the rate___.

lessons.title: Reaction Rate Graphs and Interpreting Rate Data (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: interpret graphs showing changes in concentration or volume over time to determine reaction rate and identify when a reaction is complete
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time something started quickly and then slowed down — a phone battery draining, a song getting popular, traffic clearing. Why does the rate change over time?
lessons.do_now: A graph shows the volume of gas produced in a reaction over 5 minutes. The curve rises steeply at first, then levels off. What is happening to the reaction rate over time? Why might it slow down?
materials: Rate graph analysis worksheet with 4 different reaction graphs (printed)
Graph paper (for students to construct their own graphs)
Data set from Alka-Seltzer experiment (previous lesson)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Reaction Rate Graphs and Interpreting Rate Data. Project two graphs side by side: Graph A shows concentration of reactant decreasing over time; Graph B shows concentration of product increasing over time for the same reaction. Ask: What is the relationship between these two graphs? When one goes down, the other goes up — can students explain why using conservation of matter?

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Reaction Rate Graphs and Interpreting Rate Data. Students analyze four different reaction rate graphs on their worksheet. For each graph, they: (1) identify whether the graph shows reactant consumption or product formation, (2) determine the time interval with the fastest rate (steepest slope), (3) estimate the rate during that interval (change in concentration divided by change in time), (4) identify when the reaction is essentially complete (curve flattens). They compare graphs showing the same reaction at two different temperatures.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Reaction Rate Graphs and Interpreting Rate Data. Teacher explains: The rate of a reaction at any moment equals the slope of the concentration vs. time curve. A steep slope means a fast rate; a flat slope means the reaction has slowed or stopped. Rate typically decreases over time because reactant concentration decreases, leading to fewer collisions. Students annotate their graphs with slope lines and rate labels.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Reaction Rate Graphs and Interpreting Rate Data. Students use their Alka-Seltzer data from the previous lesson to construct their own rate graph. They plot volume of gas produced vs. time, draw a best-fit curve, and calculate the average rate during the first 30 seconds and the last 30 seconds. They explain the difference using collision theory.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Reaction Rate Graphs and Interpreting Rate Data. Exit ticket: Given a graph showing gas volume produced over time for two trials — one with a catalyst and one without — students (1) identify which curve represents the catalyzed reaction and explain how they know, (2) compare the final gas volume for both trials, and (3) explain why a catalyst changes the rate but not the total amount of product.

differentiation.approaching: Provide pre-labeled axes on graph paper with scale markings; include a step-by-step guide for calculating slope: 'Pick two points. Subtract the y-values. Subtract the x-values. Divide.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the graph analysis and graph construction as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate instantaneous rate by drawing tangent lines at three different points on their curve and compare to average rate over the same intervals.
differentiation.ell: Provide annotated example graph with bilingual labels for all axes and features; use sentence frames for graph description: 'Between ___ and ___ seconds, the rate is ___ because the slope is___.'
differentiation.iep: Reduce graphs to analyze from four to two; provide graph construction template with axes pre-drawn and data points partially plotted; allow partner work.

lessons.crse_connection: Highlight the contributions of Jacobus van't Hoff, the first Nobel Prize winner in Chemistry (1901), who studied how temperature affects reaction rates. Connect to modern applications: pharmaceutical companies use rate data to determine drug shelf life and expiration dates — a topic of environmental justice since communities in low-income areas often have less access to fresh medications.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: 'The reaction rate, the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, can be determined by calculating the slope of a concentration-time graph.' 'The curve flattens at the end, an indication that the reaction has reached completion, because all of the limiting reactant has been consumed.'

vocabulary.definition: The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, often expressed in mol/L per second
The overall change in concentration divided by the total time elapsed for a given interval

cer.phenomenon: Two students study the same decomposition reaction. Student A runs the reaction at 25 degrees C and Student B runs it at 50 degrees C. Both plot concentration of reactant vs. time. lessons.title: Dynamic Equilibrium (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: describe dynamic equilibrium as the state where the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and explain why concentrations remain constant even though both reactions continue

lessons.do_now: A sealed bottle of soda appears to have stopped fizzing. But when you open it, CO2 escapes rapidly. Was the CO2 really 'gone' while the bottle was sealed, or was something else going on?
materials: Two graduated cylinders and two different-sized straws per group (equilibrium simulation)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Dynamic Equilibrium. Sealed soda demo: Hold up a sealed bottle of clear soda. Ask: Is anything happening inside this bottle right now? Students may say no. Then shake it and open it — the vigorous fizzing proves CO2 was actively dissolving and un-dissolving even though it appeared static. Introduce the concept: at equilibrium, both forward and reverse processes occur continuously at equal rates.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Dynamic Equilibrium. Straw transfer activity: Each group has two graduated cylinders — one filled with 50 mL of colored water (reactants) and one empty (products). Two students simultaneously transfer water between cylinders using different-sized straws (one large, one small). They record the volume in each cylinder every 30 seconds for 5 minutes. Initially, more water moves from the full to the empty cylinder, but as volumes equalize, the rates of transfer become closer until volumes stabilize.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Dynamic Equilibrium. Teacher connects the activity to chemical equilibrium: the large straw represents the forward reaction and the small straw the reverse reaction. At first, the forward rate is greater because there are more 'reactant' particles. As products accumulate, the reverse rate increases. Equilibrium is reached when forward rate equals reverse rate. Key point: concentrations are constant but not necessarily equal — the system is dynamic, not static. Students draw equilibrium concentration-time graphs showing both reactants and products leveling off.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Dynamic Equilibrium. Students examine the PhET equilibrium simulation, adjusting initial concentrations and observing how equilibrium position changes. They answer: If you start with more reactants, do you get more products at equilibrium? Does the system still reach a state where rates are equal? Students record observations and compare with their straw activity results.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Dynamic Equilibrium. Exit ticket: A student says 'At equilibrium, the reaction has stopped because the concentrations aren't changing.' (1) Explain why this statement is incorrect. (2) Draw a rate-time graph showing the forward and reverse rates approaching equilibrium. (3) Label the point where equilibrium is established.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-drawn rate-time graph template with the forward rate curve started; include a checklist of equilibrium characteristics: 'At equilibrium: forward rate ___ reverse rate; concentrations are ___; reactions are still ___.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the straw transfer activity and graphing as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Predict how using two straws of the same size would change the equilibrium position and graph the expected concentration-time curves. Test the prediction with the simulation.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual dynamic/static equilibrium comparison chart with diagrams; use the straw analogy as a visual anchor throughout the lesson; sentence frames for exit ticket.
differentiation.iep: Partner with peer for straw activity; provide pre-formatted data table; allow verbal explanation for exit ticket question 1; reduce to two questions.

lessons.crse_connection: Connect equilibrium to the carbon cycle and ocean acidification — a critical environmental justice issue. As atmospheric CO2 increases, the equilibrium CO2(g) + H2O(l) -> H2CO3(aq) shifts right, making oceans more acidic. This disproportionately affects coastal fishing communities in the Global South, many of them indigenous or low-income. Highlight the work of Sylvia Earle, marine biologist and National Geographic Explorer, who has advocated for understanding ocean chemistry.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'dynamic equilibrium': At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant because___. The forward and reverse reactions are both still occurring, but the concentrations appear unchanged, so___. A sealed soda bottle appears to have stopped fizzing, but CO2 molecules are still dissolving and escaping because___.

cer.phenomenon: A sealed container holds nitrogen dioxide (NO2, a brown gas) in equilibrium with dinitrogen tetroxide (N2O4, a colorless gas) according to the equation 2NO2(g) <-> N2O4(g). A student observes that the brown color in the sealed tube does not change over several hours. The student concludes that all the NO2 has reacted and the reaction is complete.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the student's conclusion is incorrect because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the definition of dynamic equilibrium and evidence from the straw transfer activity to explain why the color remains constant while both reactions continue.
cer.reasoning_frame: The constant brown color indicates that the concentration of NO2 is___. However, this does not mean the reaction has stopped because at equilibrium, the forward reaction (NO2 -> N2O4) occurs at the same rate as___. If we could track individual molecules, we would see___.

lessons.title: Le Chatelier's Principle (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: predict how changes in concentration, temperature, or pressure will shift a system at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
lessons.circle_prompt: Think of a time when something in your life was balanced and then something changed — a new sibling, moving to a new school, a schedule change. How did things adjust to find a new normal?
lessons.do_now: The equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) <-> 2NH3(g) + heat exists in a sealed container. If we suddenly add more N2, predict what will happen to the amount of NH3. Explain your reasoning.
materials: NO2/N2O4 sealed tubes in hot and cold water baths (demo)
CoCl2 equilibrium color change demo materials (cobalt chloride, HCl, water)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Le Chatelier's Principle. Demo: Place sealed tubes containing the NO2/N2O4 equilibrium mixture into hot water and ice water. Students observe the tube in hot water becoming darker brown (more NO2) and the tube in cold water becoming lighter (more N2O4). Ask: The same chemicals are in both tubes. Why does temperature change the color? Introduce Le Chatelier: when a stress is applied, the system shifts to counteract the stress.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Le Chatelier's Principle. Prediction activity: Students work in groups with whiteboards. Teacher presents a series of equilibrium systems with specific stresses applied. For each, groups predict the direction of shift (left, right, or no change) and explain their reasoning: (1) Adding more reactant, (2) Removing product, (3) Increasing temperature for an exothermic reaction, (4) Decreasing volume (increasing pressure) for a reaction with more gas moles on one side. After each prediction, teacher reveals the answer and class discusses.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Le Chatelier's Principle. Teacher formalizes Le Chatelier's principle: When a system at equilibrium is subjected to a stress (change in concentration, temperature, or pressure), the system shifts in the direction that partially counteracts the stress. Key rules: (1) Adding a substance shifts away from it; removing shifts toward it. (2) Increasing temperature shifts toward the endothermic direction; decreasing shifts toward exothermic. (3) Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer moles of gas. (4) A catalyst does NOT shift equilibrium — it only speeds up reaching equilibrium.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Le Chatelier's Principle. Application: The Haber process for making ammonia (N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, exothermic). Students determine optimal conditions to maximize ammonia yield: high pressure (4 gas moles -> 2 gas moles), low temperature (favors exothermic direction), but low temperature slows the rate. Industrial compromise: moderate temperature with a catalyst. Students explain why each condition helps or hinders.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Le Chatelier's Principle. Exit ticket: For the reaction 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <-> 2SO3(g) + heat, predict and explain the effect on equilibrium of: (1) adding more O2, (2) increasing temperature, (3) decreasing the volume of the container, (4) adding a catalyst.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Le Chatelier's decision flowchart: 'Was a substance added? -> Shift away from it. Was temperature increased? -> Is the reaction exo or endo? -> Shift toward endo.' Include color-coded arrows on the prediction worksheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the prediction activity and Haber process analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on one industrial application of Le Chatelier's principle (Contact process for sulfuric acid, or Ostwald process for nitric acid) and explain the economic trade-offs between yield and rate.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual Le Chatelier's principle reference card with arrow diagrams in English and native language; use the analogy of a seesaw to represent equilibrium shifts.
differentiation.iep: Reduce exit ticket stresses from four to two; provide Le Chatelier's rule card for reference; allow partner work during prediction activity.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the Haber-Bosch process in its historical context: Fritz Haber developed the process to fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia for fertilizer, feeding billions but also enabling explosives in World War I. Highlight the ethical complexity of scientific discoveries. Also connect to acid rain: the equilibrium SO2 + H2O <-> H2SO3 shifts right with increased SO2 pollution, disproportionately affecting communities near coal-burning power plants — many of which are located in low-income areas and communities of color.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'Le Chatelier's principle': Adding more reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right because___. Increasing temperature favors the endothermic direction, but industries want maximum product yield, so they must find a compromise because___. A catalyst does not shift equilibrium, so___.

vocabulary.definition: When a system at equilibrium is subjected to a stress, the system shifts in the direction that partially relieves the stress
The equilibrium moves toward producing more reactants (reverse reaction is favored)

cer.phenomenon: A chemical plant produces sulfur trioxide (SO3) using the Contact process: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <-> 2SO3(g), delta H = -198 kJ. The plant operates at 450 degrees C with a vanadium pentoxide catalyst. A new engineer proposes lowering the temperature to 200 degrees C to increase the yield of SO3, since the reaction is exothermic.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the engineer's proposal would increase the equilibrium yield of SO3 but is NOT practical because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use Le Chatelier's principle to explain the equilibrium shift, and collision theory to explain why lowering temperature creates a rate problem.
cer.reasoning_frame: According to Le Chatelier's principle, decreasing temperature for an exothermic reaction shifts equilibrium toward ___ because___. However, at 200 degrees C, the reaction rate would ___ because___. The current temperature of 450 degrees C is a compromise between ___ and___.

lessons.title: Equilibrium Expressions and Keq (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: write an equilibrium expression (Keq) for a reversible reaction and use the value of Keq to predict whether products or reactants are favored at equilibrium
lessons.circle_prompt: If a scoreboard shows one team leading 75-25, what do you know about the game? What if the score is 50-48? What does the ratio tell you?
lessons.do_now: Two reversible reactions are at equilibrium. Reaction A has mostly products and very little reactants. Reaction B has mostly reactants and very little products. Which reaction has gone 'further' toward completion? How could we use a number to describe this?
materials: Concentration data tables for 5 equilibrium systems (printed)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Equilibrium Expressions and Keq. Ratio analogy: Show two photos — a stadium that is 90% full (products favored, Keq much greater than 1) and a nearly empty stadium with most people still outside (reactants favored, Keq much less than 1). Ask: If the ratio of people inside to people outside is large, what does that mean? Introduce Keq as the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations at equilibrium.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Equilibrium Expressions and Keq. Students receive concentration data for five equilibrium systems at a given temperature. For each, they calculate the ratio [products]/[reactants] in various ways until they discover that the correct equilibrium expression uses concentrations raised to the power of their coefficients. Teacher guides: For aA + bB <-> cC + dD, Keq = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b. Students verify this formula gives a consistent Keq value from different data sets for the same reaction.

lessons.title: Rates and Equilibrium Review (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: apply collision theory, Le Chatelier's principle, and equilibrium expressions to analyze complex reaction systems and solve multi-step problems
lessons.circle_prompt: Share a food or drink that changes when you add something to it — like lemon in tea or salt on a watermelon. What happens and why do you think it changes?
lessons.do_now: For the reaction CO(g) + 2H2(g) <-> CH3OH(g) + heat: (1) Write the Keq expression. (2) Predict what happens to Keq if temperature increases. (3) Predict the effect on the amount of CH3OH if more H2 is added.
materials: Equilibrium scenario cards (set of 12 for group activity)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Rates and Equilibrium Review. Rapid review game: Teacher reads equilibrium scenarios and students respond with hand signals: thumbs up for shift right, thumbs down for shift left, flat hand for no change. Scenarios include changes in concentration, temperature, pressure, and addition of catalysts. Keep pace fast to build fluency.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Rates and Equilibrium Review. Scenario card activity: Groups receive complex equilibrium scenario cards that require integrating multiple concepts. Example: 'A factory runs the reaction A(g) + B(g) <-> 2C(g), delta H = +150 kJ. Current Keq = 0.05. The manager wants more product C. Evaluate three proposals: (1) increase temperature, (2) increase pressure, (3) add a catalyst. For each, predict the effect on rate, equilibrium position, and Keq value.' Groups present their analyses on whiteboards.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Rates and Equilibrium Review. Class discussion synthesizing key distinctions: (1) Rate vs. equilibrium — catalysts affect rate but not equilibrium position. (2) Le Chatelier shifts are temporary adjustments — the system reaches a new equilibrium. (3) Only temperature changes Keq. Students complete a concept map linking collision theory, rate factors, dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle, and Keq.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Rates and Equilibrium Review. Multi-step problems: Students solve three problems that combine rate and equilibrium concepts. Example: Given a rate graph and equilibrium data, students identify the point where equilibrium is reached, calculate Keq, then predict how a specified stress would change the graph.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Rates and Equilibrium Review. Unit 7 formative assessment: Six questions covering collision theory, rate factors, rate graphs, dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle, and Keq calculations.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a completed concept map as a reference tool during the review; include a summary card with all major rules (collision theory, Le Chatelier, Keq rules).
differentiation.on_level: Complete the scenario analysis and multi-step problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze a real industrial equilibrium system (ammonia synthesis or sulfuric acid production) using actual operating conditions and Keq data, and write a recommendation for optimizing yield.
differentiation.ell: Bilingual concept map with visual icons; allow oral presentation of scenario card analysis; provide sentence frames for written responses.
differentiation.iep: Reduce formative assessment to four questions; provide reference cards for all major concepts; allow extended time; partner support during scenario activity.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how traditional fermentation processes in West African, Korean, and Latin American cuisines represent empirical understanding of reaction rates and equilibrium. Highlight how Korean onggi pottery is specifically designed with porous walls that allow air exchange, controlling the rate and equilibrium of kimchi fermentation. Connect to the work of Lloyd Hall, an African American chemist who revolutionized food preservation by understanding how to control reaction rates to prevent spoilage.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion: Start with 'Equilibrium shifts.' Students expand: 'When a system at dynamic equilibrium experiences a stress such as a change in concentration, temperature, or pressure, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partially counteracts the stress, eventually establishing a new equilibrium with different concentrations but at the same Keq value if temperature is unchanged.'

vocabulary.definition: The specific set of concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium for a given set of conditions
A change in the relative amounts of reactants and products in response to a stress, as predicted by Le Chatelier's principle

cer.phenomenon: A chemical company manufactures methanol (CH3OH) using the reaction CO(g) + 2H2(g) <-> CH3OH(g), delta H = -90 kJ. Current operating conditions are 250 degrees C and 100 atm with a copper-zinc catalyst. A consultant recommends switching to 100 degrees C to increase yield.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the consultant's recommendation would ___ the equilibrium yield of methanol but would ___ the production rate because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use Le Chatelier's principle to predict the equilibrium shift and collision theory to predict the effect on rate. Explain why the current conditions represent an industrial compromise.
cer.reasoning_frame: Lowering the temperature would shift equilibrium ___ because___, increasing the equilibrium concentration of methanol. However, at 100 degrees C, the rate of the reaction would ___ because___. The current conditions of 250 degrees C with a catalyst represent a compromise between ___ and___.

units.title: Acids, Bases & Salts
units.anchoring_phenomenon: Antacid tablets relieve heartburn by reacting with stomach acid. But if you take too many, your stomach can become too basic and you feel just as bad. How do chemists measure and control the balance between acids and bases?
essential_questions: What makes a substance an acid or a base, and how do different theories define them?
How does the pH scale quantify the strength of an acid or base, and what do pH values tell us about hydronium ion concentration?
What happens at the molecular level during a neutralization reaction, and what products are formed?
units.crse_theme: Students explore acids and bases through cultural and environmental lenses — the chemistry of traditional food preservation (pickling in vinegar across many cultures, lime in nixtamalization), the pH of natural dyes used in textile traditions from India and Central America, and the environmental justice implications of acid rain on communities near industrial zones.
investigations: Investigation 8: Acid-Base Titration — Determining the Concentration of an Unknown Acid

lessons.title: Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry Theories of Acids and Bases (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: define acids and bases according to both the Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry theories and identify conjugate acid-base pairs in a reaction
lessons.circle_prompt: What sour foods do you enjoy? What about bitter foods? Do you know what makes them taste that way?
lessons.do_now: Look at these three formulas: HCl, NaOH, NaCl. One is an acid, one is a base, and one is a salt. Sort them and explain what pattern in the formulas helped you decide.
materials: pH test strips and solutions set: lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution, ammonia, milk, soapy water (1 set per group)
Litmus paper (red and blue, 1 pack per group)
Safety goggles and gloves (1 per student)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry Theories of Acids and Bases. Mystery solution challenge: Show six clear, colorless solutions in labeled beakers (A through F). Tell students three are acids and three are bases, but they all look the same. Ask: Without tasting (never taste chemicals!), how could you tell them apart? Students brainstorm methods. Introduce the idea that acids and bases have different properties that can be tested.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry Theories of Acids and Bases. Station testing: Groups rotate through six solutions (lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution, ammonia solution, milk, soapy water). At each station, they test with red litmus paper, blue litmus paper, and pH strips. They record results in a data table and classify each as acid, base, or neutral. Students look for patterns: What do all acids have in common? All bases?

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry Theories of Acids and Bases. Teacher introduces two definitions. Arrhenius: An acid produces H+ ions (hydronium, H3O+) in water; a base produces OH- ions in water. Bronsted-Lowry (broader): An acid is a proton (H+) donor; a base is a proton acceptor. Students identify conjugate acid-base pairs in reactions like HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl- (HCl donates H+ to H2O, so HCl is the acid and H2O is the base; H3O+ and Cl- are the conjugate acid and conjugate base).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry Theories of Acids and Bases. Students classify 8 reactions using both Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry definitions and identify conjugate pairs. They encounter an example where Bronsted-Lowry works but Arrhenius does not (e.g., NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl, no water involved) to understand why the Bronsted-Lowry definition is more broadly applicable.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry Theories of Acids and Bases. Exit ticket: (1) Define acid and base according to the Bronsted-Lowry theory. (2) In the reaction NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-, identify the acid, base, conjugate acid, and conjugate base. (3) Explain why NH3 is a base even though it does not contain OH-.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Venn diagram comparing Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry definitions; include a color-coded conjugate pair identification guide with arrows showing proton transfer.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the solution testing and conjugate pair analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research amphoteric substances (like water and amino acids) and explain how the same substance can act as both an acid and a base depending on the reaction partner.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual acid-base vocabulary cards with molecular diagrams; use color-coded arrows (red for proton donated, blue for proton accepted) in all examples; sentence frames for classification.
differentiation.iep: Pre-formatted data table with litmus results partially filled in; reduce conjugate pair practice to 4 reactions; provide labeled example to reference.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the traditional use of natural acid-base indicators across cultures: red cabbage juice indicators used in European folk chemistry, turmeric as an indicator in Indian traditions (turns red in basic solutions), and the use of wood ash (basic) in West African indigo dyeing to set the dye. Highlight Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish scientist whose acid-base theory was initially rejected as his doctoral thesis — he later won the Nobel Prize for it.

Water can act as either an acid or a base, but in this reaction it accepts a proton, so___. The Arrhenius definition only applies to reactions in water, but the Bronsted-Lowry definition is broader because___.

At each station, they test with red litmus paper, blue litmus paper, and pH strips. They record results in a data table and classify each as acid, base, or neutral. Students look for patterns: What do all acids have in common? All bases?

explain.description: Whole-class discussion of CER responses; address remaining misconceptions. Building on previous days: Teacher introduces two definitions. Arrhenius: An acid produces H+ ions (hydronium, H3O+) in water; a base produces OH- ions in water. Bronsted-Lowry (broader): An acid is a proton (H+) donor; a base is a proton acceptor. Students identify conjugate acid-base pairs in reactions like HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl- (HCl donates H+ to H2O, so HCl is the acid and H2O is the base; H3O+ and Cl- are the conjugate acid and conjugate base).

elaborate.description: Extension or enrichment activity connecting to real-world applications. Building on previous days: Students classify 8 reactions using both Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry definitions and identify conjugate pairs. They encounter an example where Bronsted-Lowry works but Arrhenius does not (e.g., NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl, no water involved) to understand why the Bronsted-Lowry definition is more broadly applicable.

evaluate.description: Summative check — quiz or performance task covering all concepts from the sequence. Building on previous days: Exit ticket: (1) Define acid and base according to the Bronsted-Lowry theory. (2) In the reaction NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-, identify the acid, base, conjugate acid, and conjugate base. (3) Explain why NH3 is a base even though it does not contain OH-.

differentiation.approaching: Review key concepts from the full sequence before assessment. Provide a Venn diagram comparing Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry definitions; include a color-coded conjugate pair identification guide with arrows showing proton transfer.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the solution testing and conjugate pair analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Complete extension challenge connecting to real-world applications. Research amphoteric substances (like water and amino acids) and explain how the same substance can act as both an acid and a base depending on the reaction partner.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual acid-base vocabulary cards with molecular diagrams; use color-coded arrows (red for proton donated, blue for proton accepted) in all examples; sentence frames for classification.
differentiation.iep: Pre-formatted data table with litmus results partially filled in; reduce conjugate pair practice to 4 reactions; provide labeled example to reference.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the traditional use of natural acid-base indicators across cultures: red cabbage juice indicators used in European folk chemistry, turmeric as an indicator in Indian traditions (turns red in basic solutions), and the use of wood ash (basic) in West African indigo dyeing to set the dye. Highlight Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish scientist whose acid-base theory was initially rejected as his doctoral thesis — he later won the Nobel Prize for it.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion using 'Bronsted-Lowry Acid': Start with 'Bronsted-Lowry Acid is important.' Expand by adding when, where, why, and how details to create a complex sentence that demonstrates understanding of the concept.

vocabulary.definition: A proton (H+) donor in a chemical reaction
The ion formed when a hydrogen ion (H+) combines with a water molecule; present in all acidic solutions

guided_notes_outline: Section 3: Bronsted-Lowry Theory — Proton Donors and Acceptors

cer.phenomenon: A student tests household ammonia (NH3 dissolved in water) and finds that it turns red litmus blue, has a pH of 11, and feels slippery. However, ammonia's formula does not contain OH-. A classmate claims that ammonia cannot be a base because it has no hydroxide ions.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that ammonia IS a base even though its formula does not contain OH- because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the litmus and pH data, the equation NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-, and the Bronsted-Lowry definition to explain.
cer.reasoning_frame: According to the Arrhenius definition, a base must ___. While NH3 does not contain OH- directly, when it dissolves in water it ___ because___. Under the Bronsted-Lowry definition, NH3 is a base because it ___ from water, making NH3 a proton ___ and water a proton___.

lessons.title: pH Scale, Indicators, and pH Calculations (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: use the pH scale to classify solutions as acidic, basic, or neutral and calculate pH from hydronium ion concentration
lessons.circle_prompt: If you had to rank your five favorite drinks from most sour to least sour, what order would they be in? What do you think is chemically different about the sour ones?
lessons.do_now: Solution A has a pH of 2 and Solution B has a pH of 5. A student says Solution A is 3 times more acidic than Solution B. Is this correct? Explain your reasoning.
materials: pH paper and pH meters or probes (1 per group)
Solution set: 0.1 M HCl, 0.01 M HCl, 0.001 M HCl, distilled water, 0.001 M NaOH, 0.01 M NaOH, 0.1 M NaOH
Indicator solution set: phenolphthalein, bromthymol blue, methyl orange, litmus

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: pH Scale, Indicators, and pH Calculations. Show a large pH scale poster with common substances plotted (battery acid at 1, lemon juice at 2, vinegar at 3, coffee at 5, milk at 6.5, pure water at 7, baking soda at 9, ammonia at 11, bleach at 13). Ask students to identify the pattern. Reveal: each step on the pH scale represents a tenfold change in H3O+ concentration — pH is logarithmic. So Solution A (pH 2) is actually 1000 times more acidic than Solution B (pH 5).

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: pH Scale, Indicators, and pH Calculations. Two-part exploration. Part A: Students measure the pH of seven solutions (serial dilutions of HCl, water, and serial dilutions of NaOH) using pH paper and record results. They notice the pH changes by 1 for each tenfold dilution. Part B: Students test the same solutions with four indicators (phenolphthalein, bromthymol blue, methyl orange, litmus) and record the color at each pH. They construct an indicator reference chart showing the color-change range of each indicator.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: pH Scale, Indicators, and pH Calculations. Teacher formalizes: pH = -log[H3O+]. At pH 7, [H3O+] = 1 x 10^-7 M (neutral). Below 7 is acidic (more H3O+). Above 7 is basic (less H3O+, more OH-). Also: [H3O+] x [OH-] = 1 x 10^-14 at 25 degrees C (Kw). Students practice converting between pH and [H3O+]: If [H3O+] = 1 x 10^-3, pH = 3. If pH = 9, [H3O+] = 1 x 10^-9.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: pH Scale, Indicators, and pH Calculations. Application problems: (1) A lake has a pH of 4.5 due to acid rain. Calculate [H3O+]. (2) A student measures [OH-] = 1 x 10^-4 M. Find [H3O+] and pH. (3) Which indicator from the reference chart would be best for detecting whether milk (pH ~6.5) has become acidic (spoiled)? Justify your choice using the indicator ranges.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: pH Scale, Indicators, and pH Calculations. Exit ticket: (1) Calculate the pH of a solution with [H3O+] = 1 x 10^-5 M. (2) A solution has a pH of 11. Calculate [H3O+] and [OH-]. (3) How many times more acidic is a solution with pH 3 than a solution with pH 6?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pH conversion chart showing pH values from 1-14 with corresponding [H3O+] concentrations already listed; include step-by-step calculation template: 'pH = -log[___] = -log[1 x 10^-___] = ___.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the pH measurement, indicator charting, and calculation practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate pH for concentrations that are not exact powers of 10 (e.g., [H3O+] = 3.5 x 10^-4 M) using the log function on a calculator, and explain why pH is not always a whole number.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual pH scale with color coding and bilingual labels; use sentence frames for explaining calculations; allow verbal explanation of indicator choices.
differentiation.iep: Provide pre-formatted calculation workspace with blanks to fill in; allow use of pH conversion chart during exit ticket; reduce problems from three to two.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss acid rain as an environmental justice issue: sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions from coal plants and factories create acid rain that lowers the pH of lakes and soil. Communities in Appalachia and the Adirondacks have experienced ecological damage. Highlight how pH monitoring helped advocate for the Clean Air Act. Also discuss how soil pH affects agriculture — the traditional practice of adding lime (CaO, a base) to acidic soil has been used by farmers worldwide for centuries, from Roman agriculture to modern sustainable farming.

cer.phenomenon: A blueberry farmer tests soil pH and gets a reading of 8.0. Blueberries grow best in soil with pH between 4.5 and 5.0. The farmer adds elemental sulfur to the soil, which bacteria oxidize to produce sulfuric acid according to the reaction: 2S + 3O2 + 2H2O -> 2H2SO4.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that adding sulfur will ___ the soil pH to the optimal range because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the pH scale, the reaction equation, and knowledge of acids to explain how sulfur addition changes [H3O+] and therefore pH.
cer.reasoning_frame: The current pH of 8.0 means the soil is ___, with [H3O+] = ___. The farmer needs to ___ the pH, which requires ___ the [H3O+]. The sulfur is oxidized to ___, which is a strong acid that ___ in water to produce ___ ions, thereby ___ the pH.

lessons.title: Neutralization Reactions and Titration (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: write balanced equations for neutralization reactions, predict the products (salt + water), and determine the concentration of an unknown acid or base using titration data
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever used baking soda to clean something or to settle an upset stomach? What do you think it does chemically?
lessons.do_now: If you mix equal amounts of a strong acid (HCl) and a strong base (NaOH), what do you think will happen to the pH? Will the mixture be acidic, basic, or neutral? Explain.
materials: Titration data table and calculation worksheet (printed)
Safety goggles, gloves, and aprons (1 per student)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Neutralization Reactions and Titration. Demo: Teacher adds a few drops of phenolphthalein to NaOH solution (turns pink). Then slowly adds HCl drop by drop while students count. At the equivalence point, the pink color disappears. Ask: What happened? Where did the base go? How many drops of acid did it take to 'cancel out' the base? Introduce the concept of neutralization.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Neutralization Reactions and Titration. Titration lab: Students perform a titration of an unknown concentration HCl with standardized 0.1 M NaOH. Using a burette, they add NaOH to the acid (with phenolphthalein) until a persistent pink color appears. They record the volume of NaOH used, repeat for two more trials, and calculate the average. Then they use the equation M1V1 = M2V2 (for 1:1 mole ratio) to determine the molarity of the unknown HCl.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Neutralization Reactions and Titration. Teacher formalizes neutralization: Acid + Base -> Salt + Water. For Arrhenius: H+ + OH- -> H2O. The salt is formed from the cation of the base and the anion of the acid. Students write balanced equations for: HCl + NaOH, H2SO4 + KOH, HNO3 + Ca(OH)2. Teacher explains the titration calculation: at the equivalence point, moles of acid = moles of base (adjusted for stoichiometry).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Neutralization Reactions and Titration. Students solve titration problems: (1) 25.0 mL of H2SO4 is neutralized by 30.0 mL of 0.20 M NaOH. Find the molarity of the acid (note: 2:1 mole ratio). (2) Identify the salt produced in each of the three neutralization reactions from the Explain phase. (3) Predict the pH at the equivalence point for a strong acid-strong base titration.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Neutralization Reactions and Titration. Exit ticket: (1) Write the balanced equation for the neutralization of phosphoric acid (H3PO4) with sodium hydroxide (NaOH). (2) In a titration, 20.0 mL of 0.15 M HCl is neutralized by 15.0 mL of NaOH. Calculate the concentration of NaOH. (3) Name the salt produced.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a neutralization equation template: '___ acid + ___ base -> ___ salt + H2O.' Include a step-by-step titration calculation guide with a worked example showing MaVa = MbVb.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the titration lab and calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze a titration curve (pH vs. volume of base added) to identify the equivalence point, half-equivalence point, and buffer region. Compare strong acid/strong base curves with weak acid/strong base curves.
differentiation.ell: Provide visual step-by-step titration procedure with photographs; bilingual calculation templates; color-coded equation balancing guide (acid in red, base in blue, salt in green, water in black).
differentiation.iep: Partner for burette readings; provide pre-balanced equations for practice; reduce titration calculations to one trial; allow extended time; enlarged data table.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how antacid medications use neutralization reactions — calcium carbonate (Tums), magnesium hydroxide (Milk of Magnesia), and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) all neutralize excess stomach acid (HCl). Connect to traditional remedies across cultures: the use of alkaline mineral waters for digestive relief in many European and Middle Eastern traditions. Highlight Alice Ball, an African American chemist at the University of Hawaii who developed the first effective treatment for leprosy using chaulmoogra oil — her work involved understanding acid-base chemistry of organic compounds. She died at 24, and her male colleague initially took credit for her work.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'neutralization': When an acid reacts with a base, a salt and water are formed because___. Both HCl and H2SO4 are acids, but H2SO4 requires twice as much NaOH to neutralize it because___. The phenolphthalein turned from pink to clear, so we know___.

vocabulary.definition: A chemical reaction in which an acid and a base react to produce a salt and water
The point in a titration where the moles of acid exactly equal the moles of base

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What is Neutralization? — Acid + Base = Salt + Water
Section 4: Titration — The Laboratory Technique

materials: Titration data table and calculation worksheet (printed)
Safety goggles, gloves, and aprons (1 per student)

engage.description: Present a novel scenario that requires synthesis of concepts from Days 1-2. Building on previous days: Demo: Teacher adds a few drops of phenolphthalein to NaOH solution (turns pink). Then slowly adds HCl drop by drop while students count. At the equivalence point, the pink color disappears. Ask: What happened? Where did the base go? How many drops of acid did it take to 'cancel out' the base? Introduce the concept of neutralization.

explore.description: CER activity — students construct evidence-based arguments about the topic. Building on previous days: Titration lab: Students perform a titration of an unknown concentration HCl with standardized 0.1 M NaOH. Using a burette, they add NaOH to the acid (with phenolphthalein) until a persistent pink color appears. They record the volume of NaOH used, repeat for two more trials, and calculate the average. Then they use the equation M1V1 = M2V2 (for 1:1 mole ratio) to determine the molarity of the unknown HCl.

explain.description: Whole-class discussion of CER responses; address remaining misconceptions. Building on previous days: Teacher formalizes neutralization: Acid + Base -> Salt + Water. For Arrhenius: H+ + OH- -> H2O. The salt is formed from the cation of the base and the anion of the acid. Students write balanced equations for: HCl + NaOH, H2SO4 + KOH, HNO3 + Ca(OH)2. Teacher explains the titration calculation: at the equivalence point, moles of acid = moles of base (adjusted for stoichiometry).

elaborate.description: Extension or enrichment activity connecting to real-world applications. Building on previous days: Students solve titration problems: (1) 25.0 mL of H2SO4 is neutralized by 30.0 mL of 0.20 M NaOH. Find the molarity of the acid (note: 2:1 mole ratio). (2) Identify the salt produced in each of the three neutralization reactions from the Explain phase. (3) Predict the pH at the equivalence point for a strong acid-strong base titration.

evaluate.description: Summative check — quiz or performance task covering all concepts from the sequence. Building on previous days: Exit ticket: (1) Write the balanced equation for the neutralization of phosphoric acid (H3PO4) with sodium hydroxide (NaOH). (2) In a titration, 20.0 mL of 0.15 M HCl is neutralized by 15.0 mL of NaOH. Calculate the concentration of NaOH. (3) Name the salt produced.

differentiation.approaching: Review key concepts from the full sequence before assessment. Provide a neutralization equation template: '___ acid + ___ base -> ___ salt + H2O.' Include a step-by-step titration calculation guide with a worked example showing MaVa = MbVb.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the titration lab and calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Complete extension challenge connecting to real-world applications. Analyze a titration curve (pH vs. volume of base added) to identify the equivalence point, half-equivalence point, and buffer region. Compare strong acid/strong base curves with weak acid/strong base curves.
differentiation.ell: Provide visual step-by-step titration procedure with photographs; bilingual calculation templates; color-coded equation balancing guide (acid in red, base in blue, salt in green, water in black).
differentiation.iep: Partner for burette readings; provide pre-balanced equations for practice; reduce titration calculations to one trial; allow extended time; enlarged data table.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how antacid medications use neutralization reactions — calcium carbonate (Tums), magnesium hydroxide (Milk of Magnesia), and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) all neutralize excess stomach acid (HCl). Highlight Alice Ball, an African American chemist at the University of Hawaii who developed the first effective treatment for leprosy using chaulmoogra oil — her work involved understanding acid-base chemistry of organic compounds. She died at 24, and her male colleague initially took credit for her work.
