cer.evidence_source: Use the neutralization reaction between HCl and the basic compounds in pool water, knowledge of salt formation, and the small concentrations involved.
cer.reasoning_frame: When HCl is added to basic pool water, it reacts with ___ to form ___ and water. The chloride ions produced are the same ions found in ___, which is already added to pools. The small volume of acid needed to change the pH from 8.5 to 7.4 produces a very ___ concentration of Cl- because___.

lessons.title: Salt Formation, Hydrolysis, and Acid-Base Review (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: predict whether a salt solution will be acidic, basic, or neutral based on the identities of the parent acid and base, and apply all acid-base concepts to solve multi-step problems
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time when mixing two things that seemed neutral created something unexpected — like mixing ingredients in cooking that changed the flavor in a surprising way.
lessons.do_now: Sodium chloride (NaCl) dissolved in water has a pH of 7. Sodium acetate (NaCH3COO) dissolved in water has a pH of about 9. Both are salts. Why might one salt solution be neutral and the other basic?
materials: Salt solution set: NaCl, NaCH3COO, NH4Cl, Na2CO3, KNO3 (0.1 M each)
pH paper or meters (1 per group)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Salt Formation, Hydrolysis, and Acid-Base Review. Testing salt solutions: Each group tests the pH of five salt solutions and records whether each is acidic, basic, or neutral. Results are surprising — some salts produce acidic solutions, some basic, and some neutral. Ask: What determines the pH of a salt solution if the salt itself is ionic and seems 'neutral'?

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Salt Formation, Hydrolysis, and Acid-Base Review. Pattern analysis: Students organize the five salts by identifying the parent acid and parent base for each (e.g., NaCl comes from HCl + NaOH). They classify each parent as strong or weak. They discover the pattern: salt of strong acid + strong base = neutral; salt of weak acid + strong base = basic; salt of strong acid + weak base = acidic. Students test this pattern against their pH data.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Salt Formation, Hydrolysis, and Acid-Base Review. Teacher explains hydrolysis: when a salt dissolves, its ions can react with water. If the anion comes from a weak acid, it acts as a base (accepts H+ from water, producing OH-). If the cation comes from a weak base, it acts as an acid (donates H+ to water, producing H3O+). Students write hydrolysis equations for acetate ion and ammonium ion to see this in action.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Salt Formation, Hydrolysis, and Acid-Base Review. Cumulative review: Students complete multi-step problems that integrate all Unit 8 concepts. Example: Identify the acid, base, salt, and water in a neutralization reaction; write the equation; predict the pH of the salt solution; calculate the concentration of the acid from titration data.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Salt Formation, Hydrolysis, and Acid-Base Review. Unit 8 formative assessment: Six questions covering Arrhenius and Bronsted-Lowry definitions, pH calculations, neutralization equations, titration calculations, and salt hydrolysis predictions.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a salt hydrolysis decision tree: 'What is the parent acid? Strong or weak? What is the parent base? Strong or weak? Use the chart to predict pH.' Include a reference table of common strong acids and bases.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the salt testing, pattern analysis, and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the pH of a salt solution quantitatively using Ka and Kb values, and explain buffer systems (how a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base resists pH change).
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual strong acid/base reference list; visual hydrolysis reaction diagrams with arrows showing proton transfer; sentence frames for predictions.
differentiation.iep: Reduce formative assessment to four questions; provide all reference charts during assessment; allow partner work for salt testing; extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the chemistry of traditional soap-making across cultures — wood ash (potassium carbonate, a basic salt from hydrolysis) combined with animal fats in a saponification reaction. This process has been practiced for millennia in African, European, and Middle Eastern cultures. Highlight the tradition of black soap (ose dudu) from West Africa, where cocoa pod ash provides the alkaline solution needed for saponification. Also discuss how blood pH is maintained at 7.35-7.45 through buffer systems, and how understanding acid-base chemistry is critical in medicine.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion: Start with 'Salts affect pH.' Students expand: 'Salts formed from the neutralization of acids and bases affect the pH of their aqueous solutions through a process called hydrolysis, in which the ions of the salt react with water molecules to produce either hydronium or hydroxide ions, depending on whether the parent acid or parent base was weak.'

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Oxidation, Reduction, and Oxidation Numbers. Demo: Place an iron nail in copper sulfate solution. Within minutes, the nail develops a reddish-brown coating (copper) and the blue solution fades. Ask: Iron went into the solution and copper came out. What was exchanged between them? Introduce the idea that electrons were transferred from iron to copper — this is a redox reaction.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Oxidation, Reduction, and Oxidation Numbers. Students learn the oxidation number rules systematically: (1) Free elements = 0, (2) Monatomic ions = charge, (3) Oxygen = -2 (usually), (4) Hydrogen = +1 (usually), (5) Sum of oxidation numbers = charge of species. Using these rules, students assign oxidation numbers to every atom in 10 compounds and ions. Then they examine 5 chemical equations, track changes in oxidation numbers, and identify which atoms were oxidized (increased) and which were reduced (decreased).

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Oxidation, Reduction, and Oxidation Numbers. Teacher formalizes definitions: Oxidation = loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number). Reduction = gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number). Mnemonic: OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain). The species that is oxidized is the reducing agent (it causes reduction in the other species). The species that is reduced is the oxidizing agent. Students apply these terms to the iron-copper reaction from the demo.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Oxidation, Reduction, and Oxidation Numbers. Students analyze three more redox reactions: (1) Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 (metal dissolving in acid), (2) 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO (combustion of magnesium), (3) Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag (single replacement). cer.claim_starter: I claim that the student is correct — a redox reaction occurred because___.
cer.evidence_source: Assign oxidation numbers to copper and silver before and after the reaction, identify the electron transfer, and connect the color changes to the chemical change.

lessons.title: Half-Reactions and the Activity Series (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: write and balance half-reactions for redox processes and use the activity series to predict whether a single replacement reaction will occur spontaneously
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about competitions or rankings — sports teams, music charts, or even food rankings. What makes one thing 'more active' or 'better' than another on a list?
lessons.do_now: A student places a zinc strip in copper sulfate solution and observes a reaction. Then the student places a copper strip in zinc sulfate solution and observes NO reaction. Why does one combination react and the other does not?
materials: Activity series reference table (printed and on reference table)
Metal strip samples: Zn, Cu, Mg, Fe, Pb (small pieces)
Solution set: ZnSO4, CuSO4, MgSO4, FeSO4, Pb(NO3)2 (in well plates)
Safety goggles and gloves (1 per student)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Half-Reactions and the Activity Series. Show a video of sodium reacting violently with water (very active metal) and gold sitting unchanged in acid (very inactive metal). Ask: What makes some metals more 'eager' to give up electrons than others? Is there a ranking? Introduce the activity series as a ranking of metals by their tendency to be oxidized.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Half-Reactions and the Activity Series. Micro-scale lab: Using well plates, students test combinations of metals and solutions to build their own activity series. They place small pieces of Zn, Cu, Mg, and Fe into solutions of CuSO4, ZnSO4, MgSO4, and FeSO4. For each combination, they record whether a reaction occurs (evidence: color change, metal depositing). From the pattern of which metals displace others, they rank the metals from most to least active.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Half-Reactions and the Activity Series. Teacher connects the results to the activity series on the reference table. Rule: A more active metal will replace a less active metal from solution. Students learn to write half-reactions: Oxidation half-reaction (metal loses electrons, e.g., Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-) and Reduction half-reaction (ion gains electrons, e.g., Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu). The overall reaction is the sum of the two half-reactions with electrons canceling.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Half-Reactions and the Activity Series. Prediction practice: Students use the activity series to predict whether 8 proposed reactions will occur. For those that will occur, they write balanced half-reactions and the overall equation. Key application: Can iron displace hydrogen from HCl? (Yes — Fe is above H on the activity series.) Can copper? (No — Cu is below H.)

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Half-Reactions and the Activity Series. Exit ticket: (1) Write the oxidation and reduction half-reactions for Mg + FeCl2 -> MgCl2 + Fe. (2) Will a reaction occur if copper metal is placed in aluminum sulfate solution? Use the activity series to justify. (3) A jeweler wants to plate a ring with gold. Should the ring be the anode or cathode? Explain.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a half-reaction writing template: 'Oxidation: ___ -> ___^_+ + ___e-. Reduction: ___^_+ + ___e- -> ___.' Include an activity series with a 'more active' arrow and a highlighted rule.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the micro-scale activity series lab and prediction practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the thermite reaction (Al + Fe2O3) and explain why aluminum can reduce iron oxide, calculate the energy released, and describe a real-world application (railroad welding).
differentiation.ell: Provide visual activity series with color-coded metals and arrows showing electron transfer direction; bilingual prediction sentence frames; labeled diagram of half-reactions.
differentiation.iep: Reduce prediction problems from 8 to 5; provide activity series with highlighted sections for each problem; partner for lab work; allow reference table during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the history of bronze and iron ages as revolutions in human technology driven by understanding which metals could replace others from their ores. The Haya people of Tanzania developed advanced iron smelting techniques around 2,000 years ago that achieved temperatures rivaling modern blast furnaces. Also discuss how the activity series explains why gold and platinum are found as free metals in nature (they are the least active) while alkali metals are never found free — connecting to the economics and colonialism of gold mining.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: 'The activity series, a list of metals ranked by their tendency to lose electrons and undergo oxidation, allows us to predict whether a single replacement reaction will occur spontaneously.' 'Zinc, a more active metal than copper, spontaneously displaces copper ions from solution because it has a greater tendency to be oxidized.'

vocabulary.definition: An equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction separately, including the electrons transferred
A reaction that occurs naturally without continuous external energy input once initiated

cer.phenomenon: A student's silver ring tarnishes (turns black) when exposed to air containing traces of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) gas. The tarnish is silver sulfide (Ag2S). The student tries to clean the ring by soaking it in aluminum foil and baking soda solution. The tarnish disappears and the ring is shiny again.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the aluminum foil cleaned the silver ring because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the activity series to explain why aluminum can reduce silver sulfide back to silver metal, and write the half-reactions.
cer.reasoning_frame: Aluminum is ___ active than silver on the activity series, meaning it has a greater tendency to___. In this reaction, aluminum is ___ (loses electrons) and silver ions in Ag2S are ___ (gain electrons). The half-reactions are: Oxidation: ___. Reduction: ___. This works because aluminum ___ silver on the activity series.

lessons.title: Electrochemical (Voltaic) Cells (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: diagram and explain how a voltaic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy, identifying the anode, cathode, salt bridge, and direction of electron flow
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about all the batteries you use in a day — phone, laptop, remote control. Have you ever wondered how a battery actually produces electricity from chemicals inside?
lessons.do_now: A lemon battery can light a small LED. The setup uses a zinc nail and a copper penny stuck into a lemon. Which metal do you think loses electrons (anode) and which gains them (cathode)? Use the activity series to predict.
materials: Voltaic cell construction kit per group: Zn and Cu electrode strips, ZnSO4 and CuSO4 solutions, salt bridge (KNO3 in agar or filter paper soaked in KNO3), beakers, wires, voltmeter
LED bulbs or small motors (1 per group)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Electrochemical (Voltaic) Cells. Build a lemon battery in front of the class: insert a zinc nail and copper penny into a lemon, connect wires to a voltmeter. Students see a voltage reading. Ask: The lemon is not plugged into a wall outlet — where is the electrical energy coming from? The chemical reaction between zinc and the acid in the lemon produces electrons that flow through the wire. This is an electrochemical cell.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Electrochemical (Voltaic) Cells. Lab: Each group constructs a Zn/Cu voltaic cell. They set up two beakers — one with Zn in ZnSO4, one with Cu in CuSO4 — connected by a salt bridge and external wire to a voltmeter. Students record the voltage, then connect an LED or small motor. They observe which electrode gets smaller over time (anode, Zn) and which gets larger (cathode, Cu). They draw and label a complete diagram of their cell.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Electrochemical (Voltaic) Cells. Teacher formalizes voltaic cell anatomy: (1) Anode — oxidation occurs, more active metal, negative terminal, gets smaller. (2) Cathode — reduction occurs, less active metal, positive terminal, gets larger. (3) Salt bridge — allows ion flow to maintain electrical neutrality. (4) External wire — electrons flow from anode to cathode (from Zn to Cu). Students write the half-reactions and label all components on their diagram.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Electrochemical (Voltaic) Cells. Application: Students examine the chemistry of common batteries. For a lithium-ion battery (used in phones), they identify the half-reactions from the sample cluster (Li -> Li+ + e- at the anode; CoO2 + Li+ + e- -> LiCoO2 at the cathode). They compare voltaic cells (spontaneous, produce electricity) to the concept of electrolytic cells (non-spontaneous, use electricity — to be covered next lesson).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Electrochemical (Voltaic) Cells. Exit ticket: A voltaic cell uses Mg and Ag electrodes. (1) Which metal is the anode? Use the activity series. (2) Write the oxidation and reduction half-reactions. (3) Draw an arrow showing the direction of electron flow through the external wire. (4) What is the purpose of the salt bridge?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-labeled voltaic cell diagram with blanks only for the half-reaction equations and direction of electron flow; include a 'Voltaic Cell Checklist' matching each component to its function.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the voltaic cell construction, diagram, and analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the cell potential (voltage) using standard reduction potentials from a reference table; compare predicted voltage to measured voltage and explain sources of discrepancy.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual voltaic cell diagram with all components labeled in English and native language; use arrows and color-coding (red for oxidation at anode, blue for reduction at cathode) consistently.
differentiation.iep: Partner for cell construction; provide pre-drawn cell diagram to label rather than drawing from scratch; reduce exit ticket to three parts; allow reference table use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Alessandro Volta's invention of the voltaic pile (1800), the first true battery, and how it led to the electrical age. Connect to modern battery technology and the work of John Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham, and Akira Yoshino, who shared the 2019 Nobel Prize for developing the lithium-ion battery. Discuss environmental justice issues in lithium and cobalt mining — cobalt is often mined in the Democratic Republic of Congo under dangerous conditions, including child labor, raising ethical questions about our reliance on battery-powered devices.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'voltaic cell': Zinc is the anode in a Zn/Cu voltaic cell because___. Electrons flow through the external wire from zinc to copper, but ions flow through the salt bridge in the opposite direction because___. The salt bridge is essential, so without it___.

vocabulary.definition: An electrochemical cell that converts chemical energy into electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction
A device containing a salt solution that allows ions to flow between the two half-cells, maintaining electrical neutrality

engage.description: Review warm-up connecting Day 1 vocabulary to a new example or context. Continuing: Build a lemon battery in front of the class: insert a zinc nail and copper penny into a lemon, connect wires to a voltmeter. Students see a voltage reading. Ask: The lemon is not plugged into a wall outlet — where is the electrical energy coming from? The chemical reaction between zinc and the acid in the lemon produces electrons that flow through the wire. This is an electrochemical cell.

explore.description: Structured practice — students work through increasingly complex problems with scaffolds. Continuing: Lab: Each group constructs a Zn/Cu voltaic cell. They set up two beakers — one with Zn in ZnSO4, one with Cu in CuSO4 — connected by a salt bridge and external wire to a voltmeter. Students record the voltage, then connect an LED or small motor. They observe which electrode gets smaller over time (anode, Zn) and which gets larger (cathode, Cu). They draw and label a complete diagram of their cell.

explain.description: Mini-lesson addressing patterns from practice; introduce additional complexity. Continuing: Teacher formalizes voltaic cell anatomy: (1) Anode — oxidation occurs, more active metal, negative terminal, gets smaller. (2) Cathode — reduction occurs, less active metal, positive terminal, gets larger. (3) Salt bridge — allows ion flow to maintain electrical neutrality. (4) External wire — electrons flow from anode to cathode (from Zn to Cu). Students write the half-reactions and label all components on their diagram.

elaborate.description: Partner work on application problems with real-world contexts. Continuing: Application: Students examine the chemistry of common batteries. For a lithium-ion battery (used in phones), they identify the half-reactions from the sample cluster (Li -> Li+ + e- at the anode; CoO2 + Li+ + e- -> LiCoO2 at the cathode). They compare voltaic cells (spontaneous, produce electricity) to the concept of electrolytic cells (non-spontaneous, use electricity — to be covered next lesson).

evaluate.description: Formative assessment — students solve 2-3 problems independently and self-check. Continuing: Exit ticket: A voltaic cell uses Mg and Ag electrodes. (1) Which metal is the anode? Use the activity series. (2) Write the oxidation and reduction half-reactions. (3) Draw an arrow showing the direction of electron flow through the external wire. (4) What is the purpose of the salt bridge?

differentiation.approaching: Provide completed examples from Day 1 as reference. Provide a pre-labeled voltaic cell diagram with blanks only for the half-reaction equations and direction of electron flow; include a 'Voltaic Cell Checklist' matching each component to its function.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the voltaic cell construction, diagram, and analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the cell potential (voltage) using standard reduction potentials from a reference table; compare predicted voltage to measured voltage and explain sources of discrepancy.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual voltaic cell diagram with all components labeled in English and native language; use arrows and color-coding (red for oxidation at anode, blue for reduction at cathode) consistently.
differentiation.iep: Partner for cell construction; provide pre-drawn cell diagram to label rather than drawing from scratch; reduce exit ticket to three parts; allow reference table use.

cer.phenomenon: A student builds a voltaic cell using iron and silver electrodes with appropriate salt solutions. The voltmeter reads 1.24 V. When the student removes the salt bridge, the voltage immediately drops to 0 V. The student replaces the salt bridge and the voltage returns.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the salt bridge is essential for the voltaic cell to function because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the voltage data with and without the salt bridge, and explain what happens to charge balance in each half-cell when the bridge is removed.
cer.reasoning_frame: When the cell operates, electrons flow from ___ to ___ through the wire. This causes the anode half-cell to become ___ charged (loss of negative electrons) and the cathode half-cell to become ___ charged (gain of negative electrons). Without the salt bridge, this charge buildup ___ the flow of electrons because___. The salt bridge restores balance by allowing ___ ions to migrate to the ___ half-cell and ___ ions to migrate to the ___ half-cell.

lessons.title: Electrolytic Cells and Applications (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: compare and contrast voltaic and electrolytic cells and explain how electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about something that does not happen on its own but CAN happen if you put energy into it — like pushing a car uphill. What energy source makes it possible?
lessons.do_now: In a voltaic cell, a spontaneous reaction produces electricity. What if we wanted to force a non-spontaneous reaction to happen — like separating water into hydrogen and oxygen? What would we need to provide?
materials: Electrolysis of water demo: Hoffman apparatus or simple setup with 9V battery, two graphite electrodes, water with Na2SO4 electrolyte, test tubes for gas collection
Voltaic vs. electrolytic cell comparison chart (printed)
Electroplating demo materials: copper sulfate solution, copper electrode, metal key, 6V battery

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Electrolytic Cells and Applications. Demo: Connect a 9V battery to two graphite electrodes in water with a small amount of Na2SO4. Students observe bubbles forming at both electrodes. Collect the gas at each electrode and test: hydrogen at the cathode (pops with a burning splint), oxygen at the anode (relights a glowing splint). Ask: We are using electricity to break water apart. Is this a spontaneous reaction? No — we had to force it with the battery.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Electrolytic Cells and Applications. Comparison activity: Students receive diagram templates for both a voltaic cell and an electrolytic cell. They label both diagrams side by side, identifying: energy source (spontaneous reaction vs. external battery), direction of electron flow, anode (still oxidation) and cathode (still reduction), and sign conventions. They complete a Venn diagram highlighting similarities and differences.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Electrolytic Cells and Applications. Teacher formalizes: In an electrolytic cell, an external power source forces a non-spontaneous reaction to occur. The anode is still the site of oxidation and the cathode is still the site of reduction, but the sign convention is reversed (anode is positive, cathode is negative — because the battery forces electrons to the cathode). Key applications: electrolysis of water, electroplating (coating objects with metal), refining metals like aluminum (Hall-Heroult process).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Electrolytic Cells and Applications. Electroplating demo: Teacher electroplates a metal key with copper using CuSO4 solution and a copper electrode connected to a battery. Students observe the key turning copper-colored. They identify the anode (copper electrode, being oxidized to replace Cu2+ in solution) and cathode (the key, where Cu2+ is reduced to solid copper). Students write the half-reactions and explain why the copper electrode gets smaller.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Electrolytic Cells and Applications. Exit ticket: Complete a comparison table for voltaic vs. electrolytic cells (energy conversion, spontaneity, anode sign, cathode sign, example). Then: A company electroplates silver onto jewelry. (1) Should the jewelry be the anode or cathode? (2) What should the other electrode be made of? (3) Write the reduction half-reaction at the cathode.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-filled comparison table with half the cells completed; include a visual side-by-side diagram of both cell types with matching color-coding for anode/cathode.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the comparison activity, Venn diagram, and electroplating analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the mass of copper deposited during electroplating given current, time, and Faraday's constant. Connect electrolysis to industrial aluminum production and calculate the electrical energy cost.
differentiation.ell: Bilingual comparison chart with visual cell diagrams; sentence frames for describing differences: 'In a voltaic cell, the anode is ___, but in an electrolytic cell, the anode is ___ because___.'
differentiation.iep: Provide completed Venn diagram with one additional comparison for student to add; reduce exit ticket to comparison table only; allow partner work.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the Hall-Heroult process for producing aluminum by electrolysis, developed independently by Charles Martin Hall (American) and Paul Heroult (French) in 1886. Before this process, aluminum was more expensive than gold. Highlight that Hall, an African American inventor, faced racial discrimination but persisted and revolutionized the aluminum industry. Also discuss the environmental impact of aluminum smelting, which requires enormous amounts of electricity — often generated by hydroelectric dams that displace indigenous communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'electrolysis': Water does not spontaneously decompose into hydrogen and oxygen because___. Both voltaic and electrolytic cells involve redox reactions, but they differ in energy conversion because___. The battery forces electrons to flow in the non-spontaneous direction, so___.

vocabulary.definition: An electrochemical cell that uses electrical energy from an external source to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction
The process of depositing a thin layer of metal onto an object by making it the cathode in an electrolytic cell
A battery or power supply that provides the electrical energy needed to drive electrolysis

cer.phenomenon: A rechargeable lithium-ion battery in a smartphone operates as a voltaic cell when powering the phone (discharging) and as an electrolytic cell when plugged into a charger (charging). A student asks: 'How can the same battery be both types of cell?'
cer.claim_starter: I claim that a rechargeable battery functions as both a voltaic cell and an electrolytic cell because___.
cer.evidence_source: Compare the direction of electron flow and the energy conversion during discharging vs. charging, identifying which is spontaneous and which requires external energy.
cer.reasoning_frame: When the battery is discharging, the redox reaction is ___ and chemical energy is converted to___. The anode is ___ and the cathode is___. When plugged into a charger, an external power source forces electrons in the ___ direction, reversing the reaction. This is now an ___ cell because___. The products of the discharge reaction become the ___ for the charging reaction.

lessons.title: Redox and Electrochemistry Review (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: integrate oxidation numbers, half-reactions, activity series predictions, and electrochemical cell analysis to solve multi-step redox problems
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could prevent one metal object in your life from corroding or rusting, what would it be and why?
lessons.do_now: A voltaic cell is built using Mg and Cu electrodes. Without looking at your notes: (1) Which is the anode? (2) Which direction do electrons flow? (3) Write the two half-reactions. (4) What voltage would you expect — higher or lower than a Zn/Cu cell?
materials: Redox scenario cards (set of 10 for group activity)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Redox and Electrochemistry Review. Corrosion challenge: Show images of corroded objects — a rusted bridge, a tarnished silver trophy, a green copper dome, a corroded car battery terminal. For each, students identify: What was oxidized? What was the oxidizing agent? How could the corrosion be prevented? (galvanizing, painting, sacrificial anode, electroplating).

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Redox and Electrochemistry Review. Scenario card activity: Groups receive redox scenario cards requiring integration of multiple concepts. Example: 'Design a voltaic cell that could protect an iron pipe from rusting. Choose an appropriate sacrificial anode using the activity series. Draw the cell, write half-reactions, and explain how cathodic protection works.' Groups present their solutions.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Redox and Electrochemistry Review. Class synthesis: Build a comprehensive concept map connecting oxidation numbers, half-reactions, activity series, voltaic cells, electrolytic cells, and real-world applications. Teacher addresses common misconceptions: (1) Oxidation does not always involve oxygen. (2) The anode is not always negative — it depends on the cell type. (3) Electrons flow through the wire, but ions flow through the solution.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Redox and Electrochemistry Review. Multi-step practice: Three cumulative problems covering the full range of unit content. Example: Given a reaction, assign oxidation numbers, write half-reactions, predict spontaneity using the activity series, and design an electrochemical cell to carry out the reaction.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Redox and Electrochemistry Review. Unit 9 formative assessment: Five questions covering oxidation number assignment, half-reaction writing, activity series prediction, voltaic cell diagram interpretation, and voltaic vs. electrolytic cell comparison.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a unit summary reference sheet with key definitions, rules, and labeled cell diagrams; include a step-by-step problem-solving template for redox analysis.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the scenario card activity and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on one advanced application of electrochemistry: fuel cells (hydrogen fuel cell vehicles), corrosion engineering, or electrochemical sensors in medicine.
differentiation.ell: Bilingual unit summary sheet; visual concept map with labeled diagrams; allow oral presentation of scenario card solutions with written half-reactions.
differentiation.iep: Reduce formative assessment to three questions; provide all reference materials during assessment; partner support during scenario activity; extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss corrosion prevention as a global engineering challenge. Highlight the contributions of Elijah McCoy, an African American inventor whose lubrication innovations prevented oxidation-related damage in steam engines (the phrase 'the real McCoy' is attributed to the quality of his inventions). Connect to modern corrosion engineering — the Statue of Liberty restoration in the 1980s required understanding of galvanic corrosion between its copper skin and iron framework.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion: Start with 'Electrons transfer.' Students expand: 'In every redox reaction, electrons transfer from the reducing agent, which undergoes oxidation and loses electrons, to the oxidizing agent, which undergoes reduction and gains electrons, and this transfer of electrons can be harnessed in an electrochemical cell to produce electrical energy or can be forced by an external power source in electrolysis.'

vocabulary.definition: Corrosion that occurs when two different metals are in electrical contact in the presence of an electrolyte; the more active metal corrodes preferentially
A corrosion prevention technique where a more active metal is used as a sacrificial anode to protect a less active metal

cer.phenomenon: An underground steel pipeline carries natural gas. To prevent rusting, engineers attach zinc blocks to the outside of the pipe at regular intervals. Over time, the zinc blocks dissolve away but the steel pipe remains intact. The company must replace the zinc blocks every few years.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the zinc blocks protect the steel pipe through cathodic protection because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the activity series to explain why zinc corrodes instead of iron, write the relevant half-reactions, and explain the electron flow.
cer.reasoning_frame: Zinc is ___ active than iron on the activity series, meaning it has a greater tendency to___. When connected, zinc acts as the ___ (site of oxidation), donating electrons to the iron pipe. The iron becomes the ___ (site of reduction), receiving electrons. As long as zinc is present, the iron ___ because___. This is called ___ protection.

units.title: Waves, EM Radiation & Nuclear Chemistry
units.anchoring_phenomenon: Hospitals use X-rays to see bones, UV light to sterilize equipment, and radioactive isotopes to treat cancer. All of these involve electromagnetic radiation or nuclear reactions, yet some are harmless and others can be deadly. What determines whether radiation is safe or dangerous?
essential_questions: How are wavelength, frequency, and energy related in electromagnetic radiation?
How do different frequencies of electromagnetic radiation interact with matter in different ways?
What happens to the nucleus during radioactive decay, fission, and fusion, and how are these processes different from chemical reactions?
units.crse_theme: Students explore the intersection of nuclear chemistry and society — from Marie Curie's pioneering research on radioactivity (facing gender discrimination) to the devastating effects of nuclear testing on Pacific Islander and Indigenous communities (Marshall Islands, Nevada Test Site). lessons.title: Wave-Matter Interactions and Photon Absorption (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: explain how different frequencies of electromagnetic radiation interact with matter through absorption, transmission, and reflection, and evaluate claims about the effects of EM radiation
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever gotten a sunburn? What was happening to your skin at the atomic level that made it red and painful?
lessons.do_now: A greenhouse stays warm because glass transmits visible light but absorbs infrared radiation. How does this relate to climate change and the greenhouse effect?
materials: Various materials for testing: glass, plastic wrap, sunscreen, fabric, sunglasses
UV flashlight or access to sunlight
Published claims about EM radiation (3 articles, printed excerpts)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Wave-Matter Interactions and Photon Absorption. UV bead activity: Give each student a few UV-sensitive beads. Indoors, they are white. Take them near a window or use a UV flashlight — they change color instantly. Ask: What type of radiation caused this change? Then test: Does the color change happen through glass? Through sunscreen? Through fabric? Students record which materials block UV and which transmit it.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Wave-Matter Interactions and Photon Absorption. Testing materials: Groups systematically test which materials transmit, absorb, or reflect UV radiation using the beads as detectors. They test: clear glass, sunglasses, plastic wrap, aluminum foil, sunscreen (SPF 15 vs. SPF 50), different colors of fabric, and water. They organize results in a data table. They also read two short published claims about EM radiation effects (e.g., 'Cell phones cause cancer' and 'UV water purification is safe for drinking').

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Wave-Matter Interactions and Photon Absorption. Teacher explains three wave-matter interactions: (1) Absorption — material absorbs the radiation's energy (UV absorbed by sunscreen, infrared absorbed by greenhouse gases). (2) Transmission — radiation passes through (visible light through glass). (3) Reflection — radiation bounces off (visible light off a mirror, radio waves off the ionosphere). The interaction depends on the frequency of the radiation and the molecular structure of the material.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Wave-Matter Interactions and Photon Absorption. Claim evaluation: Students evaluate the two published claims from the Explore phase using scientific evidence. They assess: Is the claim supported by evidence about EM radiation frequency, energy, and interaction with matter? They write a paragraph evaluating each claim's validity, citing specific evidence about photon energy and molecular interactions.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Wave-Matter Interactions and Photon Absorption. Exit ticket: (1) Explain why greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation but not visible light (hint: molecular vibration frequencies). (2) A company claims their product 'blocks all harmful radiation.' Evaluate this claim — what types of radiation are harmful, and what would the product need to do? (3) Why does higher SPF sunscreen provide more UV protection?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a graphic organizer with three columns: Absorption, Transmission, Reflection — students sort examples into columns; include sentence frames for claim evaluation.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the UV bead investigation and claim evaluation as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research how spectroscopy uses absorption patterns to identify unknown substances and explain how astronomers determine the composition of distant stars using absorption spectra.
differentiation.ell: Provide visual diagrams of absorption, transmission, and reflection with bilingual labels; simplified article excerpts with key vocabulary highlighted; sentence frames for evaluation paragraphs.
differentiation.iep: Reduce claim evaluation to one article instead of two; provide a claim evaluation scaffold with guiding questions; partner for UV bead investigation; extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the greenhouse effect and climate change as a global environmental justice issue — rising sea levels disproportionately threaten Pacific Island nations and coastal communities in the Global South, while industrial nations produce the most greenhouse gas emissions. Also discuss how UV water purification technology (SODIS — Solar Water Disinfection) has been deployed in developing countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America to provide safe drinking water using only sunlight and plastic bottles — an application of understanding how UV radiation interacts with biological matter.

cer.claim_starter: I claim that this product's claim is ___ (valid/not scientifically supported) because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use knowledge of EM radiation types, photon energy at cell phone frequencies, and the difference between ionizing and non-ionizing radiation to evaluate the claim.

lessons.title: Nuclear Reactions: Fission, Fusion, and Radioactive Decay (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: write balanced nuclear equations for alpha decay, beta decay, and positron emission, and compare fission, fusion, and radioactive decay in terms of changes to the nucleus and energy released
lessons.circle_prompt: The Sun has been shining for about 4.6 billion years. Where does all that energy come from? It is not burning like a campfire — so what is different?
lessons.do_now: In a chemical reaction like 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, the atoms rearrange but no atoms are created or destroyed. In a nuclear reaction, one element can change into a completely different element. How is this possible?
materials: Nuclear decay simulation cards (alpha, beta, positron — 1 set per group)
Nuclear fission and fusion diagram handout (printed)
Pennies for half-life simulation (30 per student)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Nuclear Reactions: Fission, Fusion, and Radioactive Decay. Show a dramatic video comparing a chemical explosion (TNT) with a nuclear explosion (atomic bomb test footage, historically contextualized). The nuclear explosion releases millions of times more energy from the same mass of material. Ask: Chemical reactions rearrange electrons. What is different about the nuclear reaction that produces so much more energy? The answer: nuclear reactions change the nucleus itself, converting tiny amounts of mass into enormous amounts of energy.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Nuclear Reactions: Fission, Fusion, and Radioactive Decay. Card-based nuclear decay modeling: Students use cards representing protons, neutrons, and nuclear particles to model three types of decay. (1) Alpha decay: remove a card with 2 protons + 2 neutrons (He-4 nucleus) from a uranium-238 nucleus and determine the daughter isotope. (2) Beta decay: convert a neutron card to a proton card plus an electron, modeling C-14 decay. (3) Positron emission: convert a proton to a neutron plus a positron. For each, students write the nuclear equation and verify that mass numbers and atomic numbers balance.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Nuclear Reactions: Fission, Fusion, and Radioactive Decay. Teacher formalizes: In nuclear reactions, the nucleus changes composition. Alpha decay: nucleus emits He-4, atomic number decreases by 2, mass number by 4. Beta decay: neutron becomes proton + electron, atomic number increases by 1, mass number unchanged. Fission: heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei plus neutrons and energy (used in nuclear power plants). Fusion: light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus plus energy (powers the Sun). All nuclear reactions obey conservation of mass number and atomic number. E = mc^2 explains the enormous energy: tiny mass loss converts to huge energy.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Nuclear Reactions: Fission, Fusion, and Radioactive Decay. Half-life simulation: Each student starts with 30 pennies (representing radioactive atoms). They shake and flip all pennies, remove those showing tails (decayed), record the number remaining, and repeat for 6 rounds. They graph the number of remaining atoms vs. number of half-lives and observe the exponential decay curve. Teacher connects to real-world half-lives: C-14 (5,730 years, used in carbon dating), I-131 (8 days, used in thyroid treatment), U-238 (4.5 billion years, used in geological dating).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Nuclear Reactions: Fission, Fusion, and Radioactive Decay. Exit ticket: (1) Write the balanced nuclear equation for the alpha decay of Ra-226. (2) Write the balanced nuclear equation for the beta decay of Co-60. (3) Compare fission and fusion: Which splits atoms? Which combines them? Which powers the Sun? Which powers nuclear reactors?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a nuclear equation balancing template: '___ -> ___ + ___. Check: mass numbers add up? Atomic numbers add up?' Include a reference card showing the particles (alpha = He-4, beta = electron, positron, neutron) with their mass and atomic numbers.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the card modeling, half-life simulation, and nuclear equation practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the energy released in a specific nuclear reaction using E = mc^2 and the mass defect between reactants and products. Compare to energy released in a chemical reaction.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual nuclear particle reference card with symbols and visual representations; color-coded nuclear equations (protons in red, neutrons in blue, emitted particles in green); sentence frames for comparing fission and fusion.
differentiation.iep: Pre-formatted nuclear equation templates with blanks for missing values; reduce balancing problems from five to three; partner for half-life simulation; allow reference cards during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Marie Curie's groundbreaking research on radioactivity — she was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics and Chemistry). Despite her genius, she faced significant gender discrimination. Also discuss the devastating impacts of nuclear testing on indigenous and Pacific Islander communities: the Marshall Islands (Castle Bravo test, 1954), the Navajo Nation (uranium mining leaving contaminated land and elevated cancer rates), and the environmental justice movement demanding cleanup and reparations.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'nuclear decay': Uranium-238 undergoes alpha decay because___. Both fission and fusion release enormous amounts of energy, but they are opposite processes because___. lessons.title: Nuclear Reactions: Fission, Fusion, and Radioactive Decay (Day 2 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply and compare concepts and write balanced nuclear equations for alpha decay, beta decay, and positron emission, and compare fission, fusion, and radioactive decay in terms of changes to the nucleus and energy released
lessons.circle_prompt: Share one connection you made between yesterday's topic and something in your daily life.
lessons.do_now: Recall from yesterday: explain one key idea from yesterday about how to define and describe key concepts related to: write balanced nuclear equations for alpha decay, beta decay, and positron emission, and compare fission, fusion, and radioactive decay in terms of changes to the nucleus and energy released.
materials: Nuclear decay simulation cards (alpha, beta, positron — 1 set per group)
Nuclear fission and fusion diagram handout (printed)
Pennies for half-life simulation (30 per student)

engage.description: Review warm-up connecting Day 1 vocabulary to a new example or context. Continuing: Show a dramatic video comparing a chemical explosion (TNT) with a nuclear explosion (atomic bomb test footage, historically contextualized). The nuclear explosion releases millions of times more energy from the same mass of material. Ask: Chemical reactions rearrange electrons. What is different about the nuclear reaction that produces so much more energy? The answer: nuclear reactions change the nucleus itself, converting tiny amounts of mass into enormous amounts of energy.

explore.description: Structured practice — students work through increasingly complex problems with scaffolds. Continuing: Card-based nuclear decay modeling: Students use cards representing protons, neutrons, and nuclear particles to model three types of decay. (1) Alpha decay: remove a card with 2 protons + 2 neutrons (He-4 nucleus) from a uranium-238 nucleus and determine the daughter isotope. (2) Beta decay: convert a neutron card to a proton card plus an electron, modeling C-14 decay. (3) Positron emission: convert a proton to a neutron plus a positron. For each, students write the nuclear equation and verify that mass numbers and atomic numbers balance.

explain.description: Mini-lesson addressing patterns from practice; introduce additional complexity. Continuing: Teacher formalizes: In nuclear reactions, the nucleus changes composition. Alpha decay: nucleus emits He-4, atomic number decreases by 2, mass number by 4. Beta decay: neutron becomes proton + electron, atomic number increases by 1, mass number unchanged. Fission: heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei plus neutrons and energy (used in nuclear power plants). Fusion: light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus plus energy (powers the Sun). All nuclear reactions obey conservation of mass number and atomic number. E = mc^2 explains the enormous energy: tiny mass loss converts to huge energy.

elaborate.description: Partner work on application problems with real-world contexts. Continuing: Half-life simulation: Each student starts with 30 pennies (representing radioactive atoms). They shake and flip all pennies, remove those showing tails (decayed), record the number remaining, and repeat for 6 rounds. They graph the number of remaining atoms vs. number of half-lives and observe the exponential decay curve. Teacher connects to real-world half-lives: C-14 (5,730 years, used in carbon dating), I-131 (8 days, used in thyroid treatment), U-238 (4.5 billion years, used in geological dating).

evaluate.description: Formative assessment — students solve 2-3 problems independently and self-check. Continuing: Exit ticket: (1) Write the balanced nuclear equation for the alpha decay of Ra-226. (2) Write the balanced nuclear equation for the beta decay of Co-60. (3) Compare fission and fusion: Which splits atoms? Which combines them? Which powers the Sun? Which powers nuclear reactors?

differentiation.approaching: Provide completed examples from Day 1 as reference. Provide a nuclear equation balancing template: '___ -> ___ + ___. Check: mass numbers add up? Atomic numbers add up?' Include a reference card showing the particles (alpha = He-4, beta = electron, positron, neutron) with their mass and atomic numbers.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the card modeling, half-life simulation, and nuclear equation practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the energy released in a specific nuclear reaction using E = mc^2 and the mass defect between reactants and products. Compare to energy released in a chemical reaction.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual nuclear particle reference card with symbols and visual representations; color-coded nuclear equations (protons in red, neutrons in blue, emitted particles in green); sentence frames for comparing fission and fusion.
differentiation.iep: Pre-formatted nuclear equation templates with blanks for missing values; reduce balancing problems from five to three; partner for half-life simulation; allow reference cards during exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Marie Curie's groundbreaking research on radioactivity — she was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics and Chemistry). Despite her genius, she faced significant gender discrimination. Also discuss the devastating impacts of nuclear testing on indigenous and Pacific Islander communities: the Marshall Islands (Castle Bravo test, 1954), the Navajo Nation (uranium mining leaving contaminated land and elevated cancer rates), and the environmental justice movement demanding cleanup and reparations.

cer.phenomenon: The Sun fuses approximately 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium every second. Yet the Sun has been shining for 4.6 billion years and still has enough hydrogen to last billions more. In contrast, a coal-fired power plant burns through millions of tons of coal per year to produce far less energy.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that nuclear fusion produces vastly more energy per unit mass than chemical combustion because___.
cer.evidence_source: Compare the energy source in nuclear fusion (mass-energy conversion via E=mc^2) with the energy source in combustion (bond energy changes), and use the given data about the Sun's fuel consumption.
cer.reasoning_frame: In chemical combustion, energy comes from ___, which involves rearranging___. In nuclear fusion, energy comes from ___, which involves converting a small amount of ___ into energy according to E=mc^2. Because c^2 = ___, even a tiny mass loss produces ___ energy. This explains why the Sun, despite consuming ___ tons of hydrogen per second, can sustain fusion for billions of years.

lessons.title: Nuclear Applications and Waves Review (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: evaluate the benefits and risks of nuclear technology applications and demonstrate mastery of wave properties, EM radiation, and nuclear chemistry concepts
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could use nuclear technology to solve one problem in the world — energy, medicine, food safety, or something else — what would you choose and why?
lessons.do_now: A patient receives a dose of radioactive iodine-131 (half-life = 8 days) for thyroid cancer treatment. After 24 days, what fraction of the original dose remains in the patient's body? Show your work.
materials: Nuclear applications reading set (4 short articles: nuclear medicine, nuclear power, food irradiation, carbon dating)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Nuclear Applications and Waves Review. Four corners activity: Post four signs around the room: Nuclear Power, Nuclear Medicine, Food Irradiation, Nuclear Weapons. Students move to the topic they think is most important for society to understand. Each group shares one reason for their choice. Teacher frames the discussion: nuclear technology has tremendous benefits and serious risks — understanding the science helps us make informed decisions.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Nuclear Applications and Waves Review. Jigsaw reading: Each group reads one short article about a nuclear application. Group A: Nuclear medicine (PET scans, radiation therapy using targeted isotopes). Group B: Nuclear power (fission reactors, waste storage challenges). Group C: Food irradiation (using gamma rays to kill bacteria, extending shelf life). Group D: Carbon dating (using C-14 half-life to determine age of artifacts). Each group completes a benefits-risks T-chart for their application.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Nuclear Applications and Waves Review. Groups present their application to the class. Teacher synthesizes: all nuclear applications involve the same fundamental science (radioactive decay, radiation interactions with matter) but applied in different contexts. Key distinction: the dose and type of radiation determine whether it is helpful or harmful. Students take notes from peer presentations and complete T-charts for all four applications.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Nuclear Applications and Waves Review. Cumulative review: Students work through multi-step problems integrating wave properties, EM radiation, and nuclear chemistry. Example: Calculate the energy of a gamma ray photon emitted during Co-60 decay, compare to X-ray photon energy, and explain why both are used in medical applications but require different safety precautions.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Nuclear Applications and Waves Review. Unit 10 formative assessment: Six questions covering wave calculations (c = wavelength x frequency, E = hf), EM spectrum identification, wave-matter interactions, nuclear equation balancing, half-life calculations, and fission vs. fusion comparison.

differentiation.approaching: Provide pre-organized T-chart templates with one benefit and one risk already filled in for each application; include a unit formula reference sheet for all calculations.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the jigsaw reading, presentations, and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Write a persuasive essay arguing for or against expanding nuclear power in the United States, using scientific evidence about fission, waste storage, safety, and comparison to fossil fuels and renewable energy.
differentiation.ell: Provide simplified reading excerpts with key vocabulary defined in margins; bilingual T-chart template; visual formula cards for all calculations; allow oral presentation.
differentiation.iep: Reduce formative assessment to four questions; provide all formula references; partner support during jigsaw reading; extended time; allow T-chart completion from peer presentations rather than reading.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the environmental justice dimensions of nuclear power and waste. The Yucca Mountain nuclear waste repository proposal disproportionately affected the Western Shoshone Nation. Uranium mining on Navajo Nation lands left contaminated water sources and elevated cancer rates that persist today. Contrast with the potential of nuclear power to reduce carbon emissions and combat climate change — highlighting the complexity of this issue. Also discuss Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese American physicist whose experimental work on beta decay disproved the law of conservation of parity, yet her male colleagues received the Nobel Prize for the theoretical prediction.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion: Start with 'Radiation interacts with matter.' Students expand: 'Electromagnetic radiation interacts with matter through absorption, transmission, and reflection, and the specific interaction depends on the frequency of the radiation and the molecular structure of the material, which is why high-frequency ionizing radiation like gamma rays can damage DNA while low-frequency radio waves pass harmlessly through the body.'

vocabulary.definition: The use of radioactive isotopes for diagnosis (imaging) and treatment (radiation therapy) of diseases
The process of exposing food to ionizing radiation (usually gamma rays) to kill bacteria, extend shelf life, and reduce spoilage
Materials that remain radioactive after use in nuclear power or medicine, requiring safe long-term storage

cer.phenomenon: A community near a proposed nuclear power plant is divided. Supporters argue it will provide clean energy with no carbon emissions. Opponents argue the risk of meltdown and the problem of radioactive waste make it too dangerous. Both sides present data and emotional arguments.
cer.claim_starter: I claim that the decision about building the nuclear plant should consider both ___ and ___ because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use scientific evidence about fission reactions, energy output, waste products, safety records, and comparison to fossil fuel emissions to evaluate both perspectives.
cer.reasoning_frame: Nuclear fission produces energy by ___, and the amount of energy per kilogram of fuel is ___ compared to fossil fuels. The main benefit is ___ because___. However, the main risks include ___ because___. A scientifically informed decision would weigh ___ against ___ and also consider___.

units.title: Engineering Design & Review
units.anchoring_phenomenon: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch contains an estimated 80,000 tons of plastic debris. Engineers and chemists are developing solutions — from biodegradable plastics to ocean cleanup devices to chemical recycling methods. How can chemistry knowledge be applied through the engineering design process to address real-world problems like plastic pollution?
essential_questions: How do engineers use the design process to develop solutions to complex real-world problems?
How does chemistry knowledge help us evaluate the trade-offs and constraints of proposed solutions?
How can we apply our understanding of all chemistry concepts to solve problems and prepare for the Regents examination?
units.crse_theme: Students apply chemistry to real-world problems that affect diverse communities — from clean water access in developing nations to green chemistry alternatives to hazardous industrial processes. Students examine how engineering solutions must account for social, cultural, and environmental impacts, especially on marginalized communities.
investigations: Investigation 11: Engineering Design Challenge — Solving a Chemistry-Based Problem

lessons.title: The Engineering Design Process (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: apply the engineering design process to define a problem, identify criteria and constraints, and propose a chemistry-based solution that accounts for trade-offs
lessons.circle_prompt: Think of a problem in your community or school that you wish someone would solve. What would the ideal solution look like, and what limitations might make it hard to achieve?
lessons.do_now: A city's water supply contains lead from old pipes. List three possible solutions, and for each, identify one advantage and one limitation (cost, time, effectiveness, environmental impact).

dci: ETS1.A: Defining and Delimiting Engineering Problems

materials: Case study packets: 3 chemistry-based engineering challenges (printed)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: The Engineering Design Process. Show a short video about The Ocean Cleanup project — a real engineering effort to remove plastic from the Pacific Ocean. Ask: This seems like a simple idea (scoop up plastic), but why has it taken years of design, testing, and revision? What makes real-world engineering problems so complex? Introduce the engineering design process: Define the problem, research, brainstorm solutions, evaluate trade-offs, prototype, test, and refine.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: The Engineering Design Process. Case study analysis: Groups each receive a different chemistry-based engineering challenge: (A) Designing a water filtration system for a community with arsenic-contaminated groundwater, (B) Developing a biodegradable alternative to plastic packaging, (C) Creating a low-cost battery for off-grid communities. For their challenge, groups define the problem, identify criteria (what the solution must achieve) and constraints (budget, materials, time, safety, environmental impact), and brainstorm at least three possible solutions.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: The Engineering Design Process. Teacher formalizes the engineering design process steps and key vocabulary. Criteria = what the solution must do (effectiveness, safety, durability). Constraints = limitations on the solution (cost, available materials, time, environmental regulations). Trade-offs = accepting less of one desirable quality to gain more of another. Students learn to use a trade-off analysis matrix to systematically compare solutions against multiple criteria.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: The Engineering Design Process. Groups complete a trade-off analysis matrix for their three proposed solutions, rating each solution on a 1-5 scale for effectiveness, cost, feasibility, safety, and environmental impact. They select the best solution and prepare a 2-minute pitch explaining their choice with evidence.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: The Engineering Design Process. Gallery walk presentations: Each group presents their problem, proposed solution, and trade-off analysis. Peers provide feedback using a structured rubric: Is the problem clearly defined? Are criteria and constraints realistic? Is the trade-off analysis thorough? Is the chemistry connection clear?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a partially completed problem definition template with guiding questions: 'What is the problem? Who is affected? What science is involved?' Include a sample trade-off matrix with one row completed.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the case study analysis and trade-off matrix as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the actual engineering solutions being developed for their case study problem and compare their group's proposed solution to real-world approaches, identifying what professionals considered that students may have overlooked.
differentiation.ell: Provide bilingual engineering design vocabulary cards; visual flowchart of the design process; sentence frames for the presentation: 'Our problem is___. The best solution is ___ because it scores highest on___ while still meeting the constraint of___.'
differentiation.iep: Assign a specific role in the group (problem definer, criteria lister, or matrix filler); provide simplified case study with reduced reading level; allow visual presentation instead of verbal.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how engineering design must consider equity and access. The Flint, Michigan water crisis demonstrated how engineering failures disproportionately affect communities of color and low-income residents. Highlight the work of Marc Edwards, a Virginia Tech engineer who exposed the lead contamination by applying chemistry knowledge (lead solubility and corrosion chemistry), and LeeAnne Walters, a Flint resident and mother who became a citizen scientist. Connect to green chemistry principles developed by Paul Anastas and John Warner — designing chemical processes that prevent pollution rather than cleaning it up afterward.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'engineering design': The engineering design process requires defining criteria and constraints because___. The biodegradable plastic solution scored high on environmental impact, but it scored low on cost, so the team had to consider___. A solution may be scientifically effective, but if it is too expensive for the community, so___.

vocabulary.definition: A systematic approach to solving problems that includes defining the problem, researching, brainstorming solutions, evaluating trade-offs, prototyping, testing, and refining
A compromise in which gaining one quality requires accepting less of another

materials: Case study packets: 3 chemistry-based engineering challenges (printed)

engage.description: Present a novel scenario that requires synthesis of concepts from Days 1-2. Building on previous days: Show a short video about The Ocean Cleanup project — a real engineering effort to remove plastic from the Pacific Ocean. Ask: This seems like a simple idea (scoop up plastic), but why has it taken years of design, testing, and revision? What makes real-world engineering problems so complex? Introduce the engineering design process: Define the problem, research, brainstorm solutions, evaluate trade-offs, prototype, test, and refine.

explore.description: CER activity — students construct evidence-based arguments about the topic. Building on previous days: Case study analysis: Groups each receive a different chemistry-based engineering challenge: (A) Designing a water filtration system for a community with arsenic-contaminated groundwater, (B) Developing a biodegradable alternative to plastic packaging, (C) Creating a low-cost battery for off-grid communities. For their challenge, groups define the problem, identify criteria (what the solution must achieve) and constraints (budget, materials, time, safety, environmental impact), and brainstorm at least three possible solutions.

explain.description: Whole-class discussion of CER responses; address remaining misconceptions. Building on previous days: Teacher formalizes the engineering design process steps and key vocabulary. Criteria = what the solution must do (effectiveness, safety, durability). Constraints = limitations on the solution (cost, available materials, time, environmental regulations). Trade-offs = accepting less of one desirable quality to gain more of another. Students learn to use a trade-off analysis matrix to systematically compare solutions against multiple criteria.

elaborate.description: Extension or enrichment activity connecting to real-world applications. Building on previous days: Groups complete a trade-off analysis matrix for their three proposed solutions, rating each solution on a 1-5 scale for effectiveness, cost, feasibility, safety, and environmental impact. They select the best solution and prepare a 2-minute pitch explaining their choice with evidence.

evaluate.description: Summative check — quiz or performance task covering all concepts from the sequence. Building on previous days: Gallery walk presentations: Each group presents their problem, proposed solution, and trade-off analysis. Peers provide feedback using a structured rubric: Is the problem clearly defined? Are criteria and constraints realistic? Is the trade-off analysis thorough? Is the chemistry connection clear?

cer.phenomenon: A coastal city needs to build a new desalination plant to convert seawater to drinking water. Three designs are proposed: (A) Reverse osmosis (effective but uses a lot of electricity), (B) Solar-powered distillation (low energy cost but slow output), (C) Electrodialysis (moderate energy, moderate output, but expensive membranes). cer.claim_starter: I claim that Design ___ is the best option for this city because___.
cer.evidence_source: Use the criteria (water output, energy efficiency, cost) and constraints (limited budget, growing population) to evaluate each design using a trade-off analysis.
cer.reasoning_frame: Design A excels at ___ but fails at ___ because___. Design B is strong at ___ but limited by ___ because___.
